comments.content: `malloc()` result is never checked for NULL. If allocation fails, the subsequent `pread(m, buf + carry, ...)` dereferences a NULL pointer (plus `carry` offset), causing a crash. Add a NULL check and clean up `f`/`m` before returning.
comments.suggestion_code:
unsigned char *buf = malloc(CHUNK + 64);
    if (!buf) { perror("malloc"); fclose(f); close(m); return 1; }
comments.existing_code: unsigned char *buf = malloc(CHUNK + 64);

comments.content: Potential out-of-bounds write into `buf`. The read destination is `buf + carry` with `want = CHUNK`, so up to `carry + CHUNK` bytes can be written, but the buffer is only `CHUNK + 64` bytes. This is currently safe only because `carry <= PATLEN (44) < 64`; the margin is implicit and fragile. Either size the buffer as `CHUNK + PATLEN` (or larger) explicitly, or limit `want` to `CHUNK - carry`. Also guard `buf` being NULL before this call.
comments.existing_code: ssize_t r = pread(m, buf + carry, want, (off_t)(s + off));

comments.content: `ctx` is read at `abs - 32` without verifying that `abs >= 32` (relative to the mapped range start or at least a valid file offset). If the match lies in the first 32 bytes of a mapping (e.g. a mapping starting near address 0 or a match in the first chunk), `abs - 32` underflows for unsigned values / becomes a negative file offset and `pread` reads unintended memory or fails. Clamp the context start: compute the maximum safe back-off, e.g. read from `abs - back` where `back = min(32, abs - s)` (or `abs` if `abs < 32`).

Offset arithmetic `s + off - carry + i` is fragile: `off` is advanced by `r` (the number of bytes read into the buffer excluding the carried tail), so the buffer at index 0 corresponds to address `s + off - carry`. This only holds when `carry` is exactly the number of bytes that survived from the previous chunk. A clearer/safer formulation is to track the absolute start address of the buffer (`buf_base = s + off - carry`) explicitly before the scan loop, so the math is auditable and immune to unsigned underflow if `off < carry` on the first iteration (carry starts at 0, so currently OK, but a single bookkeeping change would silently corrupt reported addresses).
comments.existing_code: unsigned long long abs = s + off - carry + i;

comments.content: `r <= 0` breaks out of the whole mapping on the first partial/error read, silently skipping the remainder of the range and potentially missing matches. `pread` may legitimately return fewer bytes than requested (short read) and may return -1 with `errno == EINTR` or `EIO` for unmapped/invalid pages inside a mapping. Handle `EINTR` by retrying, and on other errors consider advancing `off` instead of abandoning the rest of the range (or at least log the failure) so later regions are still scanned.
comments.existing_code:
ssize_t r = pread(m, buf + carry, want, (off_t)(s + off));
            if (r <= 0) break;

comments.content: Resource leak on exit paths: `f` (FILE*) and `m` (fd) are not reliably cleaned up, and `buf` is freed only on the normal path. In particular, if `open(mempath, O_RDONLY)` fails, the function returns without `fclose(f)`, leaking the FILE* handle. Add cleanup (`fclose(f)`, `close(m)`, `free(buf)`) on the early-return error path as well as before the final return.

`errors`/include note: `errno` is used implicitly nowhere here, but if `EINTR` handling is added, `#include <errno.h>` is required. Also missing `#include <errno.h>` is not a bug today; noted only for the retry fix. Ignore if not adopting `errno` handling.

comments.content: Error handling is inconsistent across accessors: `RequiredArray`/`ParseLevel`/`OptionalPreview` throw on wrong types, while `OptionalInt64`/`OptionalBool`/`OptionalString` silently coerce type mismatches to null/false. A misspelled or wrongly typed numeric field (e.g. `"level": "5"`) silently degrades to unrated instead of producing a diagnostic. Since this is described as a permissive legacy format, consider at least logging/reporting type mismatches rather than silently dropping them.

Identity logic is duplicated verbatim in both records, so any future change to identity semantics (e.g. also comparing Difficulty to disambiguate custom-difficulty charts sharing a ChartId, or switching comparer) can silently desync the preload key from the selection-match key. Extract a single shared helper / static MatchesIdentity(ChartPack?, ChartDiff?, ChartPack, ChartDiff) used by both records (and ideally by GameSession's `(pack.Id, diff.ChartId)` preload key).

Records compare by value, but their members here are reference types with reference equality. Two `ChartSelection`s built from distinct-but-equivalent `ChartPack`/`ChartDiff` instances will not be equal, and two selections with different `LoadedChart` instances will never be equal. This makes the record's compiler-generated `Equals`/`GetHashCode` misleading (and any `with`/`==` usage surprising). Either document that equality is reference-based and not meaningful for identity, or override `Equals`/`GetHashCode` to use the same identity logic as `Matches` plus `ReferenceEquals` on the loaded chart.

`Matches` has no null guards: `Pack`/`Diff` are non-nullable constructor params, but the `pack`/`diff` arguments are not validated, so passing a null `pack`/`diff` (or constructing the record with `null!`) throws `NullReferenceException` instead of returning false. Currently the only caller (`GameSession.CachePreload`) passes non-null values, but this is a public API on an immutable cross-scene DTO; make the contract explicit by null-checking arguments (or annotating them nullable and returning false).

In headless/manual-fallback mode the `_player` is never started, so the actual audio stream does not play at all (and is never stopped in `Pause` either). Any consumer relying on real audio (e.g. calibration beat source, natural-end detection) silently gets silence while the clock advances. This also means `_player.Playing` and `_playing` diverge; consider still driving the player (or documenting/enforcing that fallback is only valid when there is no real audio device).

`Pause()` computes the raw position via `GetSongTime() - UserOffsetMs/1000.0`, but `GetSongTime()` returns a *clamped monotonic* value plus the offset. If the monotonic filter held the position (e.g. output-latency compensation made the raw value keep decreasing at song start), the stored `_pausedPosition` is the inflated filtered value rather than the real playback position. Snapshot the raw position directly instead of round-tripping through the filtered/offset public API.

`StartPlayback` clamps the real-audio start to `Math.Max(0.0, fromSec)` while `_pausedPosition`/`_fixedFramePosition`/`_fallbackBaseSec` store the *unclamped* `fromSec`. After `Resume()` at a negative paused position (which the comment explicitly says is legitimate after latency subtraction), the player starts at 0 but `_pausedPosition` still holds the negative value, so the timeline restarts at 0 instead of the intended position — the subsequent monotonic floor (`Reset(_pausedPosition)`) also becomes inconsistent with what the audio is actually doing. Keep the stored start position consistent with the value actually fed to `Play()`.

`Resume()` unconditionally calls `StartPlayback` even when the clock was never paused (`_playing == true`, or `Resume()` called without a preceding `Pause()`). This restarts the stream from `_pausedPosition` (stale/0) and resets the monotonic floor, corrupting an in-progress timeline. Guard with `if (_playing) return;` (and ideally track whether a pause actually happened).

`Attach` overwrites `_manualFallback` based solely on the display server name, discarding any previously forced fallback state. If `Attach` is called after a fallback-enabled setup (or again with a new player), the mode can flip mid-timeline while `_fallbackBaseSec`/`_fallbackStartMsec` and the player's playing state are inconsistent with the new source, producing a position jump. Consider only deriving the mode when no explicit mode has been set, and clearing/reseeding the clocks when the mode changes.

`Time.GetTicksMsec()` is `ulong`; if the millisecond counter wrapped (or if `Play` is invoked so that `_fallbackStartMsec` is later than the current tick, e.g. after mode switching where fields are stale) this subtraction wraps to a huge value and the fallback clock jumps forward by an astronomical amount. Compute the delta with a guard (`now >= start ? now - start : 0`).
comments.existing_code:
pos = _fallbackBaseSec +
                  (Time.GetTicksMsec() - _fallbackStartMsec) / 1000.0;

comments.content: In fixed-frame mode the elapsed time is lost on `Pause()`/`Resume()`: `Pause()` records `_pausedPosition` but does not update `_fixedFramePosition`, and `Resume()` -> `StartPlayback` sets `_fixedFramePosition = _pausedPosition`, which is fine only if `_pausedPosition` was captured from `_fixedFramePosition`. Since `Pause` captures from `GetSongTime() - offset` (filtered value), the two can diverge. Also, `Pause` in fixed-frame mode never stops anything, so `AdvanceFixedFrame` correctly no-ops, but a `Seek` while paused updates only `_pausedPosition` while `Play()` afterwards would reset from `fromSec` — verify the fixed-frame path uses the same source of truth everywhere.

`_player` is non-null here per the earlier branch, but if the stream has finished (or was never started because `Play` failed / stream is null) `GetPlaybackPosition()` returns 0 and `+ GetTimeSinceLastMix()` adds an arbitrary bias, so `GetSongTime()` reports bogus values while `_playing` remains true. Also `GetTimeSinceLastMix()` grows unbounded when no audio is mixed (e.g. silence/no active mix) — clamp it or verify `_player.Playing` before applying the mix-age term.

comments.content: The boundary does not document (nor translate) the exception contract. `V2Integration.Load` can throw `InvalidOperationException` (legacy-direct on a v2 pack), `InvalidDataException`, `FileNotFoundException`/`IOException`, and `InvalidOperationException` from `First(...)` when the chart id is absent. Callers like `ChartPack.LoadDurationSec` do not catch any of these, so a malformed chart crashes the caller. Please at least document the thrown exception set on this method so the contract is explicit at the "stable boundary".

This file is an indirection layer with a single call site (`V2Integration.Load`) and no added behavior, tests, or contract. It is `internal static` with no state, so the "stable boundary" it provides is nominal — renaming/changing `V2Integration.Load` still forces the same edits here. Either give it real value (argument validation, exception translation, logging/tracing) or consider removing it to avoid duplicate indirection. Also confirm there are tests for the pass-through (e.g. `LegacyDirect` on a v2 pack still throws) since this facade is otherwise untested.

Deadlock/blank-screen risk: `PrepareEnterAnimation()` hides every registered item (alpha 0) before calling `TransitionDirector.ReportSceneReady(BeginEnterAnimation)`, and the only thing that makes the UI visible again is `BeginEnterAnimation`. If the callback never fires (TransitionDirector instance is null / not in `AwaitingSceneReady` and the delegate throws, or the scene is re-entered while a transition is in a stuck phase) the home screen stays fully invisible and `_Process` is disabled with no fallback. Consider a safety fallback, e.g. force-restore end state on `_ExitTree`/timeout or record whether the animation actually started and restore if it didn't.

Motion-mode change between `PrepareEnterAnimation()` and `BeginEnterAnimation()` is not handled consistently. Prepare uses the profile at _Ready time, Begin re-reads `GameSession.Settings.MotionMode`. Two concrete failures:
1. Prepare ran with an animated profile (items hidden, and shifted left if directional), but Begin now sees `Off`: the non-animated branch restores `Position`/`Modulate`, but only for items it knows about — still safe — however the reverse case is the real problem.
2. Prepare ran while mode was `Off` (nothing hidden), then mode flips to animated: `BeginEnterAnimation` sets `_enterProfile` and starts `_Process` from `_enterElapsed = 0`, so visible elements instantly snap to alpha 0 and re-fade, causing a visible flash on the first frame. Recommend capturing the profile once in `PrepareEnterAnimation` and reusing exactly that profile in `BeginEnterAnimation`.

The base position is snapshotted from `item.Position` at registration time. `HomeActions.Build`/`HomeBrandBlock.Build`/`HomeUtilityRow.Build` can register children before layout settles (anchors/offsets, containers, or any later repositioning), and `_Process`/`PrepareEnterAnimation` then write this stale snapshot back, overwriting the widget's real position. Guard against drift: re-read the current position when starting the animation (or derive the base from the widget's layout at `BeginEnterAnimation` time) rather than trusting a value captured mid-construction.

comments.content: Silent failure on unreadable roots: when `DirAccess.Open` returns null (root missing, unreadable, or `user://charts` never created on a fresh install) the whole root is skipped without any diagnostic, so a misconfigured content directory looks identical to "no packs installed". Additionally, `sub` directory names are used unchecked — a name like `..` (or containing separators) is interpolated into `$"{root}/{sub}"` and could resolve outside `root`; `ChartPack.Load` only validates paths *inside* meta.json, not the pack directory itself. Log the open failure and skip non-plain directory names.

Override semantics are silent: dev packs load first and `user://charts` second, so any user pack with the same `Id` silently shadows trusted `res://testdata/packs` content with no warning — in internal/editor builds a user-supplied pack can replace the very test data used for validation. Even if intentional (per the comment), the collision should be observable via `GD.PushWarning`. Also `pack.Id` is unvalidated (empty string is allowed), so a package with a missing/empty `id` would collapse into a single dictionary entry. Note `ChartPack.Load` returning null is already logged internally by `Load`, so skipping is acceptable.

`OS.HasFeature` does a string lookup on every access, and this property is re-evaluated on each `ScanAll` call (also exposed publicly as `ChartPack.IsEditorOrInternal`) — trivially cacheable in a static readonly field. More importantly, the release-safety of this gate is undocumented and unenforced: a shipped build only avoids `res://testdata/packs` if `internal_testdata` is a custom feature that is never declared in release export presets. Add a comment naming that requirement (or an assert/CI check) so the flag cannot silently ship test data.

comments.content: When BLEED depletes, the failure path calls `ShowResults(stageFailure: true)`, which still writes the score via `GameSession.Scores.TryUpdate(...)` (only `_auto` is excluded) and classifies a real record. A failed run therefore persists a (low) score/grade as a legitimate record and can overwrite/compare against bests. If failure is meant to be excluded from scoring, pass the failure state into the score-commit decision (e.g. skip TryUpdate when `stageFailure`) or clamp the record. Worth confirming with design and covering with a test.

`songPath` comes from `_loaded.ResolvedAudioPath`, `FileAccess.GetFileAsString(FallbackChartPath)`, and chart pack loading — none of these are validated here. If the selected pack's audio is missing/unloadable, `SongPlayback` may silently play nothing (or fail), while `_playback.HasNaturallyEnded` stays false in the audio-observable path. Combined with `GameplayEndCondition` requiring both `ChartEndReached` and `AudioEnded`, the `TracksNaturalEnd` value at construction decides whether the run can ever finish. Verify that `SongPlayback` reports `TracksNaturalEnd == false` for a stream that never starts/ends, otherwise a bad audio file leaves the player stuck at the end of the song with no results screen. At minimum, check `ResourceLoader.Exists(songPath)` before constructing playback and fail fast/fallback.

comments.content: The error branch returns after scheduling navigation but leaves the instance in a partially initialized state (`_playback`, `_endCondition`, `_noteRenderer`, `_pause` all null). `_Process` is protected only by `!_playbackStarted`, and non-`_Process` handlers (input, `_UnhandledInput`, timers, tree-exit) may touch these nulls during the frames before the transition completes. The null-forgiving `null!` fields give no runtime guard. Consider setting a `_failed` flag checked in every entry point, or disabling process/input explicitly (`SetProcess(false)` / `SetProcessInput(false)`) before returning, so a late callback can't NRE.

Also note that `_loaded = selection.Loaded` (verification path) is assigned after `ApplyLoadedSelection`, which is fine, but only `GameSession.CommitSelection` in the other branch persists the loaded chart — verify the verification path doesn't need the same commit for consistent downstream reads of `CurrentSelection.LoadedChart`.

The frame-order contract is documented only here as a comment, and the checklist flags it as fragile. Each step (`SpawnNotes`, `FlushPendingInputs`, `UpdateSustainStates`, `SweepJudges`, `FinalizeEndedMixers`) depends on prior steps mutating shared state (`_noteRenderer`, `_sustainStates`, `_engine`) with no compile-time or test-level guard. Suggest extracting this into a single named method (e.g. `RunFrame(t, currentBar, delta)`) with a unit test that pins the ordering (e.g. via an event log), so a refactor that reorders or drops a step fails a test rather than silently changing judgement behavior.

Either freeze the whole settings snapshot at `_Ready` or document that these are intentionally live.

comments.content: `_ExitTree` disposes the trace but does not stop/dispose `_playback` (audio player) or unsubscribe/navigate away. On scene teardown without going through `ExitToSelect`/`Restart`, the `SongPlayback` audio node may keep playing until Godot frees the node. Also, if the scene is exited before `StartPlayback` runs (deferred via `TransitionDirector`), the deferred `StartPlayback` callback may execute after `_ExitTree` — `StartPlayback` guards with `IsInsideTree()`, which is good, but `_playback.Play` is still skipped correctly. Consider explicitly pausing playback in `_ExitTree` for safety.

No validation of the input color range. `Color` components can be negative or > 1 (e.g. HDR/ASTC/`Color.FromHsv` edge cases, or values loaded from the settings codec). For a negative channel below -0.055, `(channel + 0.055) / 1.055` is negative and `Mathf.Pow(negative, 2.4f)` returns NaN; for channels > 1 the result is simply wrong. That NaN then propagates into `Contrast`, `DeltaE` and the warning text ("LOW CONTRAST NaN"), and the comparison `contrast < MinContrast` becomes false, so a genuinely invisible color silently produces no warning. Clamp each component to [0,1] before the transfer function.

Either format with one decimal (matching the contrast chip's `0.0`), or round toward zero / floor so the shown number is unambiguously below the threshold.

This also makes `HasWarnings` cheap instead of building the whole list just to test `Count > 0`.

Additionally, there is no guard for an empty/invalid palette; if `palette` is null the method throws `NullReferenceException` (fine if callers guarantee non-null, but worth a `ArgumentNullException`/`ThrowIfNull` for a clearer failure).

comments.content: The post-audio wall-clock only accumulates from the moment `audioEnded` is observed as `true`. In practice `SongPlayback.HasNaturallyEnded` is `TracksNaturalEnd && Clock.IsPlaying && !_player.Playing`. If the stream finishes while the clock is paused (e.g. the pause overlay is open when the audio tail runs out), `Clock.IsPlaying` is false, so `AudioEnded` is never latched, and if the player is re-started on resume (or stays stopped) `!_player.Playing` may never become true again while playing. In that case `AudioEnded` never latches and `ShouldFinish` (`ChartEndReached && AudioEnded`) never becomes true → the run deadlocks in `_Process` with no way to reach results. Consider treating "stream finished and clock not advancing" as the latch condition, or adding a time-based safety net (e.g. force finish once `EffectiveSeconds >= _chartEndTime + grace` regardless of `AudioEnded`).

`MaxStepSeconds` clamps the post-audio wall clock, but the chart clock (`_observedSeconds = Math.Max(_observedSeconds, songTime)`) is unbounded. A single sample that jumps far past the chart end (e.g. `dynamite_universe_start_sec` seeking near the end, or a clock glitch/seek producing a huge `songTime`) latches `ChartEndReached` immediately, and then the run finishes as soon as the audio ends — the "wait until chart end + 2s" guarantee is silently skipped. If the same clamp intent applies to both clocks, bound the songTime step as well (or validate it is plausible relative to `delta`).

if (double.IsFinite(songTime))
            _observedSeconds = Math.Max(_observedSeconds, songTime);

Consider documenting this explicitly or removing the early return (all updates are monotonic and idempotent anyway).

comments.content: `_particleOwners.Remove(state)` (and the analogous `_effectOwners.Remove(state)` in `ReleaseContactEffect`) silently does nothing if the entry is absent. That case is reachable: when the pool is exhausted, `UpdateSustainEffect` steals an owner's particles and already removes it from `_particleOwners` (lines 152-157), leaving the owner in `_contacts` with `ContactParticles == null` while still emitting? Actually after theft the effect is still active. However when `HitEffectLevel`/`MotionMode` are toggled Off mid-frame the release path runs every frame, and `_effectOwners`/`_particleOwners` can diverge from ownership bookkeeping. Consider asserting/logging when removal fails so pool invariants are not broken silently.

Unguarded steal fallback: when `_sustainEffectPool` is empty this indexes `_effectOwners[0]`, which throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` if `_effectOwners` is also empty (e.g. `capacity` was 0 in `PrepareSustains`, or all owners were released earlier while a new contact needs an effect). Additionally, the stolen owner is `ReleaseContactEffect`ed but the caller (`UpdateSustainEffect` for that other path) is not notified — its `ContactEffect` is nulled and it will re-acquire on its next update, which is fine, but it silently loses its localized position/span for a frame. Please guard the empty case (e.g. degrade gracefully / skip the effect) rather than indexing [0] blindly.

Same unguarded indexing as the effect pool: `_particleOwners[0]` throws when the list is empty (pool capacity is 0, or every owner already released its particles), so this steal path can crash under load. Guard the empty-list case instead of assuming capacity always exceeds concurrent live contacts.

`oldest.ContactParticles!` is force-unwrapped. If an entry can ever be present in `_particleOwners` while its `ContactParticles` is null, this throws a `NullReferenceException`. The invariant holds only if every removal from `_particleOwners` is paired with nulling the field (true today in `ReleaseSustainEffect`), so the null-forgiving operator is binding a non-obvious invariant across methods. Prefer `oldest.ContactParticles` with a null check and skip/remove stale owners to make the steal path robust.

`ReleaseSustainEffect(int headId)` uses the dictionary indexer, so any caller passing an id that was never registered in `PrepareSustains` throws `KeyNotFoundException` (e.g. `GameplayNoteRenderer.ReleaseMixerHeadView` can be called from multiple paths). Use `_contacts.TryGetValue(headId, out var state)` and no-op/log when missing. Same concern applies to `var state = _contacts[path.HeadId];` in `UpdateSustainEffect` (line 104). Idempotency of repeated Off-path calls is otherwise OK because the particle/effect fields are nulled before return.

`_contacts.Add` throws `ArgumentException` on a duplicate `HeadId` and permanently poisons initialization if `PrepareSustains` is ever invoked twice on the same instance (e.g. on restart/rebuild). Also, no cleanup of `_contacts`, `_activeBlooms`, `_activeHitParticles`, `_effectOwners`, `_particleOwners`, `_drainingParticles`, or the pools happens when notes/effects are torn down, so re-preparing after a restart would leak or double-push nodes. Consider clearing existing state at the start of `PrepareSustains`/`PrepareHits` and using `[headId] =` or a duplicate check.

comments.content: If `MotionMode` is switched to `Off` while a contact particle emitter is active, this early return leaves the emitter running: `ContactParticles` is never released, never hidden, and never added to `_drainingParticles`. It keeps emitting until the whole sustain is released. Call `ReleaseSustainEffect(state)`/`ReleaseContactParticles` in the Off branch (symmetric with the `HitEffectLevel == Off` branch above), or explicitly hide/stop it.

Same unguarded steal pattern for blooms/particles: `_activeBlooms[0]` / `_activeHitParticles[0]` throw when the active list is empty and the pool is empty (e.g. `PrepareHits` was never called, or `capacity == 0`). A defensive check that creates a new node on demand (or bails out) avoids a hard crash in the hit path.

`ContactVisual.Path` is declared `required` but is assigned only via object-initializer in `PrepareSustains`. If a future path needs a `ContactVisual` for an id not present in `_contacts`, it cannot be created without a path. This is acceptable today but the `required` + mutable-field combination makes the ownership state (`ContactEffect`/`ContactParticles`) easy to desynchronize from `_effectOwners`/`_particleOwners`. Consider encapsulating acquire/release inside `ContactVisual` so the two lists can never drift.

`_age` is never incremented. `GameplayHitParticles` has no `_Process` override, and `ResetFor`/`ResetForPool` only call `SetProcess(true/false)` without any per-frame age accumulation. `_age` stays at 0.0 forever, so `IsExpired` is always false once `_playing == true`. `GameplayEffects.RecycleExpired()` therefore never recycles these nodes; each burst stays active (still parented, still holding `ProcessMaterial`) and every new hit with an empty pool goes down the `_activeHitParticles[0]` steal path, permanently leaking nodes/material references and keeping `EmitParticles` on a fallback branch. Add a `_Process(delta)` that does `if (_playing) _age += delta;` (and stop processing once expired), or drive expiry from the emitter's `Finished` signal.

comments.content: This `Visible = false` on the retained sustain node is contradicted by the file's own contract (class doc: "断开接触时 SetEmitting(false) 停止发射，存量粒子自然消亡后自我回收；宽限内接回时重新 SetEmitting(true) 即可恢复"). Hiding the whole `Node2D` immediately hides the still-alive particles (the drain tail) and makes the reconnect path (`SetEmitting(true)` + `Visible = true`) pop back abruptly. Conversely, if `Visible` should be honoured, `_drainAge` is never advanced because `BeginRelease`/`_Process` only run when emitting stops via `SetEmitting`. Either way the drain state machine is inconsistent here; the `Visible=false` should be removed so particles fade naturally. (Noted here because it is the caller of `SetEmitting` defined in this file.)

`SetEmitting` is called from `GameplayEffects.UpdateSustainEffect` every frame while connected (`state.ContactParticles.SetEmitting(true)`), and it returns early when unchanged — fine. But when a node is released, `BeginRelease()` calls `SetEmitting(false)` which early-returns if `_emitting` is already false, then sets `_releasing = true`. The bigger problem: `IsDrained` only becomes true if `_releasing` is set; since `_Process` keeps running (`SetProcess(true)` in ResetFor) and accumulates `_drainAge` even when `_emitting` is true, the drain timer is not tied to actual emission stop. Also `BeginRelease` before any `ResetFor` (e.g. on a pooled node) sets `_releasing` on a node with `_drainLifetime = SparkLifetime`, reporting drained after 0.47s — callers may re-push a node that was never emitting. Guard `BeginRelease` with a reset/idle check.

The static `Materials` cache is keyed by the resolved `Color accent` and is never evicted or bounded. Accents come from `HitParticleAssets.Tint(accent, kind)` where `accent` originates from note colors (see `NotePaletteSpecimen` and dynamic palettes), so each distinct accent colour allocates a new `ParticleProcessMaterial` (with a `GradientTexture1D` and `CurveTexture` reference) for every layer/bucket combination — up to 4 layers × 10 buckets = 40 materials per colour. With randomized/dynamic accents this grows without bound for the whole process lifetime. Cache by a small enumerated/quantized key (e.g. quantize accent channels) or cap the dictionary.
comments.existing_code: private static readonly Dictionary<(Color Accent, int Layer, int Bucket), ParticleProcessMaterial> Materials = new();

comments.content: `Prewarm` adds a pooled node to `parent` but never schedules its removal. The `GameplayHitParticles` prewarm node relies on `IsExpired` to be recycled, which (as noted elsewhere) never becomes true because `_age` is never advanced — so the invisible, still-emitting prewarm node stays in the tree permanently. This defeats the purpose of a warm-up probe and leaks a node (plus its `PrewarmCullRect` and materials). Use a one-shot timer/`Finished` signal (or `QueueFree`) to remove the probe after warm-up.

`_liveEmitters` is incremented in `ResetFor` (only when `!prewarm`) and decremented in `Uncount`, which is called from `ResetForPool` and `_ExitTree`. Since `GameplayEffects` pools these nodes and never re-parents/frees them during play, `_ExitTree` is only called at shutdown, so the counter registers every pool reset. But because the prewarm path deliberately skips counting (`if (!prewarm)` sets `_counted = true`), the prewarmed sustain node also never calls `Uncount` — acceptable. The real risk: if `ResetFor` is called twice in a row without `ResetForPool` (possible via the `_particleOwners` steal path, which does call `ResetForPool` — ok), or if the node is somehow reset after `_ExitTree` already decremented (Godot may call `_ExitTree` then the pool manager calls `ResetForPool` on an orphan, double-decrementing), the concurrency factor will silently drift downward for the rest of the session. Consider making `_counted` the single source of truth and asserting/counting once per ResetFor, and resetting `_liveEmitters` on tree teardown.

comments.content: The lazy singletons (`_sparkTexture`, `_emberTexture`, `_shrinkCurve`, `_additive`) and the `Materials` dictionary are not thread-safe. If any layer is ever created or reset from a non-main thread (e.g. a background loading/prewarm task), two concurrent `SparkTexture()` calls can both build the image and one thread can see a non-null but not-yet-initialised object reference (the assignment happens after `CreateFromImage` returns, so this particular ordering is safe, but the `Dictionary` mutation in `SparkMaterial`/`EmberMaterial` is not). Godot resource creation must be on the main thread; at minimum guard the static caches, or document/enforce main-thread-only usage.

`LegacyScoreKey` returns `ChartId` for V2, but all consumers (`GameSession.Scores.Get/TryUpdate(packId, diff)` → `ScoreStoreCore.GetLegacy`/`_legacyRecords`) route it into the legacy-only store, which is populated from legacy JSON and never answers four-part identity queries. So the V2 branch of this key can never match a stored record — best-score display and result saving silently become no-ops whenever `TryGetScoreIdentity` fails (e.g. `GameplayDigest` missing). Make the V2 fallback explicit/rejected, or route it to the identity store, rather than returning a key with different semantics depending on format.

comments.content: `Uri.TryCreate(path, UriKind.Absolute, out _)` is overly broad as a rejection rule: on non-Windows it treats POSIX-looking values as absolute and will also accept/misclassify anything containing a scheme. Conversely the string pre-check `StartsWith('/')` is `Ordinal`, but on Windows a leading `\` is rejected only by the separate backslash check — fine — while a path beginning with `//` (UNC-ish) is rejected only because of the empty-segment rule. The real defense is the later `Path.GetFullPath` + root-prefix comparison, so this `Uri.TryCreate` call mostly adds false positives (e.g. a legitimate relative filename containing `:`-like text) while giving a misleading "URI scheme" reason. Prefer a simple explicit drive-letter check (`path.Length >= 2 && char.IsLetter(path[0]) && path[1] == ':'`) and rely on the canonicalized containment test for absoluteness.

`ValidateLegacyDirectoryChain` (and the `rootedPrefix` comparison in `IsSafeLegacyPackagePath`) compares paths with `StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase` on every platform. On case-sensitive filesystems (Linux/macOS) two distinct directories differing only in case are different packages, so a sibling directory that matches by case can pass the "escapes the package root" check even though it is actually outside the root. Use `OperatingSystem.IsWindows() ? StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase : StringComparison.Ordinal` (or a `PathComparison` helper) consistently for the containment checks.

The walk terminates and returns success only when it reaches `root` exactly. If `root` itself is a symlink/junction (e.g. the package directory under `user://charts` is a link), the loop reports `"parent directory is a reparse point: <root>"` and the package is rejected wholesale. That may be intentional, but note it is asymmetric with the `res://` short-circuit which skips the check entirely, and it also means a single linked package silently disappears (`Load` logs a warning and returns null). If linked package roots are meant to be disallowed, that should be stated in the XML doc; if they are meant to be allowed (only the leaves inside must be safe), the check should stop inspecting after the first iteration that equals `root` rather than failing on it.

`LoadDurationSec` and `LoadNoteCount` each perform a full strict decode + validation + digest via `LoadChart`, even though `LoadedChart` already carries both values. Callers needing both pay double cost, and these APIs invite list/UI code to re-decode just for metadata. Prefer an overload that takes an existing `LoadedChart`, or add a lightweight metadata load path.

Catching bare `Exception` here also swallows `OperationCanceledException` (returning `false`/"chart unavailable" instead of cancelling) and fatal `OutOfMemoryException`. Additionally only `e.Message` is logged, losing the exception type and stack needed to diagnose corrupted packages. Narrow the filter and log the exception type, e.g. `catch (Exception e) when (e is not OperationCanceledException and not OutOfMemoryException) { GD.PushWarning($"ChartPack: loading {Id}/{diff.ChartId} failed: {e.GetType().Name}: {e.Message}"); ... }`.

Format detection is all-or-nothing: presence of either `format` or `formatVersion` forces the V2 branch, so a legacy package that happens to carry a stray `formatVersion` (or a non-V2 `format` string) is rejected wholesale and silently disappears from `ScanAll` (indistinguishable to users from a missing pack). Distinguish "declares V2 with wrong version" (hard reject) from "has an unrelated `format`/`formatVersion` key" (warn and treat as legacy, or surface a clear error in the UI) so a single extra field does not brick a package.

`TryGetScoreIdentity` is documented and used as a non-throwing probe (`if (loaded.TryGetScoreIdentity(out var identity))`), but `new ScoreIdentity(...)` throws `ArgumentException` for any empty member. `packId`/`chartId` come from untrusted `meta.json` and are not validated for emptiness at load time, so `id: ""` or an empty chart id makes this method throw instead of returning false, escaping via `CompleteChartDetails`/`GameplayMain.Presentation`. Validate `Id`/`ChartId` during `Load` (non-empty, path-safe) or guard the construction (check `string.IsNullOrEmpty` on all four parts) so the probe really returns false.

comments.content: Two issues here: (1) `WithVirtualFileAccess(Load)` holds the single process-wide VirtualFileLock for the whole decode (`GD.Load` / `AudioStreamWav.LoadFromFile` do disk IO + full decode), which serializes all unrelated res:// loads and blocks V2Integration chart loading (which uses the same lock); consider narrowing the lock to just the FileAccess/Exist calls instead of the whole decode. (2) The cache is checked under AudioLock but populated under a *separate* lock acquisition, so two threads loading the same user:// path can both decode and both `Set`, meaning duplicate decode work and the first caller keeping an instance no longer in the cache. Enclose the whole load+store in AudioLock (or document the benign duplication).

The 8 MB byte cap does not bound decode memory for compressed formats, so the header parse is the only pre-decode guard — yet the parsers reject valid variants:
- PNG: requires the signature at 0..8 and "IHDR" at offset 12; a PNG with a preceding ancillary chunk is rejected (valid image dropped).
- WebP: the top-level `bytes.Length < 30` gate rejects a valid VP8L file shorter than 30 bytes even though the VP8L branch only needs 25; conversely the inner `bytes.Length >= 30` check for `VP8 ` is redundant.
Make the length checks per-branch so valid files are not dropped, keeping the post-decode DimensionsWithinLimits as the authoritative check (it is correct and currently present).

comments.content: The bounds arithmetic here is safe (offsets stay under 8 MB, no `int` overflow), but the scanner never handles SOS (0xDA): when a JPEG has no SOF before the scan (e.g. certain progressive/malformed files, or DHT-heavy streams where an entropy byte happens to be 0xFF), the loop continues into the entropy-coded data and interprets compressed bytes as markers, jumping `offset += length` arbitrarily. It terminates via the bounds checks, but results are non-deterministic as a pre-decode size guard. Add an explicit stop at SOS so the parser never scans into scan data.

Callers that refresh the same cover art/icon repeatedly will cause redundant disk IO and GPU memory churn. If this is intentional (e.g. covers must be released per chart), document it; otherwise mirror AudioCache with a bounded texture cache and an eviction hook for chart changes.

comments.content: The progress ratio is not NaN-safe. `Math.Max(0.01, state.EndTime)` does not guard against a non-finite EndTime (NaN propagates through Math.Max), and a negative `state.Time` yields a negative ratio that `Mathf.Clamp` does clamp, but a NaN/Infinity EndTime produces a NaN `pw`, which Godot then stores in `Position`/`Size` — the fill silently disappears and may poison downstream transform math. Add `double.IsFinite` validation (clamp EndTime into a sane positive range) before dividing. Note the caller (`_plan.EndTime`) is not validated here.

Exact `!=` comparison on a `double` for the ACC text cache. `LiveAcc` is a percentage produced by floating-point division on every frame, so tiny representation noise re-writes the label (full text reshaping) even though the rendered `F2` string is identical. Compare the formatted value (or quantize to 2 decimals) so the cache actually suppresses redundant reshaping, which is the stated purpose of this cache.

comments.content: `ShowResults` sets `_finished = true` first (good), but there is no check on whether a navigation/result transition is already in flight, and `_playback` is intentionally not paused here. If a stage-failure/BLEED path and natural completion both reach this method within the same frame, only the first wins — that is fine — but a second caller that already paused playback (BLEED) can still have paused the clock before losing the race. Make the guard/side-effect ordering explicit at call sites or re-assert the expected playback state here so a losing race cannot leave the song paused under a non-result screen.

`BuildStage()` dereferences `_stageRoot`/`_hudRoot` returned by `sharedStage.NoteLayer` without any null/initialization validation, and `BuildStage` can be invoked before `AddChild` completes in some Godot lifecycle orders. More importantly, if `BuildStage` is ever called twice (scene rebuild, hot reload, retry path), duplicate HUD/stage nodes and a second pause overlay will be created without freeing the previous ones — a leak that also double-wires `TogglePause`. Guard with an idempotent check (`if (_stageRoot != null) return;`) or null out/free previous roots.

The pause-button touch suppression entry (`_ignoredTouchIds.Add`) is placed after the state gate `_pause.IsPaused || TransitionDirector.IsBusy`. With `_pause.IsPaused` true the method returns early, so the press that lands on the pause button while the overlay is animating/active never registers as ignored. Its matching release is then also gated... but more importantly, the id lifecycle depends entirely on observing a matching release with `Pressed == false` in `_Input`. Godot does not deliver `InputEventScreenTouch` releases reliably when the touch is cancelled (window focus loss, touch cancel gestures, gesture recognition), so an id can stay in `_ignoredTouchIds` forever and permanently swallow that finger's future presses/drags. `ClearPointerState()` (which clears `_ignoredTouchIds`) is only invoked from `SuspendForPause` and focus-out; a stale id after a cancelled touch is not covered because focus-out may not fire. Consider also dropping ignored ids on resume/after a timeout (and/or handling `InputEventScreenTouch.Canceled` if exposed), and placing the pause-button hit test before the paused gate so an ignored press started while paused is at least tracked.

The F12 debug seek is shipped unconditionally in release builds, and it bypasses the input pipeline entirely: `_playback.Seek(...)` jumps the clock without clearing `_pointerBuffer`/hold state, so any active pointer's last positions (and their timestamps) straddle the jump, and hold/release timelines are corrupted. Worse, seeking near `_plan.EndTime` while notes are unjudged can immediately produce mass misses and corrupt the score record that the results flow / persistence consumes. Please guard it behind a debug-only build/flag (e.g. `#if DEBUG` or `OS.IsDebugBuild()` + a settings flag) and call `ClearPointerState()` before seeking.

Gate divergence between `_Input` and `_UnhandledInput`: `_Input` drops everything while `_pause.IsPaused`, but `_UnhandledInput` only checks `_pause.IsPaused` after handling Escape and does not check `TransitionDirector.IsBusy` on the paused path. More substantively, the paused early-return silently discards the mouse **release** events that occur while paused. If a mouse button is held down when pause is entered, the release press/release bookkeeping in `PointerInputBuffer` never sees the release, and after resume the pointer remains "active" at its stale position, generating phantom stationary contacts each frame and blocking holds until the user presses and releases again. Suspend already clears state (so the buffer is empty), which mitigates it, but only because of that ordering — this coupling is fragile; it would be safer to route releases through the buffer even when paused (or document/enforce the invariant that any pause path calls `ClearPointerState`).

`_pointerBuffer.Presses` is only populated from `_touches` for the *final* state of each pointer in the frame. In `CollectFrame`, a press followed by a same-frame move re-projects via `projectTouches(_touches, ... ContactPhase.Moved)`, which calls `RemoveTouches(id)` first — the `TouchSample` captured in `_presses` keeps the original `Began` phase, so that is fine. However, `RebuildTrackBuckets` runs *before* `Presses` are dispatched, and `_touchesByTrack` holds `_pointerBuffer.Touches` entries, while `ProcessPress` presumably mutates judging state. If a later `ProcessPress` depends on buckets reflecting the same pre-press state for all presses, ordering is preserved; but note that `ProcessPress` receives the press snapshot while the bucket list contains the *moved* sample for that id — any code that looks up a press id in `_touchesByTrack` will get the moved position rather than the press position. Please confirm `ProcessPress` only uses its `press.Touch` argument and never re-resolves the pointer through `_touchesByTrack`, otherwise a same-frame press+move judges against the wrong coordinate.

`(int)touch.Track` is used as an unchecked array index into `_touchesByTrack` (size 3). `ProjectHoldTouch`/`AddProjectedTouches` only produce Center/Left/Right today, but `Track` is a shared enum; if a `TouchTrackMask`/`Track` value is ever added (e.g. a 4th lane) or `GameplayMirror.Display` returns an unexpected value, this becomes an `IndexOutOfRangeException` on the hot input path with no diagnostic. Prefer an explicit switch/mapping (or bounds-check with a guard) so unsupported tracks fail loudly in tests rather than crashing a live run.

`ProjectHoldTouch` iterates the *display* tracks (Center/Left/Right) but assigns the result by the *post-mirror* track. With mirroring enabled, `displayTrack = Left` maps to chart `Track.Right`, and `displayTrack = Right` maps to chart `Track.Left` — so the assignment is consistent, but there is no guard against a mask that includes both Left and Right (e.g. overlapping regions) mapping to the same output slot: the second write silently overwrites the first with an identical-id sample, and one direction is lost. Since the mask regions are supposed to be disjoint this is latent, but a comment or an explicit assertion would make the invariant (output slot unique per input track, no silent overwrite) checkable. Consider asserting `center/left/right` are only assigned once per id.

`frameTime` is only consumed by `AdvancePressWindows`, while presses are dispatched with `press.Time` (timestamped at `_Input` arrival via `_playback.GetSongTime()`). If `frameTime` is the *current* process time but `press.Time` came from an earlier input poll, the press window may already have advanced past a unit that the press legitimately straddles. `AdvancePressWindows` compensates with a 1s margin (documented in Judgement.cs), which means a frame stall longer than 1s (e.g. a GC spike or window drag on desktop) will permanently drop legitimate presses. This is a known trade-off, but worth surfacing: the margin is a magic constant and a long hitch silently changes scoring behavior. Consider deriving the margin from a documented max-frame budget rather than a bare `1.0`.

Two correctness problems with the audio digest here:

1. `Godot.FileAccess.GetFileAsBytes` returns an empty array when the file cannot be opened (it does not throw). If `pack.AudioPathFor(diff)` is missing undecodable, the digest silently computes over empty audio, i.e. an audio mismatch is never detected — the exact failure the digest exists to catch. Capture the error code and throw.
2. The same gap exists in the virtual branch: any res:// audio — including a missing/broken imported resource — is silently digested as empty audio. Since one of the two client/server sides may be a filesystem package (full audio digest, per the comment) while the other is res://, an empty digest on res:// is not guaranteed to match the counterpart digest; the comment's claim of "same identity on both ends" only holds when both sides take the virtual path.

Returning `null` for "present but not decodable / zero length" makes the duration hook silently skip the preview and last-judgement bounds checks (`ValidateEntry` only validates when duration is non-null). `ValidateResolvedAudio` already rejects undecodable audio, but a decodable stream reporting length 0 (or a `-1`/NaN length) also disables the bounds validation without any diagnostic. Prefer failing loudly instead of degrading to "no bound check". Same applies to the virtual-branch copy at line ~112.

The Default-mode fallback swallows every `InvalidDataException` from `LoadLegacyAsV2` and silently degrades to the direct path. That is intended for empty-timeline charts, but it also masks genuine conversion defects (cyclic/dangling sustains, unsupported note types, cross-track sustains, invalid bar times, decodable-but-broken audio) — the chart then plays through a completely different code path with no v2 digest and no diagnostics. At minimum log the exception before falling back so these regressions are visible, and consider distinguishing the "cannot be represented in v2" case from other conversion errors.

`First` here throws a bare `InvalidOperationException` with no context. Its result is only used for `ReferenceEquals` index lookup below, which could reuse the existing helper (`V2PackageValidator.ValidateEntry` already derives the index via `ReferenceEquals` when `entryIndex < 0`). Passing `-1` and dropping this lookup would remove duplicated brittle logic and give a proper diagnostic instead of an opaque exception.

A `Press` that does not project onto this track still yields `ContactPhase.Began` (action is Press). `MixerRuntime.Apply` stores `_touches[id]` *before* the geometry check (MixerRuntime.cs:91-94), so a finger that lands elsewhere but happens to be inside this path's bounds can be treated as a *began* contact and become the controller (`Placed = true, Controller = id`). Phase should follow the per-track projection: `Began` iff the projection is on this track and the pointer was not already tracked here.

comments.content:
This method (and `Display`) relies on the `MirroredDisplay` mapping being an involution, and the doc comment states that as a guarantee without any guard. Two concrete consequences worth addressing:
1. It is only correct as long as the mirror stays symmetric about `MirrorAxis`; the "inverse" of the visual mapping is logically a separate operation (screen→chart). If the geometry later becomes asymmetric (e.g. non-uniform center range, or center width taken into account), this file will keep silently producing wrong touch coordinates instead of failing loudly.
2. `ProjectTouch` freshly allocates regardless of the mirror flag — when `Enabled == false`, `Display` just returns its input, so the whole wrapper is a no-op yet still goes through `GameSession.Settings` access and a tuple decomposition on every touch, every frame, in input hot paths (`AddProjectedTouches` is called per pointer phase, up to 3 tracks each). Consider an early-return `return new(id, screenTrack, screenCenter, phase);` when not mirrored, or add an assertion/test that `Display(Display(x)) == x` (the existing geometry tests only cover the shared function, not this facade).

`Display` fully covers this method (`Display(Track.Center, center).Center`), so `DisplayCenter` is a redundant second entry point to the same mapping. Having both `DisplayCenter`, `Display` and the direct `GameplayStageGeometry.MirroredDisplay` call sites (`GameplayVisualMapper`, `GameplayStageRenderer`) means the "single mapping entry" claimed in the class doc is not actually enforced, making it easy to introduce a call that forgets to apply mirroring. Consider removing `DisplayCenter` (or routing all callers through `Display`) so there is exactly one place mirroring is applied.

There is no test coverage for this facade itself: existing tests (`tools/core-tests/Gameplay/GameplayGeometryTests.cs`) only exercise `GameplayStageGeometry.MirroredDisplay/MirroredTrack`, and the round-trip / `Enabled == false` paths of `ProjectTouch` and `Display` are untested. Since these are the sole input path used by judgement, add tests asserting: (a) `Display(Display(t, c)) == (t, c)` for both tracks and Center, (b) `ProjectTouch` returns the input unchanged when `Enabled` is false, and (c) side-track touch maps to the opposite track while center stays Center. This also documents the involution assumption relied on above so a future geometry change breaks a test instead of gameplay.

comments.content: HitTiming.Exact is mapped to the Late suffix because the ternary only special-cases Early. JudgeEngine produces Exact whenever |delta| < 1e-9 (see JudgeEngine.Judge/JudgePress), so a Great/Good hit that lands exactly on the note time — quite likely when the input sample and note time share the same rounded song position — will be displayed as "GREAT L" / "GOOD L". The Exact case should be handled explicitly (e.g. no suffix, or fold it into Early/Late only where it is semantically meaningful).

Passing `unit.Category` (ScoreCategory) to the renderer couples the view layer to scoring categories. The renderer resolves the note by `noteId` and then re-derives visual type from `note.Type`; if `unit.Category`/`unit.NoteId` are ever not part of the loaded chart (e.g. synthetic/auto-generated units or a plan built from a different chart snapshot), `GameplayNoteRenderer.ResolveNoteView` silently returns on `_noteById.TryGetValue` failing, so a hit is scored but the note view stays on screen / the effect is never emitted with no diagnostic. Consider asserting/logging once on lookup failure so mismatches are detectable, and verify at plan-build time that every unit.NoteId exists in `_noteById`.

comments.content: `_motionInFlight` is only cleared by the tween's `FinishEntry`/`FinishExit` callbacks. If the tween is killed before reaching `TweenCallback` (e.g. `ForceCloseForResult` kills the tween while an entry tween is mid-flight), the flag stays `true` forever. On the next gameplay the entry animation would never finish, buttons remain disabled and `Toggle()` returns early — permanently stuck. `ForceCloseForResult` handles this explicitly, but the same hazard exists whenever `BeginEntry`/`BeginExit` kill a live tween (`_tween?.Kill()`), and it is fragile because the invariant lives in the callback rather than at the kill sites. Clear `_motionInFlight` whenever a tween is killed before starting a new one, or make the kill sites funnel through a `KillTween()` helper that also resets the flag.

For non-animated profiles `BeginExit` calls `FinishExit()` synchronously from within `Toggle()`, which is itself invoked from the button's `Pressed` handler / or HUD `TogglePause`. That means `_onResume()` (host `_playback.Resume()`) runs while Godot is still dispatching the input/press callback and before the disabled state change — reentrancy into the host's playback and input state is unguarded. Consider deferring the resume via `Callable.From(FinishExit).CallDeferred()` so pause/unpause is always applied after the current frame's input processing, and so behaviour matches the animated path (which always defers to the next frame via the tween callback).

The resume button is wired as `_resumeButton.Pressed += Toggle;` and Toggle itself re-checks `_finished()`/`_motionInFlight`, so resume is protected. But the resume button stays `Disabled = false` for the whole time the overlay is visible (including during the entry motion), meaning a user can click "继续" mid-animation and it silently does nothing — while Retry/Quit are disabled for the same window. As written, Retry/Quit silently swallow clicks during the animated entry but resume does not, which is confusing UX.

RescanPacks only validates that the pack *id* still exists. If the pack survived the rescan but its charts changed (chart removed/renamed, package revision bumped, or audio path changed), `CurrentSelection` and every `Preloads` entry keep pointing at `ChartPack`/`ChartDiff`/`LoadedChart` objects captured from the previous scan. GameplayMain consumes `CurrentSelection.Pack`/`Diff` directly, so a deleted chart id or stale absolute `DirPath`/`ResolvedAudioPath` would be used at play time. Re-scan should re-resolve the selection and cached diffs against the *new* pack objects (e.g. `Packs.FirstOrDefault(p => ids match)?.ChartOf(diff.ChartId)`), and drop any preload whose diff no longer exists or whose package revision changed.

A single removed/unreadable pack wipes the entire preload cache and, via `ClearPreload()`, strips `LoadedChart` from `CurrentSelection` with `with { LoadedChart = null }` (which also changes the `CurrentSelection` object/equality). That can null a perfectly valid committed chart from a still-existing pack (possibly just committed for the next gameplay scene) and force a full re-load. Invalidate per entry: remove only the preloads belonging to the vanished pack, and only clear `CurrentSelection.LoadedChart` when its own pack is affected, leaving the underlying `CurrentSelection` object intact otherwise.

`_init` is set before `Settings.Load()`/`Scores.Load()`/`RescanPacks()` run, so if any of them throws (corrupt settings/score file, IO error, `ScanAll` failure) the static flag stays `true` while the session is only half-initialized; all later `EnsureInit()` calls become no-ops and the app runs with empty packs/scores permanently. Set the flag only after all steps complete successfully (or use a dedicated `_initializing` guard + `_initialized` flag). Note also that this is not thread-safe: parallel first calls (e.g. a deferred callback) could observe `_init == true` mid-load and use partially-loaded state.

`CommitSelection` calls `GetPreload`, which is a *mutating* LRU touch (moves the key to the tail). Committing the selection for playback therefore silently changes eviction order and can cause a different preload to be evicted right after even if the user never navigated. Consider a read-only `PeekPreload` for lookups that should not affect LRU order.

The legacy `gameplayEffectsEnabled` migration only runs when `hitEffectLevel` is Undefined. Because `Encode` always writes both `gameplayEffectsEnabled` and `hitEffectLevel`, any pre-existing settings file that already contains a (possibly default/empty) `hitEffectLevel` value will ignore `gameplayEffectsEnabled`. More importantly, `JsonValueKind.Null` is not Undefined either: a file with `"hitEffectLevel": null` falls through to `ParseString`, which returns "full" even if `gameplayEffectsEnabled` was `false`. The intended "legacy boolean wins when the new field is absent" rule should be expressed explicitly (missing or Null), otherwise the migration is fragile and silently drops the user's OFF choice.

The magic slot count `10` and the factory color array are duplicated here, in `RestorePalettes`, and (per `GameSettings.NormalizeNotePalettes`) in `NotePalette.SlotCount`/`NotePalette.CreateLibrary`. All three copies must agree; if `NotePalette.SlotCount` ever changes, `Decode` will silently produce a snapshot with the wrong number of slots and `ApplySnapshot` will take the "reset whole library" branch. Extract a single `const int SlotCount = 10` (or reuse `NotePalette.SlotCount`) and a single factory-color source instead of repeating the literals in two methods of this file.

`Encode` serializes whatever `NotePalettes` the snapshot holds, but `RestorePalettes` assumes exactly 10 entries (`data[i]` for i in 0..9). A snapshot with >10 palettes is silently truncated on reload; a snapshot with <10 entries causes `RestorePalettes` to synthesize default/empty slots because `entry is null`, and — since `Colors` is only applied when `entry?.Colors is { Count: >= 6 }` — all previously saved colors for the missing entries are lost. Also `slot.Colors.ToList()` will NRE if a palette slot was constructed with null colors, and the colors are written without any hex validation/hygiene. Normalize the list to exactly the slot count (pad/truncate) in `Encode` before serializing, and guard `slot.Colors` against null/invalid entries so `Encode` output is always loadable back with identical content.

The codec round-trips `ActiveNotePalette` verbatim with no clamping to the valid slot range and no check that the target slot is non-empty, even though the rest of the file already has `RestorePalettes` results available to validate against. Decode it after `RestorePalettes`, then clamp to `0..slots.Count-1` and fall back to 0 when `slots[index].Empty` (mirroring `GameSettings.NormalizeNotePalettes`). Relying on the caller to fix this makes `Decode` alone unsafe for any other consumer (e.g. tests/tools) and would apply an unconfigured preset if a save file is hand-edited or written by an older build.

CanAdvance probes the external start-gate path with File.Exists on every _Process frame (GameplayMain calls it per frame). Each call is a syscall/stat on a path that is outside the Godot VFS, so a typo'd gate path is silently treated as "gate absent forever" and the run hangs until timeout with no diagnostic, and a relative gate path is resolved against the current working directory here but against GetFullPath inside SignalReady/ResolveLocalPath - i.e. the gate is checked at one place while other paths are normalized elsewhere. Normalize gate paths through ResolveLocalPath once at construction, and (optionally) rate-limit the existence probe so gate polling does not hit the filesystem every frame.

ResolveLocalPath is duplicated verbatim in V2IntegrationVerification and V2IntegrationTrace (only the trace copy has a subtle comment difference). Dispose is not idempotent/thread-safe: after the first call the second Flush on a disposed StreamWriter throws ObjectDisposedException, and Write after Dispose silently... actually throws as well but only after the file handle is gone. GameplayMain disposes in _ExitTree, and an exception path or a duplicate _ExitTree/teardown would surface as an unhandled exception during shutdown, losing the trace tail. Guard with a disposed flag (also adding an explicit `IDisposable` double-dispose safe pattern) and wrap the flush in try/finally so a failed flush cannot prevent the handle from being released.

The trace writer is created inside the constructor and only owned by the returned instance; if the caller fails to dispose it (early return, exception during startup after CreateTrace, process crash), the buffered JSONL tail is lost because StreamWriter buffers by default and nothing flushes periodically. Since the whole point is a comparable trace, flush after each Write (or use a bounded AutoFlush policy, e.g. flush every N frames) so an aborted verification run still yields a usable prefix, and document that callers must dispose via try/finally.

For an A/B comparison harness whose contract is bit-identical traces across legacy/v2 runs, prefer writing to a buffer and a single Write, and (optionally) pin double formatting so trace diffs are not polluted by runtime formatting changes.

comments.content: `LoopPositionUnwrapper.Advance` wraps when `raw < lastRaw - loopSeconds*0.5`. Because the compensation term `+ GetTimeSinceLastMix() - GetOutputLatency()` is added *before* unwrapping, the output latency (often 20–100 ms, and on the very first frames the position may be negative) shifts raw near the loop boundary; a negative first sample (`_lastRaw = -1` sentinel means the first call is always accepted, fine) combined with `GetPlaybackPosition()` reporting `length` instead of `0` at the wrap point can yield a raw position > `BarSeconds`, i.e. the unwrapped timeline can jump a full extra bar or the wrap can be missed. At minimum clamp/validate raw into `[0, BarSeconds)` or apply the compensation *after* unwrapping, and consider a sanity check (max expected delta) before accumulating `_baseSeconds`.

`Pause()` only pauses `_clock`. On the non-fallback path `_clock.Pause()` calls `_player.Stop()` so audio stops, but `_loopUnwrap` is not frozen and `_fallbackStartMsec` is not advanced — after resume the unwrapped position is based on a rewound `GetPlaybackPosition()` (the same stream restarts at 0), so `_lastRaw` (near 2s) vs the new raw (~0) is interpreted as *one* wrap, silently offsetting the timeline by up to a bar. Either reset `_loopUnwrap` on pause/resume, or drive position from `_clock.GetSongTime()` while paused/just-resumed. Also, `Pause()` is a no-op before `Start()`, which is fine, but it depends on `_clock` being non-null — `SongPositionSeconds` has no such guard for `_clock` in the `ManualFallback` branch (null-ref if called before `Start`).

`AttributedNote` uses `Math.Round` (banker's rounding), so at exactly half-bar positions (`songSec/BarSeconds` exactly N+0.5) the attribution flips to the *earlier* note when N is even (e.g. 0.5 → 0 → note 1) but to the *later* note when N is odd (e.g. 1.5 → 2 → note 3). This is inconsistent at the ±half-bar boundary, which matters because the ±150ms stray gate and duplicate gate both key off this value. Worse, when `BarSeconds/2 < 150ms` (fast BPM / short bar), a hit up to 150ms early can still be attributed to the *next* note, so the same physical note can be attributed two different ways on repeated taps within the window — bypassing the `attributedNote == LastSampledNote` duplicate guard (e.g. tap at -140ms lands on note N, tap at +10ms lands on note N+1) and counting one note twice. Use a deterministic half-up rule (e.g. `(int)Math.Floor(songSec / BarSeconds + 0.5)`) so the boundary is consistent, and consider whether the duplicate guard should compare against a tolerated note range or the last-sample timestamp instead of exact note index.

These two formulas disagree on the same input: for `songSec = 1.9 * BarSeconds`, `PassedNoteCount` = 2 so `WarmupBaseNote` = 2 and warmup covers notes 2 and 3, but `AttributedNote` = 3, meaning the first post-Ready hit (which lands late relative to bar 2) is still treated as warmup — and the note after it is too, so the player effectively gets an extra warmup note. Conversely, when `songSec` is just under a bar line the round-based attribution can be one ahead of the floor-based base, shifting the warmup window forward. Compute the base from the same attribution function used for the gate, e.g. `WarmupBaseNote = AttributedNote(songSec)`.

comments.content: `Restart` sets `WarmupBaseNote = 0` while the constructor leaves it at the default 0 as well, so the "no warmup base yet" state is indistinguishable from a real base of 0. If any code path reads `WarmupBaseNote` before the first `Hit` (e.g. the UI showing which notes are warmup, or a partial-sample display), it will report notes 0/1 as warmup even though sampling has not started. Consider resetting to -1 with a `WarmupStarted`-style flag (or documenting that `WarmupBaseNote` is only valid while `Phase != Ready`). `TargetSamples` being preserved is fine since `TrySetTargetSamples` is re-enabled by the `Ready` phase check.

`TryAdd` also rejects non-finite deviations, but that case is reported as `Stray` and, because `LastSampledNote` is not updated, a subsequent valid tap on the *same* note would be accepted — which is the correct behavior. However, a non-finite `songSec` (e.g. NaN from an uninitialized playback position) also makes `AttributedNote` and `Phase` transitions meaningless (`(int)Math.Round(double.NaN)` is an unspecified cast result), yet the first-hit path still sets `WarmupBaseNote` from it. Guard the entry point: reject non-finite `songSec` up front (throw or return `Ignored`) instead of relying on the downstream `TryAdd` fallback, which only catches the sample itself.

if (!_stats.TryAdd(deviation))
            return new HitResult(HitOutcome.Stray, deviation, attributedNote);

comments.content: `Phase`, `TargetSamples`, `_stats` and the note bookkeeping (`WarmupBaseNote`/`LastSampledNote`) are all mutable and unsynchronized. If `Hit` can be invoked from both input handling and the render/audio tick (or from multiple input devices in the same frame), `Count >= TargetSamples` is a check-then-act on `_stats.Count` and can produce more than `TargetSamples` samples or a torn `Phase`. Since this is documented as a shared UI/kernel class, either make `Hit`/`Restart`/`TrySetTargetSamples` guarded (lock or a single-thread-affinity assertion/`Debug.Assert`) or document explicitly that it is not thread-safe and must be driven from the main thread only.

`DeviationMs` / `AttributedNote` are public with no validation, and negative `songSec` is treated as a valid timeline position (`Math.Round` on negative halves rounds away from zero for .5 in some cases / to even otherwise), producing note indices ≤ 0 that can collide with `LastSampledNote = -1` sentinel semantics (`AttributedNote = 0` is fine, but `-1` from `Math.Round(-1.5)` is not distinguishable from "no sample"). Additionally, if `BarSeconds` is extremely small the `songSec / BarSeconds` ratio can overflow `int` on the cast. Validate that `songSec >= 0` (or clamp) and use a checked/saturating cast, or document that negative/invalid times are caller's responsibility.

comments.content: _Process is switched off via SetProcess(false) when the scene settles: after the enter tween callback and in the frozen branch. Nothing guarantees it is switched back on afterwards. ApplyPhase() (called from RestartSampling and from RegisterHit on phase change) only mutates state and never calls SetProcess(true) in the animated path; SetProcess(true) is only reached in the initial/not-animated branch. So with an animated motion profile, after the enter animation finished (or after Complete settled), clicking "再测一次" leaves the loop stopped: lane dim never animates, hit readout fade never runs, stray readout never expires and the strip median fade never advances. Call SetProcess(true) at the start of ApplyPhase.

Touch/click dedup: on platforms where touch emulates mouse (Godot `input_devices/pointing/emulate_mouse_from_touch`, enabled by default) a single tap delivers both an InputEventScreenTouch and a derived InputEventMouseButton. Both branches here register a hit, so the same physical tap is counted twice: the second one becomes a Duplicate (or stray) and the readout is refreshed twice, corrupting the samples this screen exists to measure. React only to non-emulated events, e.g. skip InputEventMouseButton when `Input.IsEmulatingMouseFromTouch()` (or Device == -1), or ignore mouse events while a touch is active.

RestartSampling resets `_sampling` but not `_visualState`, `_swapPhase` or the group alpha. ApplyPhase() only calls SetGroupAlpha on SwapGroup(), which selects the group by `_visualState`, and it is re-evaluated on each call. If a restart or phase change happens while a swap is in FadeOut/FadeIn, the previously faded group is left at alpha 0 forever (and the swapped-in group can change mid-fade), leaving mismatched content or invisible panels. Reset `_swapPhase = Idle`, `_swapElapsed = 0` and both content roots' modulate before calling ApplyPhase.

`_medianFade` is forced to 0 on Complete and then animated only inside the frozen branch of _Process. Combined with the SetProcess(false) paths (see the other finding), if the loop is stopped the strip's MEDIAN line stays invisible forever. Also `_medianFade` is a field declared in the middle of the class (below _Process) which makes the fade contract hard to follow; move it next to the other animation state fields.
comments.existing_code: _medianFade = complete ? 0f : 1f;

comments.content: One-shot timer captured in a lambda: `_navigating` and `_localTransitionBusy` are set true before creating the timer, but if the node leaves the tree or the timer never fires, `NavigateToSettings()` never runs and the screen stays permanently busy with all actions disabled (while the offset was already saved). The callback also never resets the busy flags when it does not navigate. Prefer a Tween/CreateTimer tied to the node and reset busy state on exit/failure.

The stepper gating is written in more than one place: `SetResultActionsEnabled(!_navigating)` followed by `_targetMinus.Disabled = !ready || _navigating` / `_targetPlus.Disabled = ...`, which uses a different formula and can recompute to a conflicting state (e.g. if `_navigating` became true before `ApplyPhase` runs while a tween is in flight). `RefreshReadouts()` also duplicates the strip data assignment (see separate finding). Consolidate the stepper gating into one helper computing the phase/`_navigating` state so the Ready-only lock cannot drift.

A stray tap sets `_lastHitKind = HitReadout.Stray` and `_lastHitMs = 0.0` but never refreshes the label text, so until the next RefreshReadouts (1 second later, at the timer end) the LAST HIT label still shows the previous accepted/warmup number, contradicting the documented "stray tap 的读数显示 —". Call RefreshReadouts() after setting the stray state.

`_stage.QueueRedraw()` runs unconditionally every frame even after Complete has settled (the loop can remain active as long as any fade condition is unmet), redrawing the stage with unchanged content. Cache the last note-progress list and dim value and skip the redraw when they did not change.

Feeding `-remaining * SideDistanceScale` into `MissDistancePx` makes the first miss fallthrough frame jump inconsistently with subsequent stage-px steps. Use `Mathf.Max(0f, -remaining)`, and remove the now-dead `SideDistScale` constant (which is also unused elsewhere) to avoid re-introducing the chart-unit/screen-unit confusion.

comments.content: `SetDepthAlpha` is driven from `UpdateViews` every frame (`v.SetDepthAlpha(v.IsMissFalling || ... || v.Model.Track != Track.Center ? 1f : TopFadeAlpha(v.Position.Y))`), so this call in a host-updated geometry helper is redundant and silently overrides the center-track top-edge depth fade for the frame it runs. It also reads like geometry code mutating alpha state. Either drop it or document why the hold head must bypass the birth-zone fade; keeping both writers for the same property makes future fade changes error-prone.

`clipToJudgeLine` mirrors `track` internally (only to pick the Beyond/intersection line), but the caller (`GameplayNoteRenderer.UpdateLinkView`) then writes the clipped points with `WriteLinkPolygon`/`WriteLinkFrame` using the *raw* `link.Track`, so thickness axis (wa/wb applied along y for side tracks vs x for center) matches — fine. However nothing here clamps `k` to `[0,1]`; `GameplayVisualMapper.ClipToJudgeLine` computes `k = numerator / denominator` and only rejects `b` beyond the line, so a segment whose `a` is beyond by construction (e.g. `anchoredEarlyHold` pinning `a` to `PositionAt(from, 0f)` while the interpolated `a` was past) yields `k` outside `[0,1]` and extrapolates both endpoints and half-widths. Consider asserting/clamping the result here (`wa`/`wb` negative → degenerate polygon) since this wrapper is the single projection chokepoint.

`SongPositionSeconds()` can be called before `StartBeatLoop()` (e.g. a frame where `_draw`/`_process` runs but start has not happened, or after the source was torn down). `CalibrationBeatSource.SongPositionSeconds()` then reads `_clock.ManualFallback` / `_audioReady` while `_clock` and `_beatPlayer` are still `null!`, so it throws a NullReferenceException (or, for the `Time.GetTicksMsec() - _fallbackStartMsec` branch, returns a huge bogus time because `_fallbackStartMsec` is still 0). Song time is `0` before start, so guard it here to make the contract explicit and crash-free.

`Math.Max(0.1, x)`/`Math.Max(0.05, fallSeconds)` do not guard NaN: `Math.Max` returns NaN when either operand is NaN, so a NaN fall-speed multiplier or `fallSeconds` propagates into `FallSeconds`/`speed`, and then into `NoteProgresses`, where the `raw is < 0.0 or > 1.0` guard does not reject NaN (all comparisons with NaN are false) so NaN progress reaches `DrawNote`/`Mathf.Lerp` and breaks the preview. Validate with `double.IsFinite` before clamping and return a sane positive default otherwise.

The two bounds use different rounding: `Ceiling` for the first and `Floor` for the last. The exact-bar-head case (`songSec == N * BarSeconds`) is therefore sampled in both the first sample after the head and, because `raw = (songSec - (head - fall)) / fall == 1.0` there, in the frame at `songSec`. Both are legitimate (the note is exactly on the judgment line), but note the fall window at its very end: `raw == 1.0` is included, so a note is drawn while its head is on the judgment line, and `raw == 0.0` is also included, so it spawns exactly at the top. This means consecutive notes overlap in time at the boundary and that the same visual frame can contain both a `0.0` and a `1.0` note — verify this is the intended rendering semantics, and please add unit tests pinning this boundary behavior (e.g. `songSec = 0`, `songSec = N*BarSeconds`, and `fallSeconds` smaller and larger than `BarSeconds`). Currently there is no test coverage for `NoteProgresses`.

        var lastBar = (int)Math.Floor((songSec + fall) / BarSeconds);

comments.content: `(int)Math.Round(valueMs)` is the real hazard here: `ClampOffset` is public and documented as "clamping", but an unchecked double→int cast for a non-finite/out-of-range value is *undefined behavior* in C# (on x64 it yields `int.MinValue`, in checked contexts it throws). So `ClampOffset(double.PositiveInfinity)`/`NaN`/`1e12` can return `-300` (i.e. flip sign) or throw, instead of clamping. `SuggestedOffsetMs` defensively sanitizes its inputs, but direct callers of `ClampOffset`/`QuantizeOffset` get no such protection (e.g. `QuantizeOffset(NaN)` → NaN). Clamp the double first, then round/cast.
