comments.content: `Advance` accepts any `double` without validation. A NaN/Infinity `rawPositionSeconds` (e.g. from an unstarted/glitched `AudioStreamPlayer` or a NaN loop length path) is stored into `_lastRaw` unchallenged; after that, `rawPositionSeconds < _lastRaw - ...` is always false for NaNs, so rollovers are never detected again and the returned timeline becomes NaN/Infinity forever — silently breaking warmup/note counting with no diagnostic. Reject non-finite input (return the last valid position or throw) rather than corrupting the internal state.

Rollover detection uses `_lastRaw >= 0.0` as the "has a previous frame" sentinel, which conflates "not yet initialized" with "a genuinely valid raw position of exactly 0.0". Two consequences: (1) the very first frame is never treated as a rollover candidate; (2) after `_lastRaw == 0.0`, the *next* frame skips rollover detection, so a real wrap that lands the raw position at ~0 for two consecutive reads (or a first frame that is actually a post-wrap read) is missed — the timeline lags one full loop, so warmup never ends. Use an explicit `bool _hasLast` flag instead of a magic sentinel value. Note also nothing handles a mismatch between the actual stream loop length and `loopSeconds` (a seek/loop-length change will mis-accumulate `_baseSeconds`); worth at least documenting that the stream length must be fixed for the lifetime of the instance.

Firing `Pressed` on mouse/touch DOWN (rather than on release within bounds) diverges from Godot's native `Button` semantics and causes two real problems: (1) a user who presses and drags off the control still commits the action, and (2) for a touch press followed by a mouse-emulated click (or any duplicate event), the same physical tap can emit `Pressed` twice, double-triggering scene transitions. Consider emitting on release only when the release position is still inside `GetRect()` (tracking a `_pressed` flag on down, clearing it on `MouseExited`/out-of-bounds release), or at least ignoring the event when `_pressAmount` is still active / debouncing.

`_Draw` clamps the cut against the CURRENT `Size` (`Mathf.Min(_cut, Mathf.Min(Size.X, Size.Y) * 0.4f)`) and then caches the resulting polygon. The resize handler clears the cache, which is correct today, but the caching contract is implicit and fragile: any future path that changes `Size` without a `NotificationResized` (e.g. setting `Size` before entering the tree, or `Scale`/`PivotOffset` driven layout) will draw a stale polygon. Safer to key the cache on the values it was built from, e.g. store `_cachedSize`/`_cachedCut` and rebuild in `_Draw` when they differ, eliminating the need for `_Notification` bookkeeping.

In the `_disabled` branch `fg` is a fixed dark color (0.35, 0.40, 0.55). For `ButtonStyle.Solid` the button background is `_accent` (cyan), but the disabled branch replaces the fill with a dark color, so this is only consistent because the disabled branch ignores `_styleKind`. Still, the disabled text contrast depends entirely on the hard-coded fill values and is not derived from theme colors (`UiFonts.Text`); on light/accent themes this may become unreadable. Prefer deriving the disabled fg from `UiFonts.Dim`/`UiFonts.Text` so theme changes stay centralized.

Layout edge cases around the text block: (1) When `AlignLeft` is true and the control is narrower than 56px, `textW = Size.X - 56f` becomes negative, which makes `DrawString`'s wrap width invalid (text can be clipped or rendered oddly). (2) In the two-line branch, the glyphs are drawn with `DrawString` using baseline positions computed from `Size.Y * 0.40f + _fontSize * 0.34f`; the last line's baseline is roughly `Size.Y*0.4 + _fontSize*0.34 + subSize + 8`, so a tall `FontSize` (e.g. 40+) or a short button height (~48px) pushes the sub-line below the bottom edge and it gets clipped. Clamp `textW` to a minimum and derive line positions from measured string height (`font.GetStringSize`) instead of constants.
comments.suggestion_code: var textW = Mathf.Max(0f, _alignLeft ? Size.X - 56f : Size.X);

comments.content: `CommitPulse` discards an in-flight pulse by resetting `_commitDuration`/`_commitAmount` to 0, but it does not `QueueRedraw()` in the early-return path, so any previously drawn pulse frame can remain on screen until another redraw happens. Minor, but consider calling `Refresh()` before the non-animated `return`. Also note that `CommitPulse` can be called every frame by a caller (e.g. a focus/hold handler) and would then permanently freeze the pulse at 0 (each call resets `_commitElapsed` to 0 and `_commitAmount` to 0), never producing animation — document/enforce re-entrancy expectations.

`MotionProfile` performs a settings lookup and profile resolution on every access. It is read in `_Process` (every frame, per button), in `_Draw`, in `SetHover`, `TriggerPress` and the setters. On screens with many buttons this is a per-frame dictionary/static-cache look per control and adds GC/branching on a hot path. Cache the profile and invalidate it when the setting changes (the settings object can raise a change event), instead of resolving it each call.

Since this is a pure utility shared by UI state, treat non-positive/non-finite delta as "no time elapsed" (return `current`) and reject non-finite inputs.

The paths that are easiest to regress — `tau <= 0` returning target verbatim, the exact `SnapPixels` boundary (0.5px snaps, 0.51px does not), monotonic convergence and frame-rate independence (one 100ms step ≈ two 50ms steps), and the degenerate delta cases above — should have unit tests, especially since the same model is duplicated in the editor assembly and cross-checking behavior depends on tests rather than shared code.

comments.content: The whole `_Draw` output is derived from `Size`, but nothing invalidates it when the control is resized. `SetAnchorsPreset(FullRect)` (here) and callers that later set `Size` (e.g. `new NeonBackground { Size = UiLayout.DesignSize }`) change `Size` after the first draw, so the background keeps the old dimensions until an unrelated redraw happens. Connect the resized signal (or override `_Notification` for `NotificationResized`) and call `QueueRedraw()`.

The loop step is a hard-coded `120f`, but Godot viewports may run at arbitrary/windowed resolutions, so `half` (= full diagonal) is not bounded by the design resolution. On a 4K-class viewport this is ~2*4400/120 ≈ 73 `DrawLine` calls with antialiasing on every redraw — acceptable, but the line count and dash spacing are not resolution-independent, so the perspective-line density visibly changes with window size. Prefer a step derived from the diagonal (e.g. a fixed number of evenly spaced offsets) so the visual density is stable, and skip the pass entirely when `half` is not positive.

There is no guard for a degenerate/zero size. Before the first layout settles `Size` may be `(0, 0)`, in which case the three glow circles get radius 0 (drawing zero-radius circles) and the line loop below is skipped only implicitly. More importantly, a `(0, height)` transient produces a vertical band of lines/lines of zero length. Adding an early return for non-positive sizes both avoids wasted draw commands and makes the intent explicit.

The opaque `UiFonts.Bg` rect is drawn over the entire control, but the glow-3 circle radius is `size.X * 0.28f` — i.e. the visual content does not cover the whole rect. If this control is ever combined with a parent clip or drawn with a partial redraw region, stale pixels from the previous size/frame can remain along the trailing edge (this ties into the missing resize invalidation above). Either guarantee full-control redraws by overriding `_Draw` only after a full `QueueRedraw` from resize, or explicitly cover the control rect via `clip_contents`/`DrawRect` before the glow lines (already done for the base fill) so partial updates cannot leave artifacts.

comments.content: `_frozenTag` is never registered for the entrance animation (unlike every other control built here). It is invisible during the intro, so this is harmless today, but `PrepareEnterAnimation` records base positions only for registered items while `PlayEnterAnimation` tween-drives registered items in parallel — if this label ever becomes visible during/after the intro it will skip the staggered shift/fade and appear abruptly, inconsistent with the rest of the stage group. Register it with `EnterGroup.Stage` for consistency (hiding happens via `CommitPhaseVisuals`, so registering it is safe).

`TapZone` is derived from `(StageX, LaneTop, StageWidth, LaneBandHeight)`, i.e. it is assumed to sit strictly below the header (y=120) and strictly above the bottom strip (y=956). Nothing enforces this: if `LaneTop`/`LaneBandHeight` (or `BarHeight`, `StripY`) are edited, taps silently land on the header/back button area or the bottom strip, which the XML doc explicitly claims cannot happen. A cheap build-time invariant (e.g. `Debug.Assert` in `BuildStage`, or a static ctor check comparing against `BarHeight` and `StripY`) would turn a silent input-routing regression into a loud failure.

comments.content: The Newton loop and the bisection fallback are coupled incorrectly. When Newton exits via the `slope < epsilon` break (which happens for curves like `Exit` where the derivative is ~0 near t=0/t=1), `parameter` may already have been clamped to the boundary, and worse, the bisection phase assumes `[0,1]` brackets the root but starts from `low = 0, high = 1` *without* resetting `parameter` to a valid bracket state (it only uses `parameter` as the first probe). More concretely, the Newton step is allowed to escape its bracket, so the final 8 bisection iterations can converge to a sub-optimal point (8 iterations of bisection give only ~1/256 resolution ~ 0.0039, coarser than the 1e-5 epsilon used as the “done” condition). The two tolerances are inconsistent: the early-out claims 1e-5 accuracy, but the fallback cannot achieve it. Also the derivative guard `Math.Abs(slope) < 0.00001f` breaks out on slopes that are small but perfectly serviceable (e.g. 1e-6 with a moderately sized error), needlessly discarding the fast path. Consider bracketing Newton properly (bisect only within the current bracket, use a larger slope guard, and run more bisection iterations or until the bracket width itself is below epsilon).

NaN (and +/-Infinity is handled by clamp only for infinities) slips through: `Math.Clamp(float.NaN, 0f, 1f)` returns NaN, the `is <= 0f or >= 1f` check is false for NaN, and NaN then flows into the solver producing NaN output that will poison every downstream Lerp (transforms/colors go NaN and the node may disappear indefinitely). This is a public helper called from many screens, so a single divide-by-zero or uninitialized duration upstream yields NaN. Guard it explicitly and return a safe value.

The public `CubicBezier` accepts arbitrary control points but assumes the x control points lie in [0,1] so that `Sample(t,x1,x2)` is monotonic and the bisection bracket `[0,1]` is valid. CSS permits x outside [0,1]? No — CSS restricts x1/x2 to [0,1] while y may overshoot; but this method does not validate that, and callers (e.g. `SongCardMotion.cs`) pass literal values. If an x outside [0,1] is ever supplied, the x-curve is no longer monotonic and the solver can return incorrect/non-monotonic results. Either validate x1/x2 (throw or clamp) or document the precondition in the XML doc.

comments.content: The semantic curves are compiled into `tools/core-tests` (see `CoreTests.csproj`) but there is no test file exercising them. Since every animation in the UI depends on these curves and the solver is hand-rolled, a regression (e.g. in the Newton/bisection tolerance, or a changed control point) would silently alter all animation feel without any failing test. Add unit tests asserting: endpoint mapping (0→0, 1→1), monotonic non-decreasing output across the domain for each named curve, and approximate known values (e.g. `Standard(0.5f)`). The `Exit`/`Signal` curves are especially worth testing because their zero-derivative endpoints stress the solver fallback.

`progress` is used directly in `Mathf.Lerp`/`Mathf.InverseLerp` without validation. The upstream producer applies `Math.Max(0.05, fallSeconds)` and a range filter that NaN slips through, so a non-finite or out-of-range value can draw the note outside the lane band and drive `glow` beyond [0,1] (halo alpha > intended). Since this is a public settable property consumed from another file, clamp here as the last line of defence.

`CalibrationStrip` does not validate its numeric inputs: a NaN `Samples` entry makes `x` NaN (invalid draw), an out-of-range value draws bars outside the strip (over the panel border), and a NaN/non-finite `MedianMs` produces a NaN marker position and a garbage label (`MEDIAN +NaN ms`) or places the marker outside the strip. Clamp/skip non-finite values before mapping, and clamp both samples and the median to ±`MaxAcceptedDeviationMs`.

When the final step lands only when easing is not exactly 1 (e.g. `UiEase.Standard` returns 0.9999f for float precision at raw == 1.0), the settle branch forces `_fade = 1f` but `changed` was computed against the pre-clamped `next`, so it may return `false` even though the exposed `Fade` jumped to 1. The caller (`CalibrationScreen`) only re-applies `Modulate` when `AdvanceFade` returns true, so the label can be left mid-fade (e.g. alpha 0.9999). Compute `changed` after the settle clamp, or force `changed = true` in the settle branch.

`BeginFade` runs before `_Ready` in some paths? Either way, `BeginFade`/`AdvanceFade` call `profile.HoverDuration` but nothing guards a zero duration. `UiMotionProfile.Off` has `HoverDuration == 0.0`, and while `IsAnimated` is false for `Off`, the `Reduced` profile's durations are non-zero but user-configurable. More importantly, if `HoverDuration` is 0 while `IsAnimated` is true, `_elapsed / 0.0` yields `+Infinity` (or NaN for `0/0`), clamped to 1 → fade jumps immediately with no visible animation. Add a defensive `if (profile.HoverDuration <= 0.0)` fast-path to snap to 1.

Setting `Disabled = true` mid-hover leaves `_hover = true` and the hover fade stuck at its hovered value (the `_Draw` uses the fade value when animated, ignoring `_disabled`), and re-enabling while the pointer is still over the control leaves it visually un-hovered because no new `MouseEntered` fires. Reset `_hover` and restart the fade (or `SetProcess(true)`) when transitioning to disabled so a disabled control never renders the hover colour.

`AcceptEvent()` is only called on the press-down event; the matching release (`Pressed: false`) and mouse-motion events still propagate. `CalibrationScreen._UnhandledInput` only reacts to `Pressed: true`, so the tap is not double-counted, but downstream UI handlers that react to releases can see an unpaired event. Also, the button has no focus handling, so while `MouseFilter` defaults to `Stop`, the control silently swallows events that Godot's `BaseButton` would normally route. Consider also consuming the release for symmetry (mirror the same pattern in both `StepperButton` and `HoverLabel`).

`DrawDashed` has no guard for non-positive `dash`/`gap`. If `dash <= 0` or `gap <= 0`, then `remaining` starts at <=0, `step = Mathf.Min(remaining, length - walked)` becomes <=0, `walked` never advances and the inner `while` spins forever (UI freeze). It is only safe today because all call sites pass positive values derived from `u` (`size/26`), but `size` comes from callers such as `GlyphIcon._Draw` where `Size.X` could be 0 giving `u = 0` -> `dash = 0` -> infinite loop. Also `width` could become 0 making the dash invisible. Add an early guard.

`size` is not validated: `u = size / 26f`, so `size <= 0` (e.g. a `Control` whose `Size.X` is 0 on the first `_Draw`, or a minimized/hidden layout) yields `u <= 0` and any `width` yields `w <= 0`. Negative/zero line widths make strokes invisible or degenerate, and `u = 0` propagates into `DrawDashed` as the zero-dash infinite-loop case. Either guard `size <= 0` by returning early, or clamp `u`/`w` to a small positive minimum.

Every glyph draw allocates: `List<Vector2>`/arrays in the `Bleed`, `Mirror`, `Auto`, `Funnel` cases (`outline.ToArray()`, collection expressions `[P(...), ...]` creating new arrays). Since `UiGlyphs.Draw` is called from `Control._Draw`, which is re-invoked on every redraw/resize (and `GlyphIcon` sits inside hover/selection-driven widgets), this causes GC churn on the UI thread. Consider reusing a static/thread-local scratch `List<Vector2>` cleared per call, and caching the immutable path arrays per glyph kind (they only depend on `topLeft`/`u`, so cache by kind and offset by `topLeft` when drawing).

comments.content: Closure of the Bleed outline relies on the arc's last point exactly hitting `P(5, 17)`, the start of the second cubic. The loop runs `i = 0..arcSteps` with `t = Pi*i/arcSteps`, so at `i = arcSteps`, `t = Pi` => `P(13,17) + (-1, ~0)*8u` = `P(5,17)` only up to floating-point rounding of `Mathf.Sin(Mathf.Pi)` (~1e-7); the second cubic `SampleCubic` starts at `i=1`, so it never re-adds `P(5,17)` and the visual join is fine but the returned outline's last point is `P(13,3)` from the second cubic, not a closed loop. Then `DrawPolyline(..., antialiased: true)` does not close the path, so the top vertex at `P(13,3)` is fine but the tiny Y offset (~1e-5 px) can create a hairline notch. Prefer explicitly appending the exact shared endpoints (`P(13,3)` and `P(5,17)`) instead of depending on trig identity, or add a `closed` call by re-appending `outline[0]`.

`DrawDashed`'s state machine can go negative and double-toggle: `remaining` is decremented by `step` and the `if (remaining <= 0.0001f)` check can flip even when `step` was clamped to exactly fill the remaining length (two adjacent toggles for zero-length draws), and if `remaining` ever starts `<= 0` the inner loop spins forever. Use `remaining = Mathf.Max(0f, remaining - step)` and a consistent epsilon, and reject non-positive `dash`/`gap` up front. Also, when a dash straddles a segment boundary the two independently antialiased `DrawLine` calls meet at the shared vertex with a visible seam (notably at the Auto rounded-rect corners); consider a small overlap or a single polyline pass.

There are no tests for the geometry helpers. Boundary conditions worth covering: `size = 0`, negative `width`, a single-point path in `DrawDashed`, zero/negative `dash`/`gap`, and the Bleed outline closure (first == last sampled vertex) and Auto rounded-rect closure (`path[0] == path[^1]` modulo the duplicated `P(3+radius, 3)`). The default arm `_ => Full` silently maps any unrecognized `UiMotionMode` value (new enum member added later, or an out-of-range cast like `(UiMotionMode)42`) to the most expensive profile — full motion, loop, echo. This masks bugs and is the least safe fallback for accessibility modes. Since the enum is closed and only 3 values exist, list `UiMotionMode.Full` explicitly and let the default arm fall back to `Off` (or throw), so unknown values cannot accidentally enable motion.

`Apply` has no argument validation. It is a public entry point called directly with arbitrary `Font` values (e.g. `UiLabels.Apply(_title, UiFonts.Cjk, ...)`), and `UiFonts.Tech`/`TechBold` are `GD.Load<Font>` results that return `null` when the asset path is wrong or the font is not yet available. Passing `null` into `AddThemeFontOverride` silently overrides the theme's default font with a null resource, degrading to invisible/incorrect text with no error — hard to diagnose. Guard here (skip the font override when `font` is null) or fail loudly, and validate `label` for null so caller mistakes surface immediately instead of a generic NRE deep in Godot. Also, `size` is unvalidated: a 0/negative size produces invisible labels through every named variant; consider asserting `size > 0`.

`Cjk` replaces the label's font wholesale with a `SystemFont` whose `FontNames` list relies on fonts installed on the host machine (`Microsoft YaHei`, `PingFang SC`, `Noto Sans CJK SC`, `sans-serif`). On platforms without any of these (minimal Linux/SteamOS images, containers, some CI runners) there is no fallback and CJK strings render as tofu boxes. Additionally, because the whole font is swapped rather than a fallback chain being added, mixed Latin+CJK strings lose the SpaceGrotesk Latin glyphs used elsewhere, so typography is inconsistent. Prefer keeping the Tech font as primary and appending the CJK font to its `Fallbacks` (or bundling Noto Sans SC) instead of replacing the font outright.

When a motion mode with `AllowLoop == false` is active, `_elapsed` keeps growing while redraws stop, so nothing is redrawn — but more importantly the frame is only ever repainted if something else invalidates the control (e.g. a resize or a later switch back to Full). Explicitly request a redraw when the profile's `AllowLoop` value changes (cache the last profile/mode and compare) so the accessibility state is actually applied.

Consider reducing segments (24-32 is ample at these radii), lowering the redraw rate (e.g. throttle to ~30 FPS for the loop), or drawing the static parts (metal arcs/constraint arms) once into a cached canvas/texture and only animating the glowing elements.

Wrap `_pulseTime` modulo the pulse period (`Mathf.Tau * 3f / 4f` scaled) or use `Mathf.Wrap`/fmod.

When motion mode changes from Off to Reduced/Full, `_staticFrameApplied` is reset and playback resumes — but if the player was stopped while a previous state left `SpeedScale` at the Off/normal value, calling `Play(_clipName, -1.0, speed, false)` with an explicit speed is fine. However, when the mode changes Reduced→Full (or vice versa) while playing, `_motionPlayer.SpeedScale = speed` is only reached in the `else` branch — good — but `Play` uses `customBlend = false` and passes a `-1` duration; that is okay. The real risk is that `Play(..., fromEnd: false)` restarts the clip from time 0 with no fade, so a user toggling Off→Full snaps the model abruptly to frame 0 rather than resuming. If a smooth resume is desired, restore the previous playback position instead of restarting. Also `_motionPlayer.SpeedScale = speed` is assigned every frame while playing, which is redundant (see per-frame work note).

The camera fit math only accounts for elevation (`Cos/Sin(elevation)`) but ignores the azimuth component for the horizontal extent, i.e. the projected width should be `size.X * cos(azimuth) + size.Z * sin(azimuth)`, not just `size.X / 2`. With the configured 22° azimuth the camera is off-axis, so `halfHorizontal` under-estimates the projected width and the model can be clipped on the sides (also the vertical term ignores X/Z cross terms). Compute the extents from the actual camera orientation (e.g. project the AABB corners into camera space) for a robust fit.

comments.content: `ComputeAabb` recurses only into direct children and `MeshInstance3D`s, and it never stops recursion at hidden nodes; more importantly, at the time it runs (`CallDeferred` in `_Ready`) the model may not yet have a valid global transform chain if it is parented under a scene still being attached. Since `GetAabb()` returns the local AABB, `GlobalTransform * GetAabb()` is correct, but the loop does not handle `MultiMeshInstance3D` or `GPUParticles3D` and silently ignores any non-Node3D wrappers. Also `aabb = new Aabb()` initialised then immediately replaced by `first` flag — fine — but there is no version that accounts for animated poses (the animation may move meshes outside the bind-pose AABB, causing the model to clip during playback). Consider using the animation's trimmed bounds or including a safety margin for animated parts.

`modelScene.Instantiate<Node3D>()` will throw (or return null / print error) if the root of the GLB is not a Node3D — `Instantiate<T>` raises an error via `GD.PushError` and returns null when the cast fails. The returned value is not null-checked before `model.Name = ...` / `root.AddChild(model)`, so a mismatched asset crashes the home screen. Add a null check and add the generic `Instantiate()` with a type check instead. Same pattern applies to `_haloMaterial.Shader is null` which is checked but then returns with `halo` never added, leaving partial state (the shader load also occurs after the TextureRect is constructed).

Setting `BackgroundMode = BGMode.Color` with a fully transparent `BackgroundColor` means the `Sky` assigned below is never used as the background or for reflections — but `ReflectedLightSource = Sky` and `AmbientLightSource` are set expecting the sky material's radiance. In Godot, reflection from sky works via the sky radiance map regardless of background mode, so `Sky` reflection still resolves, but the `ProceduralSkyMaterial` colors set here (sky top/horizon/ground) only contribute to reflections/ambient, while the actual visible background is transparent. This looks unintended (the sky colors are dead when BackgroundMode is Color transparent) — either use `BGMode.Sky` for reflections-only via `ReflectionSource.Sky` explicitly or drop the unused Sky configuration; otherwise future maintainers may assume the sky is visible.

comments.content: `delta` is not validated. If the game is paused/unpaused or the window is dragged, `delta` can spike and `_pulseTime` jumps, and when `delta` is NaN/infinite the shader parameter becomes NaN, producing a black/artefact halo. Other systems in this codebase guard with `double.IsFinite(delta)` (see ResultScreen). Add a `if (!double.IsFinite(delta) || delta <= 0) return;` (or clamp) for robustness.

CREDITS / LOGIN are documented as permanently disabled placeholders (grey, non-interactive, no route, no arrow), yet they are still passed to `register`, which puts them into Main's entrance-animation list. Every home entry re-runs the fade/directional motion on two dead labels, adding elements the navigation layer has to care about and keeping "disabled-but-present" affordances alive. Since they are purely decorative, either build them without `register` (or with a separate static/decor layer) or drop them entirely until a real route exists. Additionally, nothing in this helper stops these placeholder labels from later becoming focusable if the MouseFilter is relaxed — a guard (e.g. `FocusMode = Control.FocusModeEnum.None`) would make the "no input" intent explicit rather than implicit through MouseFilter only.

The build description is rendered into a fixed 616x18 label with no clipping, autowrap, or ellipsis. Godot's Label does not clip by default (`clip_text = false`), so the longest known string ("v0.1.2 · INTERNAL TESTDATA · DO NOT DISTRIBUTE", ~43 chars at font size 11) may render wider than 616 and overflow to the left of the intended footer band, or overlap other content, rather than being truncated. Enable clipping and/or handle overflow explicitly, e.g. `label.ClipText = true`, or truncate long descriptions with an ellipsis before assigning `Text`.

`buildDescription` is used unconditionally. `BuildDescription()` in Main falls back to "UNCLASSIFIED EXPORT" so it never returns empty today, but this helper is public-internal API: if a caller passes `null`/whitespace, Label renders a blank fixed-height footer band and the build-identity failure is silently hidden (the footer looks intentionally empty). Add an explicit guard, e.g. fall back to a visible placeholder such as "v? · UNKNOWN BUILD" (or throw) when the input is null/whitespace, so a missing version can never pass as normal.

The three label rectangles are hardcoded magic coordinates (1512/62, 1670/58, 1240/1020) tied to the 1920x1080 reference canvas, and the vertical anchors for CREDITS (y=62, h=18 → bottom 80) and LOGIN (y=58, h=20 → bottom 78) are inconsistent, so the two items on the same row will not share a baseline. Named constants (as done in HomeActions/HomeBrandBlock) or a single row layout computed from a shared baseline would remove the drift and make later layout tweaks safe.

comments.content:
Redo cannot undo an already-committed change. `EndGesture()` pushes the changed gesture onto `_undo` and clears `_redo`; then `PushBounded(_undo, _current)` adds a second, identical entry. After that redo, a single `Undo()` restores `_current` to the redo target and leaves `IsDirty == true`, so the applied baseline is lost until a second undo runs. This also contradicts the stated contract that a gesture is one history step.

Concrete counterexample:
1. `SetColor(...)` (creates undo entry A0), `Undo()` → `_undo` empty, `_redo = [A1]`, at A0.
2. `BeginGesture(); SetColor(...)` (now at B1). `CanRedo == false` (GestureChanged), so calling `Redo()` returns false with no state change.
3. `EndGesture()` commits B1: `_undo = [A0]`, `_redo` cleared.
4. Call `Redo()` again: `CanRedo == true`, `EndGesture()` is a no-op, then `PushBounded(_undo, _current)` adds B1 again, and `Pop(_redo)` moves history to the pre-redo state → the redo history entry is duplicated.

Fix: `Redo()` should not push the current state to `_undo` after a no-op `EndGesture()`. If the live gesture is supposed to block redo, `CanRedo` must also exclude redo when a gesture is open (or the gesture must be committed before `_redo` is consulted), and the extra `PushBounded` should be removed since `EndGesture()` already records the post-gesture state.

The redo-clear branch is only reached when `EndGesture` runs inside `Undo()`, which then immediately pops `_undo` and pushes the current state onto `_redo`. That means the user's previously valid redo branch is silently discarded. E.g. undo, then start a drag and undo again: the pre-drag redo items are gone, and `_redo` now only holds the post-drag state. This is consistent with "a new change clears redo", but it is surprising for the `Undo()` caller, which expects undo to be reversible. Consider having `Undo()` bypass `EndGesture`'s redo clearing by routing through the same history-management helper, so a gesture that is undone immediately does not destroy an unrelated redo stack. Either way, please add a test covering "begin gesture → change → Undo" ordering.

`CanUndo` includes an uncommitted gesture (`GestureChanged`), but `IsDirty` does not. So `_current` can differ from `_applied` while `IsDirty` is false. A caller that enables save/apply only on `IsDirty` will not persist a live drag, and `AcceptApplied()` calls `EndGesture()` first: it commits the in-progress gesture into `_undo` and then sets `_applied` to the gesture-final state, so the baseline and history become out of sync with respect to the UI gesture (a subsequent `Undo` jumps to the pre-gesture state instead of the pre-(post-accept) state). Document this contract explicitly, or make `IsDirty` consistent with `CanUndo`.

comments.content: `ResetSlot` calls `ReplaceSlot` without passing an `activeIndex`, so it keeps the current selection. That is intended by the XML doc. However, if `slot` is currently empty, it returns false, which is right. Still, note that `ResetSlot(0)` resets slot 0 to factory colors while `ResetColor` also resets the *active slot*. Consistency looks fine, but there is no guard preventing `_factoryColors` from being mutated later (it is a private raw array stored in the draft). `NormalizeColors` returns a fresh array, so today it is safe, but `ClearSlot` and `ResetSlot` hand this same array instance to `new PaletteSlotSnapshot`, whose ctor does `Array.AsReadOnly(Colors.ToArray())`. That is a defensive copy, so OK. No action required beyond confirming this stays true.

`nowMsec + Msec` can wrap around on `ulong` when `nowMsec` is within `Msec` of `ulong.MaxValue`. In that case `Until` returns a tiny value, `Blocks(nowMsec, unlockMsec)` becomes `nowMsec < unlockMsec` → false, and the 120 ms anti-passthrough window silently disappears. Although Godot's `Time.GetTicksMsec()` would take centuries to get there, the helper is public/pure and its documented contract (`now + Msec`) is broken at the wrap point. Saturate instead:

```csharp
public static ulong Until(ulong nowMsec) =>
    nowMsec > ulong.MaxValue - Msec ? ulong.MaxValue : nowMsec + Msec;
```

comments.content: The window is exclusive at `unlockMsec`: the tick exactly equal to `unlockMsec` unblocks. Also note `Blocks` cannot distinguish "guard expired" from "unlockMsec never set"; callers passing a default `0` unlock value get `false` (unblocked), which is the permissive failure mode. Please document the semantics explicitly in the doc comment (e.g. "blocked while `nowMsec < unlockMsec`; the unlock tick itself is allowed").

comments.content: `AmbientFrameIndex` returns 29 (the last entry frame) both when the atlas failed to load and during the brief window before `Poll()` completes — different meanings collapsed into one value, and this idle-frame behavior is implicit. For a non-loaded atlas, returning `29` while `At(29)` falls back to `_still` is only safe because `At` checks `_frame`; make the intent explicit (e.g. return a named `IdleFrameIndex` constant and early-return when not loaded) and document that callers must treat it as frame 29 of the idle pose.

The long-press flow has several real correctness problems:

1. **Long-press then tap fires BOTH menu and selection.** When `_Process` reaches `LongPressSeconds` it emits `MenuRequested` and clears `_holding`, but the matching release still arrives and calls `EndHold()`, which emits `Chosen` (a long press commonly ends outside the control, so this selects a slot *and* opens the context menu). A flag must be set when the menu is emitted so the subsequent release is swallowed.
2. **`Chosen` fires even when the release happens outside the slot.** `_GuiInput` with default `MouseFilter.Stop` keeps receiving the release after the pointer leaves the control, and there is no position check, so dragging off a slot still selects it — inconsistent with `TechButton`'s inside-on-release semantics.
3. **Mouse and touch releases are not matched to the press.** Any left-button release or any `ScreenTouch` release ends the hold, regardless of which pointer started it (a second finger's release cancels a hold begun by the first). At minimum, filter `Canceled` (a canceled press currently counts as a release and emits `Chosen`) and track the owning touch index.

A single guarded state-machine (owner = mouse/touch index, `longPressed` flag, release-inside check) is needed; the current code can emit neither, one, or both signals depending on pointer motion and timing.

The key release is consumed here (`SetInputAsHandled` and return) even when it is not an activation-capable key event, and more importantly `_keyOwner` is never cleared when `_Input` bails out earlier because `CanInteract` became false — that path calls `CancelInteraction()` so it is fine — but the bigger issue is the mirror of the mouse path: a key release is accepted for ANY keyboard device, including emulated input, because `_keyDevice` is recorded from the press but `InputEvent.DeviceIdEmulation` is not excluded at press time in `_GuiInput`. Emulated key presses (e.g., from automation/replay) can therefore drive the button and emit `Pressed`, whereas pointer input is deliberately blocked for emulation. Add `key.Device == InputEvent.DeviceIdEmulation` rejection in `_GuiInput`.

`FinishInteraction(HasFocus())` will emit `Pressed` on the key *release* even if the key press was followed by focus loss inside the same frame or the release arrives after the control was disabled (the `CanInteract` guard is re-checked inside `FinishInteraction`, which covers the disabled case). However, there is no `key.Canceled` check: a canceled key (OS/focus change) is treated as a normal release and activates the button. Add `key.Canceled` to the release handling and call `CancelInteraction()` instead, mirroring the pointer path's `Update.Cancel`.

`HeldChanged` balance issue for momentary buttons: `Momentary` setter calls `CancelInteraction()` *before* assigning `_momentary`, which is correct, but `_held` is only ever reset in `CancelInteraction`. If a consumer toggles `Momentary` from false to true while a pointer is being held, `CancelInteraction` runs (no `_held` set, fine). The real gap is `BeginInteraction`: for momentary buttons it emits `HeldChanged(true)` but `FinishInteraction` calls `CancelInteraction()` which emits `HeldChanged(false)` — good. Verify by inspection that every `_held = true` has a paired `CancelInteraction`; the current code is consistent, but note `_ExitTree`/`_Notification`/`Enabled` all funnel through `CancelInteraction`, so this is fine. No action needed if confirmed elsewhere.

Add `CancelHold()` to `_ExitTree`/`_Notification(VisibilityChanged)`.

comments.content: `Shader` resources are `Resource`-derived and Godot objects; creating one inside a static field initialiser runs at class-load time (possibly before the Godot runtime/scripting context for a given engine instance is fully ready) and it is never disposed. For hot-reload / editor re-entry this can leak the previous instance, and if the shader fails to compile there is no diagnostics because `GetShaderRid`/`Shader.SetCode` errors are silent. Prefer creating the `Shader` inside `_Ready` (assign and `Dispose` in `_ExitTree` if not shared), or at minimum create it via `GD.Load<Shader>`/`Shader.SetCode` in `_Ready` and check `GetShaderRid().IsValid`.

If `SvField` is ever re-entered (`_Ready` may be called again after an `_EnterTree` cycle, e.g. reparenting), `_Ready` unconditionally `AddChild`s new `_surface`/`_ring` nodes without removing the previous ones — duplicate children accumulate and the `_material` is recreated. Guard with `if (_surface.GetParent() == null)` / `if (!IsAncestorOf(_surface))`, or create these children in the constructor instead of `_Ready`. Additionally, the `ShaderMaterial` is never disposed on `_ExitTree`.

Unbalanced `DragStarted`/`DragEnded`: `DragStarted` is emitted immediately after `TryBegin`, then the code re-checks `_pointer.Active`/`IsVisibleInTree()` and may `return` before applying/starting the drag. If a consumer's `DragStarted` handler calls `CancelInteraction()` (e.g. it pushes an undo snapshot and something re-layouts), `_pointer.Reset()` emits `DragEnded` *inside* `EmitSignal(DragStarted)` — reentrancy where the end fires before the start's own emit returns. More simply, if `IsVisibleInTree()` turns false between emit and the re-check, the pointer stays active with no `SetProcessInput`-driven end until a later release. Start the drag and apply the first position *before* emitting `DragStarted`, or capture-then-emit in a state that guarantees `DragEnded` follows exactly once. Same pattern in `SvField._GuiInput`.

`TryBegin` accepts an `InputEventScreenTouch` press with `Pressed: true` but does not check `Canceled: false` — unlike the `InputEventMouseButton` pattern just above it. A canceled touch press (Godot can deliver `Pressed=true, Canceled=true` when the touch is canceled by the OS before it registers) would then start a gesture whose only matching read is `Pressed=true, Canceled=true`, which `Read` maps to `Update.Cancel` — so it is recoverable, but it still briefly acquires the pointer and, for `SvField`/`HueBar`, emits `DragStarted` then immediately `DragEnded`. Add `Canceled: false` to the pattern for symmetry and to avoid spurious start/end pairs.

`Read` returns `Update.None` for a `InputEventMouseButton` release with a matching device but does not verify the release is for the same button as the press — the pattern does check `ButtonIndex: MouseButton.Left`, matching the press, so OK. However `InputEventScreenDrag`/`InputEventScreenTouch` events from *other* devices (e.g. a second touch device) are filtered by `e.Device != _device` which is correct. One remaining concern: mouse `InputEventMouseMotion` with `ButtonMask` cleared returns `Update.Cancel` and the caller `FinishInteraction(false)` — that is intended. No change needed beyond the `Canceled` note above.

`_pairOrder` has exactly 5 elements (6 channels minus the current one), so `_pairOrder[0..1]` is currently safe. However, nothing guarantees that contract: `_pairOrder` is initialized to the empty array (`private int[] _pairOrder = [];` in NoteColorsScreen.cs) and `RefreshObservation` indexes `_pairOrder[0]` (line 204) unconditionally. If the channel count ever changes (or `Refresh` is reached without a prior `RefreshObservation`), this throws `IndexOutOfRangeException`. Also, `_pairButtons[i]` is indexed assuming exactly two comparison buttons exist. Add a cheap guard/defensive loop bound so a degenerate order fails gracefully instead of crashing the screen.

`_pairOrder[0]` is dereferenced without checking for an empty order (see the guard comment below). Additionally, `_pairOverride` is validated only against `!= _channel`; it is never validated against the palette range or against membership in `_pairOrder`. A stale override carried across a preset/slot switch whose palette has a different channel layout would index `palette.Get((NoteColorChannel)pair)` (line 205) and `Types[pair]` with an out-of-range value. Validate the override (0 <= requested < Names.Length && requested != _channel, ideally `_pairOrder.Contains(requested)`) before use, and fall back to `_pairOrder[0]` when the order is empty.

However, `DrawSetTransform` is called *after* the early return, and in Godot every `_Draw` invocation is expected to be stateless per frame — if any later code path (or the container's own drawing) relies on the default transform being in effect, the explicit `DrawSetTransform(Vector2.Zero, 0f, Vector2.One)` reset at the end is the only guarantee, and it will be skipped if anything between set/reset throws (e.g. a bad polygon). comments.content: `Present` clears neither `_wordmark.Scale`, `_wordmark.Modulate`, nor the stale `_halo`/material state before starting. On a second run (retry from the results screen re-enters `ResultFlow` → `Present`), the node is still holding the previous run's transform/alpha until `ApplyFrame()` runs — which it does immediately here, so Scale/Modulate are fine. But `Visible = tex is not null` (see previous comment) and, more importantly, `_wordmark.Texture` from a previous outcome can briefly persist if the new load returns `null` (Godot does not clear the old texture when the load fails). Explicitly reset `_wordmark.Texture = null` (and `Material = null`, `Scale = Vector2.One`, `Modulate = Colors.White`) at the top of `Present` so a failed load can never show the previous outcome's wordmark. Also `HaloOf`'s `_` fallback returns `DefaultHalo` for `None`, while the wordmark is hidden — harmless today but worth a comment tying it to `HasWordmark`.

Fixed after the `_material ??=` line. If `GD.Load<Shader>` returns `null` (shader file missing from the export or renamed), `ShaderMaterial { Shader = null }` is constructed and cached. `SetShaderParameter` on a material with a null shader is silently ignored in Godot (or logs an error), and because `_material` is now non-null, every subsequent `Present` will keep reusing the broken material — the wordmark renders unshaded (or invisible) with no warning and no path to recovery. Validate the shader load and fall back to leaving `_wordmark.Material = null` (unshaded plain texture) rather than caching a shaderless material.

`ApplyFrame` is also called from `_Input` immediately after `_timeline.Skip()`. `Skip()` sets `Elapsed = Duration`, so `MarkScale` is 1.0 and `MarkAlpha` is 1.0 — fine. But when `HasWordmark` is false (`_timeline` is `Plain`), the block is skipped entirely, so on a *second* run with `HasWordmark == false` the wordmark retains whatever `Scale`/`Modulate` the previous run left (the node stays `Visible = false`, so invisible, but the stale values are a latent trap). Reset the wordmark's `Scale`/`Modulate` unconditionally in `ApplyFrame` (or in `Present`) rather than inside the `HasWordmark` branch. Also, `QueueRedraw()` is called every frame including from `_Input`, which can double-redraw in the same frame — harmless but worth noting; the `_Draw` body early-returns when `_timeline is null`, so first-frame safety is already covered.

Non-Full modes are handled inconsistently: Reduced is special-cased in every accessor, but Off is not. For `Mode == Off`, `Duration` is 0 and `Elapsed` is always 0, yet `DimAlpha` evaluates to `Smooth01(0 / 0.30) == 0`, `BandAlpha` to `Smooth01(-0.04/0.24) == 0` and `MarkAlpha` to 0. That happens to be harmless for drawing (Off never renders a prelude frame), but `Glow` still returns `GlowBase` (0.85) for Off, which is a non-zero prelude light value leaking into a mode that claims to be inert. Since all these outputs are documented as "pure functions of Elapsed", make Off explicit (e.g. early-return terminal/zero values) so callers cannot accidentally sample a prelude-glow value in Off.

`EaseOutBack` deliberately over- and under-shoots (with c1 = 1.35 it peaks above 1.0 and dips below 0.0 mid-curve), so `MarkScale` can briefly exceed `StampScaleFrom` (≈1.66) and also grow *after* the peak while opacity is already committed. This is intended bounce, but the file gives no bound and no test asserts the range (`SkipAndInvalidDeltas` only checks the final 1.0). At minimum document the intended overshoot ceiling here so a future clamp of `StampProgress`/`Lerp` doesn't silently break the bounce, and add a test asserting `MarkScale` stays within the intended band across the full stamp window.

`Energy` never converges exactly to `EnergyFloor`: after a `Skip()` (Elapsed == Duration == 1.55) the decay factor is `exp(-0.95*7) ≈ 1.3e-3`, so `Energy ≈ 1.0027` rather than the documented terminal 1.0. More importantly, `Advance` clamps `Elapsed` at `Duration`, so the decay can never run to completion (it needs several seconds), meaning the stable hand-off frame keeps a residual energy offset from whichever frame the countdown happened to end on. If the shader or host samples `Energy` right at completion expecting `EnergyFloor`, that expectation is violated. Either snap to `EnergyFloor` once `IsComplete` (or once the decay factor is below an epsilon), or document that Energy is intentionally asymptotic at hand-off.

`ResultRunSequence` is a plain mutable-flag object with no synchronization or owner validation. The check-then-set on `_preludeCompleted` is not atomic; if the timer callback and the skip/input callback fire on different threads (or re-entrantly from within the same delivery), both can observe `false` and both return `true`, double-delivering the result screen — exactly the guarantee the class exists to provide. The file gives no thread-affinity contract. Either document/enforce single-thread usage (e.g. Godot main thread only, assert with `System.Threading.Thread` check) or use `Interlocked.Exchange`/`Interlocked.CompareExchange` on an int flag so the gate is genuinely one-shot.

The `>=` comparison is only safe because `Advance` clamps and `Skip` sets exactly `Duration`. For `Mode == Off`, `Duration == 0` and `Elapsed == 0`, so `IsComplete` is true before anything happens — correct, but fragile: `Advance` rejects negative deltas and non-finite values, so the boundary invariant lives entirely in those two setters. If a future path writes `Elapsed` directly (e.g. for test injection or replay seek), `IsComplete` would silently disagree with what the host draws. Consider making `Elapsed` settable only through `Advance`/`Skip` (it already is) and noting in the doc comment that `IsComplete` never depends on sub-millisecond rounding.

comments.content: Inner loop is executed for each of the 3 blocks × 2 panels on every redraw, i.e. ~2 × 3 × 19 = 114 iterations plus `DrawLine` calls per frame. Most of those lines are fully clipped by the `lo < hi` / `z > a` guards or lie in fully-opaque regions, so the bulk of the submitted draw calls may be invisible. Consider precomputing the visible band range from `lo/hi/dx` before the loop to cut wasted `DrawLine` submissions during the animation.

`Restore` leaves inconsistent state: when the pack is found but `chartId` doesn't match any chart, `PackIndex` is updated while `DifficultyIndex` keeps whatever value it had before (possibly pointing to a chart index of the *previous* pack, which may be out of range for the new pack). The caller then indexes charts by `DifficultyIndex` and could read the wrong difficulty or go out of range. Reset `DifficultyIndex` when no chart matches (or fall back to 0) before returning.

`IsVisible(int index)` indexes `_matches` without any bounds check, and `SelectPack(int index)` accepts arbitrary indices including negative/out-of-range values. The state never validates against `catalog.Count`, so a stale row index (e.g. catalog rebuilt after a pack was removed/added while the UI still holds old indices) will throw `IndexOutOfRangeException` in `IsVisible` or silently leave an invalid `PackIndex` that later crashes `catalog[PackIndex]` consumers. Guard these entry points (return false / ignore invalid index) or validate inside `SelectPack`.

`Filter` dereferences `pack.Title`, `pack.Artist` and `chart.Charter` with no null guard, and `Restore`/`NextDifficulty`/`ClampDifficulty` also assume `Charts` is non-null. The record types permit nulls (`SongBrowseEntry(string Id, string Title, string Artist, IReadOnlyList<SongBrowseChart> Charts)` and `SongBrowseChart(string Id, string Charter)`), so malformed/partial catalog data from the loader would throw `NullReferenceException` on every keystroke. comments.content: `ResetForEmptyCard` only clears the four animation flags/alphas but never recomputes `Animating`. If `ShowEmpty()` is called while any segment is in flight (text fading out, cover fading, or collapse resizing), `Animating` stays `true` forever: `Advance` will find all segments cleared, `settled` stays `true`, and it will only drop the latch on the *next* `Advance` call — but the page early-returns out of `Advance` when `Animating == false` (SongDetailCard.Animating gate), so if the empty card is shown and no further frame is pumped, the page keeps running the per-frame path indefinitely (and a pending `_collapsing` resize can never land). Reset should also recompute the latch (or explicitly clear it) so the state machine is consistent after the reset.

When motion is turned off mid-fade (`profile.Animated == false`), `HideCover`/`ShowCover` clear `_coverFading` without snapping `_coverAlpha` to the intended value (0 for hide, 1 for show). `ShowCover` does set `_coverAlpha = 1f`, but `HideCover` leaves whatever intermediate alpha was in flight, so the page applies a frozen, partially transparent cover that never recovers. Symmetrically, `StartTextFade`-driven text fading is never cancelled when `Animated` flips to false (`BeginTextRefresh` with `!profile.Animated` returns `Applied` and doesn't clear `_textFading`), so a stale fade can continue writing alpha after the setting changed. Consider clearing `_coverFading` and setting `_coverAlpha` to the profile-appropriate terminal value, and cancelling `_textFading` in the non-animated path.

If a text fade-in is still in flight and a new refresh arrives with `currentTextAlpha <= 0f` (or motion turned off), this returns `Applied` and never clears `_textFading`. The still-running fade-in loop in `Advance` keeps overwriting `_textAlpha` toward 1 and emitting `TextAlphaChanged`, so the page's `SetExtendedInfoDim(true)` (which writes 0.6/0.35 modulation) is immediately clobbered by the next simulated alpha write and the freshly applied text ends up un-dimmed / flickering. Cancel in-flight text fades on the non-animated/instant path.

If the fade-out completes but its generation is stale, `_textFading` is cleared and nothing else happens — this is correct only because the newer `BeginTextRefresh` retargeted the same fade. However, the generation check compares against `_textGeneration`, which `BeginTextRefresh` always overwrites; if the page ever bumps `currentGeneration` without calling `BeginTextRefresh` (e.g. selection changed and the card shows a different song via the instant path), the pending `_pendingText` stays stale. Since `PendingText` is also what the page writes in the `Applied` path (SongDetailCard.ShowText), it's worth documenting/asserting that every generation bump must be paired with `BeginTextRefresh`, or dropping `_pendingText` here to avoid stale reads.

comments.content: Cancelling a collapse mid-flight via `Expand` clears `_collapsing` but leaves the resize retarget in `StartResize`. That works because `StartResize` resets `_resizeElapsed`, but if the card was hidden (`cardWasHidden == true`) while a collapse was in flight (possible via `ShowEmpty`/re-show paths), `_shownHeight` is snapped to `_rowHeight` — fine. The real gap is that `Expand` never resets `_collapsing` when `profile.Directional` is false: it does clear it at the top, so that's fine too. No action needed if the page never calls `Expand` while `!IsPresenting` with a running collapse; consider asserting `cardWasHidden` matches `!IsPresenting` to make the invariant explicit.

Negative `delta` (e.g. after a time-scale/clock anomaly) is not guarded: `_resizeElapsed`, `_textFadeElapsed` and `_coverFadeElapsed` can decrease, rewinding animations (and `Math.Clamp` on progress only clamps the top). Clamping `delta` to `>= 0` at entry of `Advance` keeps all three segments monotonic and avoids a frame where e.g. a completed collapse is re-run.

Stepping is always relative to 0, not to `Min`, and the result is not re-snapped after clamping. With the default range (0–100) this happens to work, but for any non-default range it breaks: e.g. `Min=3, Max=103` can never reach 103 (the nearest step is 100), and `Min=2, Max=98` snaps to 2,7,...97 so Max is unreachable; when `Min` is not a multiple of 5 the first emitted value after a drag can be below `Min` and gets clamped to a value that is not on the step grid. Since `Min`/`Max` are public and settable, this is a latent correctness bug for future ranges. Snap relative to `Min` and keep the endpoint reachable.

Pointer mapping uses the hard-coded constants `TrackWidth`/`TrackHandle` instead of the control's actual `Size`, and `localX` is used raw without accounting for the control's position/scale. This only works because `SettingsScreen.Layout.AddSlider` happens to size the control as `TrackWidth + TrackHandle` and offset its position manually; any resize, container layout, or scaled canvas will make the grabber no longer follow the pointer. Derive the usable track length from `Size` (e.g. `Size.X - TrackHandle`) so the widget is self-consistent, matching how `_Draw` computes `trackLeft` from `Size.Y` and the knob geometry from `Size`.

Also note `_Draw` uses `TrackWidth` while `Size.X` equals `TrackWidth + TrackHandle`, so if the two ever diverge the fill/handle drawing and the value mapping will disagree.

`_dragging` is only cleared by a `InputEventMouseButton` event. If the user presses, drags outside the control's rect and releases there, the release button event is not delivered to this control (Godot only routes `_GuiInput` for events inside the rect unless mouse capture is active via `AcceptEvent` on press... which here is not durable across nodes), so `_dragging` can remain `true`. The next time the pointer merely passes over the slider, `InputEventMouseMotion` will call `ApplyAt`, silently changing the volume without the button held. Reset on mouse exit / when the button is no longer pressed, e.g. add `MouseExited += () => _dragging = false;` in `_Ready`, or check `Input.IsMouseButtonPressed(MouseButton.Left)` in the motion branch.

`InputEventScreenDrag` is applied unconditionally, without checking `_dragging` (unlike the mouse-motion branch which guards with `when _dragging`). A stray drag event (multi-touch, a second finger, or an event routed while this control is not the active touch target) will move the slider and emit `Changed`, which in turn writes settings and triggers a debounced save. Gate the drag on `_dragging` (and ideally on the touch index that started it) for consistency with the mouse path.

With an empty `_labels` array (i.e. before `Configure` is called), `_labels.Length - 1` is `-1`, so `Mathf.Clamp(value, 0, -1)` returns `-1` and a click emits `Chosen(-1)`. Callers currently call `Configure` right after construction, but the widget is public-ish and emits an out-of-range index with no guard. Add an early-return guard so an unconfigured widget is inert.

comments.content: `AdvanceGeneration` is deliberately single-threaded (Cancel, then non-atomic `++_generation`), and `SongDetailRequest` is bound into the Godot `SongSelect` node which is reached from deferred/main-thread callbacks. The assumption is only stated in the class summary; it is not enforced. If `Begin()`/`Invalidate()` are ever invoked from a different thread than `CurrentGeneration`/`IsCurrentGeneration` readers (e.g. a signal handler on a worker, or a future refactor that kicks refresh from a load callback), the ordering can leak a stale value: `Cancel()` clears the loader's `_completed` before the increment, so between those two steps a concurrent reader can observe the old generation as still "current" while the matching result has already been dropped, or a load started with the new (not yet published) generation can be treated as stale. Consider asserting the owning thread or documenting the constraint on the mutating members, and/or moving the increment before the cancel so a reader can never see a generation whose result was already discarded.

`Math.Clamp(Target + pixels, 0f, maximum)` throws `ArgumentException` when `min > max`. `SongListViewport.MaxScroll()` does guard against negative `maximum`, but this state machine is also exercised directly by tests/other callers, and `maximum` is a raw parameter. Additionally, if `maximum` is NaN the comparison semantics of `Math.Clamp` silently produce NaN, which then poisons `Display`/`Target` and makes `Step` never converge (`Math.Abs(NaN) <= SnapPixels` is false → `Animating` stays true forever). Add an explicit guard, e.g. `maximum = float.IsFinite(maximum) ? MathF.Max(0f, maximum) : 0f;` before clamping, and return early when `pixels` is not finite.

comments.content: Integer truncation `Written = (int)actual` disagrees with the write path: `SongListViewport.Write()` uses `Mathf.RoundToInt(_state.Display)` and `AcceptWrite` stores the rounded `landed`, while `Step` compares `actual != Written` against the container's integer `ScrollVertical`. Whenever `actual` has a fractional part (it can, since `Display` is a float that is only snapped by writing back to the int container), `Push` resets `Written` to a truncated value different from the container's actual value, so the next `Step` on the same frame sees a spurious `actual != Written` and treats it as an external write (cancelling inertia / re-syncing). Use the same rounding as the write path: `Written = Mathf.RoundToInt(actual)` (or `Math.Round`), to keep the state machine's notion of "what we last wrote" consistent with what was actually written.

The method returns `true` (meaning "the caller should write immediately") only for the non-animated `tau <= 0` path. But when the target is already saturated at the clamp bound (e.g. `Target == maximum` and a further push tries to scroll further down, or `Target == 0` and pushing up), the animation is started anyway with `Display != Target` possibly already equal — leading to a no-op frame loop that keeps `Animating` true until `Step` snaps. Minor, but for a pure no-change push the caller could be told nothing happened. More important: this early-out should also be taken when `Display == Target` after clamping (nothing to animate), e.g. return `true` when `Target == Display` so `Write()` happens synchronously and `Animating` is not spuriously set.

`ScrollInertia.Step` already applies the same `SnapPixels` test internally and can return exactly `target`, but this outer `reached` check is evaluated against the *pre-step* distance. For a very small `delta` (long frame stalls aside, e.g. a tiny first frame) or a large `tau`, the step moves `Display` only slightly toward `Target`; since `reached` is false the code keeps animating, and `Step` internally snaps to `target` once within `SnapPixels` — fine, but the outer check means `Display` may be set to `Target` while `Animating` is set to `true` when `ScrollInertia.Step` internally snapped but the pre-step distance was just above `SnapPixels`. That leaves one extra frame of "animating with `Display == Target`" which returns `true` (extra write) with no motion. Consider deriving `Animating` from the post-step result: `Display = reached ? Target : ScrollInertia.Step(...); Animating = Display != Target;`.

`Stop` sets `Display = actual` unconditionally. In `SongListViewport`, `StopInertia()` is called on a touch press while an inertia animation may still be mid-flight, and `Display` is the animated (float) value at that moment. If the container's `ScrollVertical` is stale relative to `Display` (e.g. a write was rejected/clamped), this silently jumps the display back to the last written position. That is probably intended, but it also drops any remaining intended motion without attempting to write final target — acceptable, though worth confirming the caller re-writes after `Stop`. No change strictly required; treat this as a note if the touch-start path doesn't need to freeze at the target position.

Dim state is hard-written as a fixed alpha and is never tracked, so it silently overrides the in-flight text fade:

1. `ShowText` during animation starts a fade-out from the *dimmed* alpha (0.6/0.35) instead of 1; when the fade lands at 0 the text is replaced and fades back to 1, so switching rows mid-refresh bumps the brightness up (dim → full) instead of settling at the intended dimmed value.
2. `Advance` calls `SetExtendedInfoDim(false)` on `TextFadeInSettled` only. There is no symmetric call on `TextAlphaChanged`, so an externally requested dim (via `ShowText`/`SettleTextDim` on the `Applied` path) is lost as soon as the next fade-in settles.
3. `SettleTextDim()` re-writes alpha 1 onto labels, discarding whatever `_motion.TextAlpha` the fade-in is currently at (ordered after `ShowCover` in the page, so the fade-in may still be running).

Store a `_dimmed` flag and route every modulation write through a single `ApplyTextModulation()` that multiplies `_motion.TextAlpha` by the dim factor, and call it from `ApplyTextAlpha`, `SetExtendedInfoDim` and `ShowEmpty`.

`ResetForEmptyCard` only resets the motion's text/cover alpha and pending text, but `ShowEmpty` never re-applies the text alpha (`_title/_artist/_charter.Modulate`). If an empty selection is reached while a text fade-out is in flight (e.g. alpha currently near 0), `SetExtendedInfoDim(false)` writes 1 to the labels so it happens to look fine — but if any other path leaves the labels modulated, the empty placeholder stays invisible/dim. More importantly the height is not reset either: `ResetForEmptyCard` leaves `_shownHeight`/`_targetHeight` untouched, so an empty card can be shown at a partially collapsed height. Consider also calling `ApplyTextAlpha()` (or the unified modulation helper) and re-applying the height here.

No guard on `listWidth`: with a narrow list (e.g. small window / scaled UI) `barWidth` and the label widths (`listWidth - InfoInsetX - 40`, `listWidth - CardPad - 320`) can become zero or negative, producing a degenerate/backwards progress bar and clipped or inverted labels. `ShowPreviewProgress` repeats the same computation without guarding, so a negative `barWidth` combined with any fraction yields a fill/knob outside the bar. Clamp with `Mathf.Max(0f, ...)` (or use a single helper for the bar geometry).

`fraction`, `elapsed` and `duration` are used verbatim. A negative or >1 fraction (e.g. clock skew, a duration corrected after the stream started, or a caller that doesn't clamp like `SongPreviewPlayer.Readout`) drives the fill width and knob outside the bar (`barWidth*fraction - 7` can be left of `BarInsetX`). Also, with `duration == 0` (stream not yet loaded / failed) the readout renders `0:00 / 0:00` as if playback finished. Clamp the fraction to `[0, 1]` (and guard non-finite values) before applying the geometry.

Unguarded input handling:
- A negative `seconds` (or `-0.4` rounding to `0`) still produces odd output (`-1:60` style values are reachable via `-0.6` → total = -1 → `-1:59`; and any total in `(-1, 0)` truncates to `0:00`), which will show up if a stream reports a negative position or duration.
- `double.NaN` / `double.PositiveInfinity` cast to `int` is undefined in C# (implementation-defined range, on .NET Core it yields `int.MinValue`/`0x80000000`), yielding garbage like `-35791394:08` instead of a sane placeholder.

Clamp the input (`double.IsFinite`, `Math.Max(0, seconds)`) or render a placeholder when the duration is unknown.

`ShowPreviewLoading`/`ShowPreviewUnavailable` write into the same `_previewTime` slot as the progress readout, and `ShowPreviewProgress` overwrites it with `elapsed / duration`. That means once the preview starts ticking, the loading/unavailable message is replaced by `0:00 / 0:00`, and after a failed preview it reads `0:00 / 0:00` rather than "预览不可用" the first time `UpdatePreviewReadout(0)` runs (called from `StopPreview`). Consider keeping the status text in a separate label or having `ShowPreviewProgress` skip the clock write while a status message is active.

The transport child is a separate `Control` at `TransportInsetX/Y`; its `_GuiInput` calls `AcceptEvent()` (and returns early when `Disabled`, i.e. during chart loading, without consuming). Godot bubbles input to the nearest ancestor that stops it, and the parent's `_GuiInput` is only skipped when the event is accepted — so pressing the transport on a disabled state will fall through and trigger `CollapseRequested`, collapsing the card. More generally, any child that doesn't consume input could collapse the card. Also, `AcceptEvent` is called even after invoking the event, which prevents the event from continuing; that's desired, but consider also handling `InputEventScreenTouch` (the transport does) for consistency on touch devices.

`SetSelectionActionsEnabled` hard-codes button state from `GameSession.GetPreload(...)` and ignores the async loading lifecycle: (1) it re-enables `_startBtn` even when the detail load failed (preload absent → false, ok) but does not reset `_detailCard.SetTransportEnabled`; more importantly (2) the enabled state here bypasses `_detailRequest` generation checks and the `ApplyEmptySelection` path — if called while `CurrentPack` has zero charts it forces `_diffBtn.Disabled = false` even though there is no difficulty to cycle, contradicting `ApplyEmptySelection`. `NavigateBack` ignores the return value of `TransitionDirector.Navigate`. `_Process` dereferences `_listViewport`, `_detailCard` (via `_cardAnimating`), `_previewPlayer` and the roots that are declared `null!`. `_Process` is enabled in `_Ready` before the deferred callbacks run, and `_listViewport` is assigned in `BuildLibrary()`. `StopPreview()` calls `_detailCard.SetTransportPlaying(false)` and `_previewPlayer`, i.e. it touches Godot controls and the player after `_detailRequest.Dispose()`. If `_Ready` failed early (or `_detailRequest` was already disposed by a prior exit/re-entry on the same instance), this throws in `_ExitTree`. comments.content: `BeginRefreshAll` clamps `_diffIdx` but immediately reads `pack.Charts[_diffIdx]` afterwards — that part is fine — yet `CompleteRefreshAll` performs the same `ClampDifficulty` + index pattern with a stale `_diffIdx` captured before the deferred call. Centralize a single `CurrentDiff` helper that always clamps and returns null for empty lists, and use it from all four call sites (`StartPreview`, `IsCurrentPreviewLoad`, `CompleteRefreshAll`, `CompleteChartDetailsLoad`, `CompleteChartDetails`) so the clamp logic cannot drift.

`StopPreview` unconditionally calls `UpdatePreviewReadout(0)` → `_previewPlayer.Readout(0)` → `_detailCard.ShowPreviewProgress(...)`. Godot `AudioStreamPlayer.GetPlaybackPosition()` on a stopped player can return the last position, and `SongPreviewPlayer.Elapsed` is computed as `GetPlaybackPosition() - _start` without clamping; when `_start > 0` and the player has never played, this yields a negative elapsed that `Readout` clamps to 0 — but `Fraction`/`Duration` are still based on the *previous* chart's duration. `StopPreview` runs on every refresh and before `_previewPlayer.Load` updates `_duration`, so the progress bar momentarily shows the old duration for the new chart. `Stop()` should reset the readout state (duration/start) or `StopPreview` should not push a progress update for a chart it hasn't loaded.

`CompleteChartDetails` is invoked with `loaded` from `CompleteRefreshAll`'s cached path without checking that `generation` is still the current generation *inside* the cached branch — it is checked at the top of `CompleteRefreshAll` and again in `CompleteChartDetails`, so this is safe, but the cached branch skips `_detailCard.ShowChartLoading()` handling and directly calls `CompleteChartDetails`, which may call `StartPreview()` → `_previewPlayer.Load(...)` with `_detailRequest.CurrentGeneration`. That value equals `generation` only because no `Begin()` happened in between (single-threaded deferred). This is correct today, but the coupling is implicit; passing the generation through `StartPreview(int generation)` would make the preview key's provenance explicit and prevent a future refactor from re-reading a generation that has already advanced.

`Advance` divides by the caller-supplied `dischargeSeconds` / `chargeCycleSeconds` without validating them. A zero divisor yields `Infinity` (or `NaN` when delta is also 0), which gets stored into `Discharge`/`ChargePhase` and permanently corrupts the state (`Discharge < 1f` becomes false, modulo on NaN stays NaN). A negative or non-finite value has the same effect. Guard the durations (use an epsilon / clamp, or treat <= 0 as "not advancing") before performing the division.

The negative-phase correction only adds `1.0` a single time. If `delta` is a negative jump larger than one cycle (e.g. a clock rollback or a long frame where delta is negative), `phase` can be e.g. -3.7 and the result stays -2.7, leaving `ChargePhase` outside [0,1). Use a robust wrap (e.g. `phase - Math.Floor(phase)`) instead of a single conditional add.

`MarkReady` overwrites `Phase`/`LockAmount` unconditionally. If it is called while already in `Discharge` (or while a Lock ramp is in progress), the discharge progress is silently discarded and the state machine jumps back to Lock, and `Discharge` is left at its old non-zero value while `Phase` is no longer Discharge — stale state that `BeginReveal(discharge:true)` will then resets to 0, but `IsDischargeRunning`/`Discharge` readers will see inconsistent values. Also note `BeginReveal(true)` while already discharging is a no-op, so a caller cannot restart the discharge timer. Make the transition rules explicit (early-return / reset `Discharge` on re-lock) so repeated MarkReady calls are idempotent and predictable.

`delta` is not validated. A negative or NaN `delta` will drive `LockAmount`/`Discharge`/`ChargePhase` backwards or into NaN (e.g. NaN propagates through `Math.Min`), and a huge single-frame delta (tab restored from background) makes the whole ramp complete in one tick. Consider ignoring non-positive/non-finite deltas and clamping the delta (e.g. to a max step) so animations stay stable after long stalls.

The public mutable state machine (`Phase`, `LockAmount`, `Discharge`, `ChargePhase` with public getters and methods that mutate them) has no synchronization. If `Advance`/`MarkReady`/`BeginReveal` are driven from different threads (e.g. input vs. animation loop) the phase/timer values can race and produce torn or inconsistent transitions. Either document/assert single-thread (UI/main thread) usage or make the transitions atomic/guarded.

`_GuiInput` unconditionally calls `StartKnobTween`, unlike `SetState` which checks `MotionProfileProvider().IsAnimated`. With MOTION OFF the toggle still animates (and creates a Tween), contradicting the instant-snap path; the resulting knob position also diverges from `SetState`'s immediate `_knob = target`, so a following `RefreshQuickSettings()` (which is invoked right after Toggled is persisted) can start a second conflicting tween from a mid-transition value. Guard on `IsAnimated` and snap instead.

Setting `Disabled` only calls `QueueRedraw()`; it leaves `_hover`/`_hoverFade` untouched and does not gate the hover handlers. A control that was hovered (or one that stops receiving mouse-exit) keeps its hover highlight and per-frame `_Process` running while disabled. Clear the hover state and stop processing when entering the disabled state, and ignore MouseEntered/MouseExited while disabled. This applies to both `QuickSwitch` and `PreviewTransport`.

All three interactive widgets accept both left mouse press and screen touch in `_GuiInput`. In Godot, an emulated mouse event is generated from touch by default (`Input.emulate_mouse_from_touch`), so a single tap can be delivered as both `InputEventScreenTouch` and `InputEventMouseButton` — emitting `Chosen`/`Toggled`/`Pressed` twice (toggle would flip back and forth). Handle only one source (mouse button) or de-duplicate, e.g. ignore mouse events that report `Device == -1`/emulated input.

`MotionProfileProvider` is `required init` but there is no runtime guard: if a widget is constructed without it (e.g. added by a path other than the current builders, or after refactoring), `_Ready`/`SetHover`/`_GuiInput` will NRE on the delegate invocation. The same applies to `QuickModeRow`, `QuickActionRow` and `PreviewTransport`. Store the resolved profile at `_Ready` (or initialize a default provider) and fail fast with a clear error in `_Ready` instead of faulting later during input handling.

`UiHoverFade.Update` re-resolves `UiMotionProfile.For(GameSession.Settings.MotionMode)` per frame for its own transition, while `SetHover`/`Settled` use `MotionProfileProvider()`. If the two ever disagree (widget provided a different profile), the fade can keep advancing or settle against a different source than the one used to decide `SetProcess`. Consider having `Update` accept the profile (or the `IsAnimated` flag) so a single source of truth governs both the snap and per-frame advance.

`_tween` is killed only when a new tween starts; it is never killed in `_ExitTree`/`_Notification(NotificationPredelete)`. If the widget is freed while a knob tween is running, the Tween (bound to the node, so it should stop, but the callback continues until the next frame) may still invoke `QueueRedraw` on a disposed node depending on Godot version/behavior. Explicitly `_tween?.Kill()` on exit for safety and to release the reference.

Once `_path` equals the failed path, the equality shortcut suppresses all future retries and `Current` reports a mismatched entry, so a transient failure permanently blanks the cover. Commit the path only after a successful decode, clear/invalidate on failure, and skip caching null textures so a valid path with no cover is distinguishable from an undecoded one.
