comments.content: `ResetForPool` leaves `Kind`, `Accent`, `SpanPx`, `Strength`, and `Intensity` from the previous use. In the pooled path (GameplayEffects.EmitBloom) ResetFor + Intensity are set immediately, so it's safe there — but NotePaletteSpecimen creates its own instance and reuses it, and any code that un-hides a pooled node before calling ResetFor would briefly render with stale parameters (e.g. a Mine-strike shape in the wrong accent). Clearing the visual-affecting state here (Visible=false plus reset Kind/Accent/Strength/Intensity to defaults) makes the pool contract self-consistent and prevents future misuse.

There is no test coverage around the frame/progress math (`IsExpired` boundary, fade at frame 0, mine extent clamping). These are pure functions of `_age`, `SpanPx`, and `Intensity`, so they'd be easy to extract/pin with a test — otherwise regressions in the fade curve are only caught visually.

Drag termination only happens if the Left-button *release* lands inside this Control. If the user drags a slider and releases outside the control/panel (or the window loses focus), `_dragging` stays >= 0 forever: any later `InputEventMouseMotion` over the page will keep calling `ApplySlider` and silently change the setting, and `EditCommitted` is never fired so the value is never persisted. Handle `_Notification(NotificationMouseExit)` (and/or focus loss) to clear `_dragging` and invoke `EditCommitted`, and consider using `GetGlobalMousePosition` feedback there as well.

`HitAt` maps the stepper minus button to `Sub = -1`, but `DrawStepper` / `HoverKey` encode the minus button as `Sub = 0` and plus as `1`. With `Sub = -1`, `HoverKey` yields `row*100 + 0` — which is the same key as the *first segment* of the same row (`Hotspot.Segment` also uses `row*100 + Sub`). Although STEPPER and SEGMENT controls never coexist on one row today, the encoding is ambiguous by construction and silently breaks if a segment row with index 0 ever shares a row key. Use `Sub = 0` consistently for the minus button in `HitAt` so the hover key space stays one-to-one.

When dragging, `ApplySlider` is called on every mouse-motion event. `PercentAt` quantizes via `Math.Clamp(percent / SliderStepPercent * SliderStepPercent, ...)` but there is no de-duplication against the last emitted value, so `SliderChanged` → `ApplySettingsSlider` → `RefreshSettingsPage()` → `QueueRedraw()` fires repeatedly for the same percentage (mouse moves within one 5% step, plus fast motions emit many events). Track the last emitted percent per slider and skip no-op emissions (also avoids a redraw storm while dragging).

Handle position is computed from the rounded pixel `filled`, while the design uses `x0 + fw − 7` (i.e. the half-handle offset). At `percent = 0` the handle's left edge is `SliderTrackLeft − 7` and at `percent = 100` its right edge is `SliderTrackRight + 7`, which is intended, but the handle is drawn from the *filled* pixel length rather than the exact track fraction — the two diverge by up to 1px. Minor; more importantly, the handle is drawn even when the row is a placeholder (`PREVIEW VOLUME`, alpha 55%) which is correct, but the value text uses `accent` for placeholders — verify this matches design intent. (Low priority, listed for completeness.)

            SliderHandleSize, SliderHandleSize);

comments.content: TryParseHex accepts 8-digit `#RRGGBBAA` input in principle? No — it enforces length 7, but `Color.HtmlIsValid` also accepts the `#RGB` shorthand form (4 chars). Since length must be exactly 7, `#F00` is rejected, while `#FF0000` is accepted — that part is fine. The real risk: `Color.HtmlIsValid` accepts named/other formats in some Godot versions, and the alpha/rounding semantics of `FromHtml` differ from `ToHex` (which drops alpha). Round-tripping through these helpers is not guaranteed exact, so callers that persist via ToHex and reload via TryParseHex may see drift. Consider documenting that only 6-digit RGB is supported and validating the characters explicitly (matching `TryNormalizeHex` in GameSettingsCodec.cs) instead of relying on `Color.HtmlIsValid`.

        return true;

comments.content: `TryParseHex` trims and prefixes `#`, so it accepts loosely formatted input (e.g. " ff0000 "). Because colors are converted with `ToHex` (alpha-dropping) and later re-parsed, the parse result may not match the original `Color` when the source color had alpha != 1. If alpha-bearing colors ever reach this path (e.g. from a color picker with alpha enabled), persistence will silently discard alpha and re-parse as opaque, changing the rendered appearance. Consider asserting/rejecting colors with non-opaque alpha at the `Set` boundary, or document that alpha is intentionally ignored.

`NormalizeName` and `IsValidName` disagree: `NormalizeName` uppercases and strips invalid characters, so `"abc!"` normalizes to `"ABC"`, but `IsValidName("abc!")` is false while `IsValidName("abc")` is also false (case-sensitive) even though `NormalizeName` would happily produce it. This mirror-duplicates the logic in GameSettingsCodec.NormalizeName and NotePaletteDraft.TryNormalizeName (three copies of the same rule), which risks drift. Consider having `NormalizeName` call `IsValidName` on its candidate and making `IsValidName` case-insensitive/consistent, and centralizing this rule in one place.

`NormalizeName` truncates to `NameMaxLength` *before* trimming, so input like `"ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOP"` (16 chars) becomes `"ABCDEFGHIJKL"` while `"ABCDEFGHIJ KL"` (with a leading-space interaction) can yield a different visible length after `Trim()`. It also permits names consisting only of spaces/hyphens to fall back to `DefaultName` but a name of only hyphens (e.g. `"---"`) is accepted as-is because `Trim()` doesn't strip hyphens — this may be an unintended valid preset name. Consider trimming before/after truncation and requiring at least one alphanumeric character.

comments.content: `Get`/`Set` use a catch-all `default`/`_` arm mapping every unknown enum value to `Mine`. Because `Set` is called with `(NoteColorChannel)i` in NoteColorsScreen (line 146/270), any out-of-range index writes into `Mine` silently rather than failing — a future channel addition or a bad index will corrupt the Mine color instead of surfacing. Prefer an explicit `NoteColorChannel.Mine => Mine` arm plus `default => throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(channel))` to fail fast.

`CopyFrom` does not guard against `other` being null (callers in GameSettings.cs line 90 index into arrays, so it may be non-null today, but nothing in the signature documents this). Since `Name` is a reference string, this copies the reference (fine for immutable strings). Recommend adding `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(other)` or annotating `[NotNull]` to make the invariant explicit, especially since it's a public mutating API.

`FactoryColors` is a public mutable `Color[]`; external code can assign into it (e.g. `FactoryColors[0] = Colors.Red`), permanently corrupting factory defaults used by `NoteColorsScreen` (line 79). Also, `MatchesFactory()` and `ResetColorsToFactory()` duplicate the channel ordering list, so the array and those methods must be kept in sync manually. Consider exposing an immutable `IReadOnlyList<Color>` / `ReadOnlySpan` and deriving `ResetColorsToFactory`/`MatchesFactory` from it to guarantee structural consistency.

The `document is null` early return only clears the time/bar-bpm labels. The title, difficulty and level labels keep the values of the previously opened chart. This is reachable today: in `OpenChart` (EditorFlow.cs) `_document` is assigned before `RefreshEditHud()`, but `_hudView.Refresh` runs on every `_Process` frame, and an exception thrown after the assignment (e.g. `AttachDocument`/`ApplyDefaultGridDivisor`) leaves a half-initialized document; if any future flow nulls/clears `_document` on return-to-Pack the stale song info stays on screen. The HUD should explicitly reset the song row when there is no document.

`_hudGrid` and `_hudPathEdit` overlap: the grid label spans x 672–1872 and the centered PATH EDIT label spans x 360–1560, both at y 23 with height 26. When the path-edit badge is visible (double-click insert / hold-mixer selection), the centered `PATH EDIT` text is drawn on top of / underneath the right-aligned `GRID … · SNAP … · AUTO` text in the x 672–1560 range. Give the PATH EDIT label a narrower box centered on 960 (e.g. x 860, w 200) so it cannot collide with the right-corner HUD line.

comments.content: `saveError` is rendered verbatim into the HUD, which is a fixed-width (1652×32) single-line label. An exception message can contain a path and/or embedded newlines (`\n` from a formatted exception message), which will break row layout or spill outside the reserved strip. Compounding this: `RefreshSaveState` is called every `_Process` frame from `StandaloneEditorMain`, and the early-out `if (_saveState.Text == text) return;` is computed on the *unclipped* text, so nothing bounds it. Consider collapsing whitespace and truncating to a bounded length before display.

`canvas.CursorBpm` is formatted with the current ambient culture (`:0.0` uses `CultureInfo.CurrentCulture`), unlike the rest of the file which uses `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture`. On a locale using ',' as decimal separator this produces e.g. `BAR 12 · 120,0 BPM`, an inconsistent HUD readout (and the file's own `SnapStepText` deliberately uses invariant culture). Use the invariant culture for the whole string.

comments.content: The difficulty color is only re-applied when one of the three tag strings changed. Switching to a chart of a different difficulty that happens to share the same `DifficultyName()` and `LevelTagText()` (e.g. two `Hard` charts both rated LV 12, or two `Custom` charts with the same `DifficultyKey` and level) leaves the label color and the underlying `chart` stale — the color still reflects the old chart. Key the color update on the selected chart identity/difficulty rather than on the rendered text.

Documentation mismatch: the XML comment says the `FREE` mode is when Z temporarily disables *time* snapping, but `SnapEnabled` (the global snap toggle, presumably a different key) also forces `FREE` here. That means with global snap on and Z active, the grid label correctly reads the step, but disabling snap globally also shows `FREE` even though X still has space snapping at fine step — acceptable, but worth confirming there is no distinct indicator for "global snap off" versus "Z toggled off". More importantly, the method is non-static while it uses no instance state; making it `static` keeps it consistent with the other stateless formatters in this class.

comments.content: `k` is not guaranteed to be in [0, 1]. This code path is only reached when `!Beyond(a) && Beyond(b)`, and with `a` on the pre-line side (e.g. Left track: a.X < LeftLineX while b.X < LeftLineX), both numerator and denominator are negative, so `k` is positive — but if `b` is beyond the line by more than `a` is before it (b.X < LeftLineX < a.X), `|numerator| > |denominator|` and `k > 1`. Then `a += (b - a) * k` extrapolates past `b` instead of staying inside the segment, producing a link polygon that overshoots/clips to the wrong side of the rail. Consider clamping (or bailing out when `k` is outside [0,1]) and, more generally, handling the fully-beyond case (`Beyond(a) && Beyond(b)`) explicitly so the contract ("return false when the whole segment is past the line") is stated rather than implied.

`WriteLinkPolygon` indexes the caller buffer at 0..3 and `WriteLinkFrame` at index 4, relying only on a comment for the length contract. A buffer of exactly 4 passes `WriteLinkPolygon` then blows up in `WriteLinkFrame`; misuse yields an `IndexOutOfRangeException` deep in the per-frame render loop. Add explicit guards (`if (buffer.Length < 4) throw new ArgumentException(...)`; `< 5` in `WriteLinkFrame`) so misuse fails early with a clear message, and document that callers must not alias the same array across both helpers (the 5th element would corrupt the polygon).

The hardcoded 2px offsets are not bounded by the actual size. When Size.X or Size.Y is smaller than ~4px (Control not yet laid out / collapsing container), points like `Size.X - 2` become negative and `cut` (clamped only by the min dimension) can exceed `Size.X - 2`, producing inverted/self-intersecting border geometry passed to DrawPolyline. Guard against a minimum size (e.g. return early when min dimension < 8) or clamp the cut/insets to the available space.

Repeated redraws for the same size create a new array only once per _Draw for waves, but this is minor. The more meaningful cost is that nothing notifies the node when Size changes, so the drawing may be stale or redrawn excessively depending on the parent. Override `_Notification`/connect to `Resized` (or override `_Notification` handling `NotificationResized`) and call `QueueRedraw()` there, rather than relying on implicit redraws.

comments.content: Text absolute sizes are clamped to a minimum of 27/13 px regardless of the area, and the baseline positions are pure fractions of Size.Y. In a small cover (e.g. 40x40 thumbnail) the 27px "NO COVER" text will overflow the width and overlap the subtitle, and both will spill outside the clip region. Also `UiFonts.TechBold`/`UiFonts.Tech`/`UiFonts.Text`/`UiFonts.Dim` are referenced without any null guard — if fonts load asynchronously or fail, DrawString will throw during _Draw. Validate/skip text drawing when the width can't accommodate the string (measure via font.GetStringSize) and when fonts are null.

A new `Vector2[segments + 1]` is allocated on every DrawWave call, i.e. three arrays (3×65 points) each `_Draw`. If redraws happen frequently (animation/resize), this creates avoidable GC churn. Consider caching the point buffer as a field and reusing it, or drawing the wave with a single reusable list.

`BarLine` is defined in `NoteType` (value 9), yet `BaseColor(NoteType)` falls through to `_ => Mixer`. Only `NoteType.BarLine => BarLine` exists — wait, it's listed, so this is fine. However `HitAccent(NoteType)` and `HitEffect(NoteType)` map `BarLine`/unknown to `BarLine` color / `Tap` effect respectively, which is acceptable but worth a test. The real divergence risk: the two enums use different defaults for unknown values (`Mixer` vs `Tap`), so a future enum addition will silently get different colors depending on which path renders the note. Consider making both defaults explicit/consistent, or throw for undefined values so the divergence is caught early.

When `burstFollowsNote` is true, negative-grade or *unknown* types fall through to `_ => HitPerfect`. That means a `NoteType.BarLine` burst or a future note type gets the Perfect white burst regardless of grade — inconsistent with the non-BurstFollowsNote branch where `Good`/`Great` are honored for Tap-like notes. Also, in the follow-note branch the `grade` is entirely ignored for Tap/ExTap (a `Good` hit still flashes full note color). Please confirm this is intentional (it likely is for per-note color), and add explicit tests for `(burstFollowsNote=true, grade=Good)` and unknown-type inputs.

`Active` and `BurstFollowsNote` are mutable public static state read on every frame from the renderer (GameplayNoteRenderer.cs:443) while `GameplayMain._Ready` writes them. Because `NotePalette` is a reference type, if `GameSession.Settings.ActiveNotePalette` were ever assigned without cloning, live mutators (e.g. the color-editing UI) would change in-progress visuals. The `Clone()` at GameplayMain.cs:101 currently guards this, but the guarantee lives in the caller, not here. Since these fields are widely read and only set at startup, consider exposing them as write-once (setter validating a not-yet-initialized flag) or passing a snapshot instance through the renderer instead of a global, so the invariant cannot be broken silently.

Per the doc comment "Miss / Mine 恒红", `EffectAccent` returns `HitMiss` for Mine before consulting `burstFollowsNote`, which is correct. But `HitAccent(NoteType.Mine)` and this hard-coded `new Color(0.93f, 0.24f, 0.33f)` are two different "mine reds" (`HitMiss` = 1.00/0.33/0.38). Duplicating the color literal here means a palette/theme change to the Miss color won't update the mine hit accent. Consider reusing `HitMiss` (or a named static `MineHitAccent`) so there is a single source of truth.

comments.content: `Close` dereferences `points[0]` without validating the input. If an empty array is passed (e.g. a caller builds points conditionally), this throws `IndexOutOfRangeException` at runtime in the middle of a draw call. Either guard against empty/null input (return an empty array) or document the precondition with a thrown `ArgumentException`.

The `cut` value is only upper-clamped; a negative `cut` (or negative/zero size) produces a degenerate, self-intersecting polygon that will render incorrectly. Since this is a shared public helper used by every custom-drawn control, clamp to a non-negative range as well.

comments.content: `Reuse` returns early for BarLine views right after `ApplyBarLineSurface`, and `ApplyBarLineSurface` does not refresh the material's `vertical` (nor its size-dependent cut) for the *new* size — actually it does pass `_vertical`, but the material's `size_px` is set from `sizePx`, fine. The real gap: `Reuse` never sets `_baseColor`, `_kind`, `_gold`, `_energy` for the BarLine path, so those fields keep whatever `ResetForPool` left (`_energy = FallEnergy`). This is currently harmless only because a BarLine view never turns into a mesh view. However `Reuse` *does* mutate `Model`, `_sizePx`, `_vertical`, `_brightness` before the early return, meaning a BarLine-created view that is reused with a non-BarLine model would silently render as a bar line while flags say otherwise. Either make pool discipline explicit (e.g. assert `model.Type == NoteType.BarLine` for a bar-line instance) or fully initialize the material fields before returning.

`BeginRecoverableHoldFallthrough` and `RestoreHoldContact` guard only `IsMissFalling`/`IsRecoverableHoldFalling` and never `IsResolved`/`_haloOnly`. A resolved view (e.g. `MarkJudged` with negative ttl, or `BeginResidual` which sets `u_mode = 1` while `_haloOnly == true`) can be grabbed by the recoverable-hold path (setting `IsRecoverableHoldFalling = true`, `IsLineAnchored = false`) or resurrected by `RestoreHoldContact` (setting `_energy = ContactEnergy`, clearing `_ttl = -1`), leaving a judged note permanently visible at contact brightness / residual never stopping, and callers may treat it as an active endpoint. Add an `IsResolved` (and `_haloOnly`) guard to both transitions.

`MarkJudged` and `BeginResidual` reset `_stateAlpha` but never touch `_depthAlpha`. Since `Modulate` alpha is the product `_depthAlpha * _stateAlpha`, a view that received a depth fade (e.g. `SetDepthAlpha(0f)` at spawn or a partial fade near the spawn zone) and is then judged inline will render with an unexpectedly low alpha — the hit flash can be effectively invisible if `_depthAlpha` was driven to ~0. Callers in `GameplayStageRenderer` do call `SetDepthAlpha` each frame for live notes, but for the residual/judged path this file should not rely on that. Reset `_depthAlpha = 1f` in both transition methods (or document the contract explicitly).

`TickTtl` divides by `_residualTtl` (and `PeakDecaySeconds`). `_residualTtl` is only assigned inside `BeginResidual`, and `ResetForPool` does not reset it. It happens to be initialized to `DefaultResidualSeconds` at field declaration, but `_haloOnly` is public state reachable via `IsResidual`, and `BeginResidual` is the only path that sets `_haloOnly = true` — so the division is safe today. Still, `_residualTtl` should be reset in `ResetForPool` (to `DefaultResidualSeconds`) so a pooled instance can never carry residual timing between uses, and the invariant should be made explicit rather than relying on the field initializer.

Add `_residualTtl = DefaultResidualSeconds;` and, when `_material != null`, reset `u_mode`/`u_opacity` so a pooled instance is fully clean before it is handed out.

comments.content: `BeginMissFallthrough` and `BeginRecoverableHoldFallthrough` return without marking the view resolved, but `BeginMissFallthrough` doesn't clear `IsRecoverableHoldFalling` / `IsLineAnchored` consistency: it sets `IsLineAnchored = false` but leaves `IsRecoverableHoldFalling` untouched (could be true from a prior disconnect), so `AdvanceMissFallthrough` would still be in both fallthrough states and `UpdateMissAlpha` would compete with the miss branch — actually since both flags can be true, `AdvanceMissFallthrough` accumulates distance for both and the return condition relies on `IsMissFalling`, so a recoverable hold that escalates to a real miss keeps `IsRecoverableHoldFalling == true` and the caller may then treat it as recoverable. Explicitly clear `IsRecoverableHoldFalling` when starting a real miss.

The public properties mutate backing fields and call `Refresh()`, which only queues a redraw. Unlike `Cut`, `Fill`/`Border`/`BorderWidth` do not invalidate caches — fine for colors, but the bigger issue is that a setter called before the node enters the tree gets no draw at all: `Refresh()` returns early when `!IsInsideTree()`, so if the value is set in a constructor/`_Ready`-less path the panel may render with stale visuals until some other event forces a redraw. More importantly, `_Draw` is not guaranteed to be invoked at all if `QueueRedraw` is skipped, so consider calling `QueueRedraw()` unconditionally (Godot safely ignores/defers it outside the tree) or force a redraw on `NotificationReady`.

Also, since `Cut` also affects geometry, the setter path is correct there — just make sure any future geometry-affecting property follows the same invalidation pattern.

A negative/NaN cut or a degenerate size yields a degenerate or self-intersecting polygon that `DrawColoredPolygon`/`DrawPolyline` will happily accept, producing garbage rendering (and possibly console errors). Clamp defensively here rather than relying on callers.

comments.content: The cache is only invalidated by `NotificationResized` and by the `Cut` setter. `Size` mutations that occur without a resize notification (e.g. `SetSize`/direct field assignment in the same frame as the first draw, or transform changes) will reuse stale points. Also `_closedPoints` is derived from `_points`, so keeping two nullable arrays in sync is error-prone: it can be rebuilt on demand from `_points` with negligible cost instead of being cached separately, eliminating a whole class of desync bugs.

`DrawPolyline` centers the stroke on the path, so half of `_borderWidth` straddles outside the polygon. Unlike an inset approach, this strokes the border centered on the edge (antialiased=true already hint to draw half-line offset), causing the outer half to be clipped by the Control's own rect/size or rendering under sibling controls, and also visually bleeding outside the intended cut-corner shape. If the design expects the border inside the shape, stroke an inset polygon (e.g. `UiGeometry.CutCorners(Size - borderWidth, cut - borderWidth/2)` offset by half the width) instead.

Missing test coverage: there are no consumers/tests in this file or the repo path exercising the caching + invalidation of `CutPanel` (cut clamping, resize invalidation, border-less path). Adding a small headless draw/inspection test that asserts `_points` are recomputed after a `Cut`/size change and that the polygon matches `UiGeometry.CutCorners` would guard the focus-area regressions above.

`Full` is the implicit 0/default value, so any uninitialized field or `default(UiMotionMode)` behaves as full motion, and the parsers (`GameSettings.ParseMotionMode`, `EditorSettings.ParseMotionMode`) fall back to `Full` for unknown/corrupt strings. An accessibility user who chose `Reduced`/`Off` can silently get full animation. Assign explicit values (`Full = 0, Reduced = 1, Off = 2`) so the member order is an explicit contract, document that `EditorSettingsPage` maps the UI option index directly via `(UiMotionMode)index`, and treat unknown/unparseable values as the motion-safe option (`Reduced`/`Off`) rather than `Full`.

comments.content: `Tech`/`TechBold` are loaded via `GD.Load<Font>` in a static field initializer with no null or resource-type guard. If the asset path/import is missing (e.g. a build that strips `assets/fonts` or a bad `.import`), `GD.Load` returns null and every consumer (`UiFonts.Tech.GetStringSize(...)` in ResultScreen, `new FontVariation { BaseFont = UiFonts.TechBold }` in the editor, etc.) will either silently render nothing or throw a NullReferenceException far from the root cause. `Cjk` is built from `SystemFont.FontNames` and assumes one of the listed OS fonts is installed; the comment acknowledges this is a placeholder. On minimal Linux/Steam Deck/container images none of "Microsoft YaHei"/"PingFang SC"/"Noto Sans CJK SC" may exist, so Chinese text silently renders as tofu boxes (this font is selected explicitly wherever CJK text is detected, e.g. `NoteColorsWidgets.cs`/`ResultScreen.cs`). comments.content: No validation of input events. NaN BarTime or NaN/Infinity Mult are silently accepted: a NaN key is ordered by `Comparer<double>.Default` as smaller than everything, so it becomes `_events[0]` and poisons `SpeedAt` for every query `barTime <= NaN` (always false) — actually it lands at the start and the early-return branch `barTime <= _events[0].BarTime` never matches, so interpolation output becomes NaN. NaN/Infinity multipliers likewise produce NaN distances that propagate into note positions in the renderer. Since the map is built from chart-authored data (`_chart.DropSpeeds`), reject or drop non-finite entries (and log) rather than silently producing NaN geometry.

The documented "later value wins on duplicates" semantics only hold for already-ordered enumerables: `events` is enumerated once in its given order and later assignments overwrite earlier ones, so the *last enumerated* entry wins, which for a shuffled/unordered source is arbitrary. Either sort/clarify the contract ("last occurrence in the given sequence wins") or make the intent explicit in code so callers don't depend on accidental ordering. Note the existing test `(2.0,0.5),(2.0,0.8)` passes for either interpretation, so it doesn't pin the semantics.

comments.content: `RemainingDistance` multiplies the whole BarTime delta by the instantaneous speed at `currentBarTime`, ignoring all intermediate events. For notes far in the future this can be wrong monotonically (a note can jump backwards when speed changes, and a note whose `noteBarTime` is beyond the last event uses the last event's speed for the entire span, not the integral over the piecewise-linear speed). This is a deliberate design (client-side tests pin the current behavior), but the doc comment should state that the result is the *linearized* distance assuming the current speed holds, so callers/tests don't treat it as a true integral. If exact piecewise integration were ever required, the segments would need to be integrated separately.

public double RemainingDistance(double noteBarTime, double currentBarTime) =>
        (noteBarTime - currentBarTime) * SpeedAt(currentBarTime);

comments.content:
The section-lookup loops (duplicated in `BarTimeToSeconds`, `SecondsToBarTime`, `BpmAtBarTime`, `BpmAtSeconds`) silently assume: (a) `Sections` is sorted ascending, (b) the first entry starts at/ before the query, and (c) every `Bpm`/`Seconds` is finite. Nothing in this type enforces those invariants — `Chart` is a public `init`-only model, so any caller/test can construct an unsorted or degenerate section list and get silently wrong (or `NaN`/`Infinity` from `Bpm == 0`) hit times.

Same for out-of-range input: a negative `bar`/`second` just extrapolates from section 0 (which is probably the right answer only if section 0 starts at 0), and values beyond the last section extrapolate indefinitely, so malformed data or an audio-offset bug becomes invisible instead of failing fast. Consider validating in the constructor / a `Validate()` method (sorted, first BarTime == 0, Bpm > 0) and asserting rather than silently extrapolating.

Inconsistent empty-timeline contract: `BarTimeToSeconds`/`SecondsToBarTime` throw on `Sections.Count == 0`, while `BpmAtBarTime`/`BpmAtSeconds` silently return a hard-coded 150 BPM. On the 3/350 legacy charts without a timeline (§1.3), timing conversions are expected to fall back, yet BPM lookup will report a fabricated 150 — if the real baked BPM differs, gameplay geometry/scroll speed is silently wrong with no signal. Either make the fallback explicit (document that 150 is the legacy default and reference the spec) or surface it (e.g. `TryBpmAtSeconds`) instead of hard-coding a magic number in two places (also duplicated in `shared/Chart/V2/Evaluation.cs`).

`NotesOf` maps every unrecognised `Track` value to `NotesRight` via `_ =>`. Because `Track` is a plain (non-`[Flags]`) enum, a corrupt/out-of-range value coming from deserialisation (e.g. a cast of an arbitrary int in a loader) would be silently folded into the right lane instead of being rejected — notes land in the wrong lane or get judged twice, and the bad data never shows up in logs. Prefer an explicit `Track.Right => NotesRight, _ => throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(track), track, ...)`.

`Note` is otherwise fully immutable (`init`), but `Second` is `set`. `DynamixChartLoader` relies on this to re-time notes after construction, which means every `Chart` in the system is a mutable object masquerading as an immutable data model: any consumer that caches a `Chart`, or shares one across the judge thread / render thread, can observe a `Note` whose `Second` disagrees with `BarTime`/`BakedSecond` mid-retime, without any synchronisation. Prefer computing `Second` once in the constructor / factory (pass the resolved `second` to `new Note { ... }`), or make it `init` and provide a `WithSecond(...)` that returns a new instance, so re-timing cannot race and cannot leave the record inconsistent.

Given the chart is immutable after load, cache it once (`private readonly Note[] _allNotes` built lazily/in ctor) or expose a pre-built `IReadOnlyList<Note>` so callers can index and cannot accidentally re-enumerate. `PreviewBarAtStagePoint` is documented as the exact inverse of the preview projection, but it is not: `PreviewDistanceForBars` returns *unscaled* units (`barDelta/visibleBars * PreviewTravelPx`), whose consumer multiplies by `SideDistanceScale` (AuthoringCanvas/Path/Placement: `SidePreviewTravelPx * SideDistanceScale`), while `PreviewBarAtStagePoint` uses `StageDistancePx`, which measures *on-screen rail pixels*. The two sides must use the same scale (either divide `distance` by `SideDistanceScale` here, or make `PreviewDistanceForBars` return scaled rail pixels and update its callers).

`SidePreviewTravelPx` and `CenterPreviewTravelPx` are both just aliases of `TravelPx`, which is misleading: the side preview only travels 691px on screen (`SideVisibleTravelPx`), and the extra `TravelPx` value is meaningful only *before* `SideDistanceScale` is applied. Frozen landmark constants (`CenterUnitPx`, `SideUnitPx`, `TravelPx`, `SideVisibleTravelPx`, `BaseFallSpeedPx`, `CenterX0`) are not pinned by any assertion — existing tests only re-derive from the same constants (`SideDistanceScale - 691f/790f`, `CenterWidthPx`), so a drift in the literal values would go unnoticed. Add a test asserting the documented screen landmarks directly: `CenterToStageX(MirrorAxis)` ≈ 963, `LeftLineX + SideVisibleTravelPx` == 875 (and mirrored right 1045), `DesignWidth - (LeftLineX + RightLineX)` == 0, and `BaseFallSpeedPx == 1026`.

comments.content: After recomputing `Second` from `BarTime`, the per-track lists are no longer necessarily sorted by time. `LoadTrack` sorted by the baked `Second`, and the BPM-derived seconds can reorder notes (e.g. when baked values are stale/zero or when a note's BarTime lies in a different BPM section). Downstream code (e.g. `Integration.ConvertLegacyChart` and the judge engine) assumes time-ordered note sequences, so ordering guarantees from the loader are silently broken. Re-sort each track after recomputing.

`DropSpeeds` events are consumed at runtime with linear interpolation "between adjacent BarTime values", but unlike `sections` they are neither sorted nor validated. Out-of-order or duplicate `BarTime` entries in the exported JSON will produce negative/zero interpolation intervals and undefined multipliers. Sort by BarTime (and dedupe/validate strictly increasing) to uphold the invariant the runtime depends on.

BPM values are not validated. `Chart.BarTimeToSeconds` divides by `s.Bpm`, so a section with `BPM = 0` (or a negative / NaN value) produces `Infinity`/`NaN` hit seconds for every note in that section — silently corrupting the whole chart. A missing `BPM` field falls back to 150, but an explicitly exported 0 does not. Validate that BPM is finite and > 0 (and that Seconds/BarTime are finite) and fail with a descriptive error instead of emitting NaN.

Unknown note types are silently dropped, but a missing `Type` property defaults to `1` (falling back to a real, valid note type). That means a malformed export without `Type` becomes a bogus Playable note instead of being skipped/rejected, and out-of-range notes disappear without any diagnostic while `TotalMainNote` still reflects the raw header count — a mismatch that will surface later as inconsistent judge/score totals. At minimum, use a sentinel fallback (e.g. -1) for a missing `Type` so it is skipped rather than coerced to type 1, and log/count skipped notes.

File I/O and JSON parse errors propagate raw: `File.ReadAllText` throws `FileNotFoundException`/`IOException`, and `JsonDocument.Parse` throws `JsonException` without any indication of which chart/file failed. Callers cannot distinguish a corrupt file from a missing one, and the failure gives no context (path) for diagnosis. Wrap these so the exception carries the offending path (e.g. `throw new InvalidDataException($"Failed to load chart '{path}'", ex)`), giving both `LoadFile` and `Load` a consistent failure surface.

The XML doc on the class claims tolerance for dangling `SubNoteId` ("由判定计划构建时处理"), but `Load` performs no consistency check at all, while `V2.Integration.ConvertLegacyChart` hard-fails on dangling `SubNoteId` and duplicate note IDs. So a chart that this loader accepts as valid will blow up later in the v2 pipeline with an opaque error. Either document the split clearly or expose a lightweight validation helper so callers can detect these issues at load time.

comments.content: FormatNumber rounding mode is not RFC 8785 compliant. `double.ToString("R")` on .NET Core 3.0+ already produces the shortest round-trip digits using round-half-to-even, which matches ECMAScript; but for values whose shortest representation requires round-half-up semantics it can differ. More importantly, the code path silently relies on platform `"R"` behavior — on .NET Framework / Xamarin / Mono the `"R"` format is documented as not always round-trippable and can emit 17 significant digits (e.g. 0.1 → "0.10000000000000001"), producing two different digests for the same chart across runtimes. Since the digest is a cross-platform contract, this needs either an explicit shortest-round-trip implementation or a target-framework guard (`#if NETCOREAPP3_0_OR_GREATER`) with a documented fallback.

        var shortest = Math.Abs(value).ToString("R", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);

comments.content: ECMAScript/JCS exponent form requires the '+' sign on non-negative exponents (handled below), but note `scientificExponent` is only reachable outside [-6, 21]. For very small values like 5e-324, `Math.Abs(value).ToString("R")` yields "5E-324"; after stripping leading zeros this stays correct. However, for subnormal/shortest forms the .NET `"R"` output for a value such as 1.7976931348623157E+308 already contains a 17-digit mantissa — fine. The real gap is that no test-visible invariant enforces the exact JCS rule that the significand in scientific form has exactly one digit before the decimal point when the digits are longer; `digits[0] + "." + digits[1..]` is correct, but this ordering/branching needs unit tests for boundary cases (1e21, 1e-7, 123456789012345678901, 0.000001, 1e-6) to lock the contract.

Integer JSON numbers beyond 2^53 lose precision through TryGetDouble and are silently rounded, which can make two distinct large integers (e.g. 9007199254740993 vs 9007199254740992) canonicalize to the same text. Since the projection only emits integer bar/numerator/denominator via `(long)` casts, this is only a risk for arbitrary JsonElement input to the public Canonicalize API. Consider rejecting integers that are not exactly representable as binary64 (compare against the raw text / BigInteger) so the canonicalizer never silently collides distinct values.

`Array.Sort` is not stable, and the comparator falls back to `CompareBytes(left.CanonicalUtf8, right.CanonicalUtf8)`. Two notes with identical time, type, and identical projected JSON will compare equal and their relative order is then unspecified — but since their canonical bytes are identical, the resulting digest is unaffected, so this is acceptable. Still, the comparator does a full byte-by-byte comparison of the canonical UTF-8 on every tie, and `CanonicalUtf8` is memoized in `ProjectedNote` (recomputed per note), which is fine. No action required beyond ensuring a test asserts determinism across shuffled input order for duplicate notes.

`Sha256Hex(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(canonical))` allocates a large intermediate string plus its UTF-8 byte array. The canonicalizer already produces a string; consider a `CanonicalizeUtf8` overload over dictionaries (or an `Encoding.UTF8.GetByteCount`/`GetBytes` into a rented buffer via `ArrayPool`) to avoid double allocation for large charts. Minor, but this is on the hot path for every digest computation.

var canonical = JsonCanonicalizer.Canonicalize(projection);
        var digest = Sha256Hex(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(canonical));

comments.content: `ProjectAndSortNotes` projects every note twice (once in the `Select` creating `ProjectedNote`, which materializes `ProjectNote`, and the `CanonicalUtf8` property computes canonical bytes eagerly for every note). For large charts this roughly doubles projection work compared with lazily computing `CanonicalUtf8` only for ties. Consider lazy evaluation (`Lazy<byte[]>` or compute-on-demand) or a cheaper tie-break key (e.g. note `Id`, if stable/unique) to avoid canonicalizing every note just for sorting.

comments.content: `BuildProjection` is public and performs no validation of `resolvedAudioSha256` or `judgePreset` (unlike `Compute`, which validates them). A caller can build a projection with `JudgePreset.Tutorial` (then `JudgePresetName` throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`) or with a malformed audio hash and get an invalid digest material without the friendly `ArgumentException`. For API consistency and to prevent divergence between `Compute` and `BuildProjection`, apply the same validation in `BuildProjection` or make it private/internal.

Iterating `foreach (var c in value)` over a string is fine, but the surrogate validation in `ValidateSurrogates` walks the string a second time. Minor: `AppendString` already validates and then re-walks; acceptable for clarity. No correctness issue.

`IsJsonSafeCanonical` does not fully enforce the canonical v2 representation that `FromJsonComponents` requires. It is only true when `Bar.Sign >= 0`, and the public constructor normalizes to `0 <= Numerator < Denominator` with a reduced fraction (and `Numerator == 0` implies `Denominator == 1`), so the remaining invariants actually hold for every instance. However, this is an implicit dependency: any future constructor/deserialization path (or a value produced by `default(ExactBarTime)`, where `Denominator == 0`) that bypasses normalization would allow `Write` (line 273) to emit JSON that `Read` then rejects on round-trip, and `Write` additionally casts `Denominator` to `long` (0 for a default value, or a truncated huge value) — a silent corruption. Make the predicate self-sufficient instead of relying on normalization side effects:

```csharp
public bool IsJsonSafeCanonical =>
    Bar.Sign >= 0 && Bar <= MaxSafeInteger &&
    Numerator.Sign >= 0 && Numerator < Denominator &&
    Numerator <= MaxSafeInteger && Denominator <= MaxSafeInteger &&
    (Numerator.IsZero ? Denominator.IsOne : BigInteger.GreatestCommonDivisor(Numerator, Denominator).IsOne);
```

Note the same implicit assumption applies elsewhere in the file (e.g. `ToString`, `IsNonNegative` uses only `Bar.Sign`), so a documented class invariant (or a debug assert) would also help.

`ToDouble` loses precision in the `maxBits > 1022` branch: right-shifting numerator and denominator by the *same* `shift` (derived from the larger of the two bit lengths) is not equivalent to scaling, and it truncates the value. Two concrete problems:

1. The quotient changes (it becomes smaller by roughly `1 << shift`) instead of being rounded, so results near 1.0 can be badly wrong. E.g. `FromFraction((1 << 2000) + 1, 1 << 2000).ToDouble()` returns ~0 instead of ~1.0.
2. If `denominator` is much larger than `numerator`, shifting by `maxBits` can zero out the denominator first, returning `±Infinity` for an ordinary finite quotient (e.g. `FromFraction(1, 1 << 1100)` returns `+Infinity` instead of ~0).

Since this feeds runtime timing/rendering (`Evaluation.cs`, `RuntimeAdapter.cs`, `EditorTime.cs`), silent wrong values are hard to diagnose. Scale each side independently based on its own magnitude (e.g. shift numerator down to ~53 significant bits and denominator to ~53 bits counter-balancing the exact difference in bit lengths), and only return Infinity when the value itself genuinely exceeds `double.MaxValue`.

The converter rejects any integer component that does not fit in `long` (`TryGetInt64`), yet the type and `MaxSafeInteger` explicitly allow components up to 2^53-1 (and `Write` casts to `long`, which is correct for that range). This is only safe because `MaxSafeInteger < long.MaxValue`, so no JSON-safe value is currently lost — but the check and error message are misleading. Reading via `System.Numerics.BigInteger.Parse(property.Value.GetRawText())` (or `TryGetInt64` fallback) after validating `ValueKind == Number` and the absence of a fraction/exponent would make the converter consistent with the declared contract and give a precise "must be an integer within 0..9007199254740991" error. Note also that `TryGetInt64` rejects `1.0`/`1e0` forms only by luck of number token shape; be explicit about rejecting non-integer tokens.

The out-of-range exception always reports `nameof(bar)`, even when it was `numerator` or `denominator` that exceeded `MaxSafeInteger`. This produces misleading diagnostics (and the parameter name is used by callers that rethrow/filter on it).

if (bar > MaxSafeInteger || numerator > MaxSafeInteger || denominator > MaxSafeInteger)
            throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(bar), "BarTime components must be JSON-safe integers.");

comments.content: `FromDouble` can be called with ordinary finite inputs (e.g. `Evaluation.cs` converts BPM values and audio offsets) and may produce a value whose components vastly exceed `MaxSafeInteger` or are negative. That is fine for internal arithmetic, but there is no guard preventing such values from reaching `Write`, where `(long)value.Bar` would silently truncate if `IsJsonSafeCanonical` were ever relaxed. Consider making `FromDouble` (or its callers) assert `IsJsonSafeCanonical` where the value is destined for serialization, and add boundary tests for `FromDouble`/`ToDouble` around `double.MaxValue`, `double.Epsilon`, negative zero, and the `maxBits > 1022` branch described above.

Chrome is the only root in the scene tree — `EnsureLayers` adds `_chromeRoot` as a child of this node, but the `ColorRect`s returned by `AddChromeLine` are parented to `_chromeRoot`. Calling `BuildCommunityStageChrome()` again (e.g. re-entering the stage, or an editor that re-runs setup on the same renderer) will add a *second* named `CommunityStageChrome` sibling next to the existing one only if `EnsureLayers` re-runs, but the real problem is the line-rect children: `AddChromeLine`'s `ColorRect` is added to `_chromeRoot` while the `GameplayBackdrop`/`ColorRect`s just below look like they should share the same container — they do; so the return value of `AddChromeLine` is fine. The actual defect here is `child.Free()` being called while iterating the live child list with no `IsQueuedForDeletion` guard: Godot's `Free()` is synchronous, so the child array mutates during the `foreach`, which can skip children on some Godot builds and leaves queued-for-deletion nodes that `FindChildren` (used by `AuthoringCanvas.ApplyBackgroundDim`) will still see. Rebuild the root instead (`RemoveChild` + `QueueFree`, or `foreach` over a `.ToArray()` snapshot).

Note: only the first user of this renderer's chrome (gameplay, line 51 of GameplayMain.Presentation.cs) is an owner — everything relies on the fact this is never called twice; that invariant is undocumented.

`Rebuild()` does not go through `EnsureLayers()` alone: it calls `foreach (var child in _noteRoot!.GetChildren()) child.Free();` — this frees *every* child of the shared note layer, which in gameplay is also where `GameplayNoteRenderer` pools NoteViews, sustain polys/frames and hit effects (`_noteRoot = sharedStage.NoteLayer`). If anything ever calls `Rebuild()`/`SetNotes()`/`SetGhostNoteIds()` on the gameplay instance, it will destroy live gameplay visuals and leave `GameplayNoteRenderer`'s pools full of dangling references (it only re-parents on `GetParent() == null`, so a freed instance in a pool will crash later). Since `_views`/`_links` are the only things this class owns, only free the nodes this class created (track them, e.g. keep a list of created nodes, or use a dedicated sub-container inside the layer) rather than all children. At minimum this ownership contract must be documented/enforced.

Also, `_notes.ToDictionary(note => note.Id)` throws `ArgumentException` on duplicate IDs. `SetNotes` is a public API fed by chart/editor data, so malformed input crashes the stage instead of degrading. Use a tolerant construction (e.g. `GroupBy(...).ToDictionary(g => g.Key, g => g.First())` or validate and log once).

`RenderedLinkCount`/`RenderedCurvedLinkCount` are documented as rendered counters, but the `if (!ShowLinks) return;` early exit leaves `_views` populated while `_links` stays empty. More importantly, when `ShowControlNodes == false` (editor sets it at AuthoringCanvas.cs:199), hold/mixer *nodes* are skipped for NoteViews but their links are still created, so links reference positions for notes that have no visible head/node — the ribbon then connects to an invisible point. Decide whether skipping control nodes should also skip their link segments, and keep the skip logic in one place so views and links stay consistent.

The curved-link branch ignores `a`/`b`'s actual path shape: it only lerps between the already-clipped endpoints with an eased `progress`, so for a non-linear `V2PathCurve` between two flattened path segments, the rendered ribbon is a straight-line-with-eased-parameter, not the curve. More concretely, the ribbon is lerped along the *chord*, which is the intended flattening approximation — but `a` and `b` have already been clipped (`ClipToJudgeLine` mutated `a`), so the eased parameter is applied to the clipped chord, producing a curve whose shape changes as the link crosses the judge line and which no longer matches the runtime `V2Curves.Progress` sampling used elsewhere. Use the unclipped path points for curve sampling and clip the sampled polyline instead.

Related: `V2Curves.Progress(curve, u)` is called for every curve type including `Hold` — verify it handles `V2PathCurve.Hold`; a hold-curve should step rather than ease.

`UpdatePreviewPositions()` recomputes `PositionAt` for notes, and then `UpdateLink` recomputes `PositionAt` again for both endpoints of every link — the same notes are positioned 2–3 times per update (each `SetPreviewBar`/`SetPreviewTime` call, and the editor calls both every dirty frame). Per-frame cost is O(notes + 3×links) with heavy `Track` switch dispatch plus, in the curved branch, a 13-point sample loop and fresh `List<Vector2>`/`float` allocations per link per frame. Cache each note's resolved position in a local array/dictionary during `UpdatePreviewPositions` and pass it into `UpdateLink`; also reuse pre-allocated point/half-width buffers (as `GameplayVisualMapper.WriteLinkPolygon` already does) instead of allocating two lists and two arrays every frame.

Two-state preview is unguarded: when a distance provider is set, `_previewBar` and `_remainingScale` are silently ignored (so `SetPreviewBar` and `SetNotes(notes, remainingScale)` become no-ops and `SetPreviewTime` is the only input). Also `Remaining()` is invoked inside `UpdateLink` for both endpoints while `Rebuild` also calls `Remaining(note)` per note — if the provider is expensive or stateful this is called repeatedly. Document the contract that the provider supersedes bar/scale, or make the fallback explicit so callers cannot accidentally combine them. In the same vein, `SetGhostNoteIds` rebuilds and then calls `SetPreviewTime(_previewTime)` while `SetNotes` rebuilds and calls `SetPreviewBar(_previewBar)` — the two paths update preview state with different inputs, so the resulting positions depend on call order (editor calls `SetGhostNoteIds` then `SetNotes` then `SetPreviewTime`, fine, but any other ordering leaves notes positioned from a stale bar).

`ShouldRenderGhost` treats a ghost `HoldHead` differently (rendered while `Remaining(tail) >= 0`), but here only the head's own `remaining` is clamped for display — if the head is behind the judge line while the tail is still ahead, the head node is drawn at the judge line (clamped to 0) instead of its true (negative) position. Result: a ghost hold whose head already passed renders a head sitting exactly on the judge line, overlapping other notes, which is visually wrong. If the intent is to hide the passed head, skip creating the view; if it's to keep the tail visible, position the head at its real coordinates and let the link clipping hide the part beyond the line.

`EnsureLayers()` recreates both layers if either pointer becomes invalid, but the surviving root is not detached — if only `_noteRoot` was freed, a fresh `CommunityStageChrome` (and a new backdrop/bars if `BuildCommunityStageChrome` re-runs) is added next to the stale one, duplicating chrome and leaking the old node. Also `NoteLayer` is handed to `GameplayNoteRenderer`/`NoteLayer` consumers; if the renderer ever recreates it, those consumers keep a freed reference and call `AddChild` on it. Prefer creating the layers once in `_Ready` (or a `_EnterTree` guard with an explicit `_layersBuilt` flag) and never reallocating them.

`Cubic.DerivativeRoots()` never compares the returned roots against `lo`/`hi` itself; it relies on callers. Every caller does filter (`u > lo && u < hi` in `Roots`, `u > 0.0 && u < 1.0` in `IsFiniteAndPositive`), so the current behavior is correct, but this primitive is easy to misuse. More importantly, in `Roots` the double root is emitted only when `root > 0.0`; when `discriminant == 0` (a double root) a single root is emitted, and the partitioning code then evaluates it — that path is fine. However near-degenerate cubics (|A| slightly greater than 1e-15 but roots exploding in magnitude) produce roots far outside the interval; the consumers filter them, but the epsilon-based quadratic fallback branch uses `-C / (2.0 * B)` without any finiteness guard, so `B` subnormal can yield `Inf`/`NaN` roots. Add an explicit `double.IsFinite` check on emitted roots so `AddReceiverBoundaries`/`IsFiniteAndPositive` never receive non-finite cut points.

Tangent (touching) crossings are systematically dropped here. The extra `Math.Abs(polynomial.Evaluate(cut)) < 1e-12` pass only catches a root that coincides with a sub-interval bound that lies on the root grid; when the polynomial just touches zero at an interior point (e.g. a path that grazes the receiver edge and bounces back, which the per-frame exit/reentry guarantee is supposed to cover), that zero is a *derivative* root, so the sub-interval endpoints around it do not change sign and the `Math.Sign(va) == Math.Sign(vb)` continue skips the whole range. The 1e-12 absolute tolerance is also scale-dependent (it is meaningless for large centers like 1e6 and far too loose for tiny widths). A tangential contact is currently reported as no contact at all, so a real touch/grazing judgement tick is silently lost. Consider explicitly reporting every derivative cut whose value is (near) zero relative to the interval's magnitude, and use a relative tolerance instead of 1e-12.

`AddReceiverBoundaries` starts the loop at `Math.Max(0, FindRuntimeInterval(from))`, but `FindRuntimeInterval` performs no range validation. For `from >= _runtimeTimes[^1]` (i.e. beyond the last path point) it returns `_curves.Length - 1`, and for any `from` past the path end the loop body immediately hits `if (start >= to) break;` only if `to` is also past the end — otherwise it evaluates the *last* interval with `start + (end - start) * cut` values that can lie outside `[from, to]` and be discarded by `AddTime`, wasting the work but also risking mis-indexing when `from > _runtimeTimes[^1]`. Passing a `from` greater than the last runtime time (e.g. a frame after the mixer tail) means the returned boundaries can be inconsistent. Add explicit clamping/validation of `from` and `to` against `[_runtimeTimes[0], _runtimeTimes[^1]]`, and guard `from <= to`.

The runtime (binary64) helpers accept non-finite input without validation, unlike their exact counterparts (`ToBarTime`, `BpmAtSeconds`). `RuntimeSecondsAt(double.NaN)` / `RuntimeBarAt(double.NaN)` / `RuntimeBpmAt(double.NaN)` all go through `FindRuntimeBarSegment`/`FindRuntimeSecondSegment`, whose comparisons with `NaN` are always false, so they silently return segment 0 instead of raising or short-circuiting. Given the class doc states these are the hot-path runtime lookups, silently producing a wrong answer for NaN is a real hazard; at minimum document the precondition or add a `double.IsFinite` guard (throwing `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`) as is done elsewhere in this file.

`V2ScrollMap` never validates its input and the runtime segment search mixes lossy comparison with strict bounds: nothing checks that event times are strictly increasing or that `Value` is finite, and `_runtimeTimes` is a `ToDouble()` projection where two distinct `ExactBarTime`s can collide. Because the search uses strict `_runtimeTimes[mid] < time` with an exact-equality early return, equal binary64 bounds make `u = (time - lo) / (hi - lo)` a division by zero (`u = NaN`) in the interpolation. Add constructor validation (strictly increasing times / finite `Value`), guard `_runtimeTimes[hi] == _runtimeTimes[lo]` (or select segments via exact `ExactBarTime` comparisons), so a malformed scroll list fails fast instead of yielding NaN speeds.

The class-level contract says runtime and exact evaluation must agree at boundaries/ticks (`RuntimeSecondsAt(ExactBarTime)` delegates here via `time.ToDouble()`). Because `_runtimeBars`/`_runtimeSeconds` are stored premultiplied from `ToDouble()`, the runtime path loses precision relative to `ToExactSeconds`; at a BPM event whose exact time does not round-trip exactly through binary64 this can put the caller in the previous segment. There is no test asserting `RuntimeSecondsAt(t) == ToExactSeconds(t).ToDouble()` at every BPM event boundary for non-representable bar times (e.g. `1/3`). Please add a boundary-equivalence test across all event and fractional tick times to confirm the two paths agree.

comments.content: `SmoothRun` is called on every `Evaluate`/`EvaluateRuntime`/`AddReceiverBoundaries` invocation and walks backward/forward linearly over the whole curve array. For a long path with many smooth intervals this turns a nominally O(log n) evaluation into O(n) per sample, which matters because `EvaluateRuntime` is the per-frame hot path and `AddReceiverBoundaries` calls `SmoothRun` once per interval. Since run starts are already known at construction time (they are exactly the intervals where `_centerSlopes[runStart] is not null`), precompute a `int[] _runStartByInterval` array in the constructor and have `SmoothRun` be a lookup.

`PchipSlopes` divides by `h[i]` without checking for zero. `h[i]` comes from `(_points[point + 1].Time - _points[point].Time).ToDouble()`, so two distinct `ExactBarTime`s whose difference rounds to `0.0` in binary64 (very close nodes, which the semantic validator permits since it only requires strict exact ordering) yield `Infinity`/`NaN` in `d[i]`. `IsFiniteAndPositive` only rejects this *after* construction, and `V2PathEvaluator` is also built outside validation (runtime adapter/tests), so the NaN slopes flow into `Hermite` and produce NaN samples instead of a clear failure. Guard `h[i] == 0.0` (e.g. fall back to a zero slope or throw a descriptive exception) in `PchipSlopes`.

comments.content: `IsFiniteAndPositive` documents that width cubics are checked "at both endpoints and every derivative root inside the interval", but `DerivativeRoots()` omits the double root when `discriminant == 0` because of the `if (root > 0.0)` condition — in that case only one (the repeated) root is yielded, which is fine. The real gap is that the check never evaluates the width polynomial at the *left* endpoint `u == 0` beyond the node loop, and more importantly it only inspects derivative roots, so a width cubic that dips below zero without an interior stationary point but with a negative value at `u` just inside the interval (possible when the Hermite slope is very negative and the dip peaks past the interval end) is missed. Since `HermitePolynomial` is a cubic whose sign changes are bounded by its derivative roots, also evaluating the cubic at the sub-interval boundaries created by the derivative roots (i.e. 0, 1 and all roots) would make the claim in the doc comment actually hold.

`AddReceiverBoundaries` runs its root solver over *every* interval from `from` to the path end for *every* receiver, and allocates a fresh `List<double>` and a `new[] { -0.5, 0.5 }` array per interval inside the loop. On the frame hot path this is avoidable garbage churn (the outer `List<double> output` is already supplied). Hoist the `{ -0.5, 0.5 }` array to a `static readonly` field and reuse a scratch list for `cuts` instead of allocating one per `Roots` call.

`V2MixerTicks.TickCount` truncates via `BigInteger.Divide(duration.ImproperNumerator * 8, duration.Denominator)` with no guard on the resulting `count` magnitude. The only bound is `duration < 0`; a chart with an extremely long tail divided into eighths can yield a count large enough that `Enumerate` runs for an unbounded time (judgement counting in `Validate.cs` and the judge engine both call `TickCount`/`Enumerate`). Document/enforce a maximum tick count so malformed or adversarial charts fail fast instead of hanging validation and gameplay.

`ResolvePackagePath` only compares against `rootPrefix` (root + one separator), so the root directory itself is rejected, but more importantly the check is purely textual and the symlink/reparse check in `ValidatePackageTree` is a TOCTOU gate: between the tree walk and the later `File.ReadAllBytes`/`Directory.Enumerate...` calls, a directory component can be swapped for a symlink/junction that points outside the root (or a file replaced by a link), and `Path.GetFullPath` will never notice because it does not resolve links. Also `StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase` makes the containment check OS-dependent (on case-sensitive Linux `Root/..` variations are handled by GetFullPath, but case-insensitive matching can accept a sibling directory differing only in case on a case-sensitive FS). Consider using `Path.GetRelativePath` + rejecting `..`/rooted results, and re-verify each resolved path (`File.GetAttributes` / `ResolveLinkTarget`) immediately before use rather than relying on the early tree scan.

`ResolvePackagePath` performs no absolute-path / rooted-path check of `relative` before combining. `Path.Combine(root, rootedPath)` discards `root` entirely; `Path.GetFullPath` then returns an absolute path outside the package. The later `StartsWith(rootPrefix)` check does catch most cases, but on Windows a relative value like `C:foo` or a path whose casing matches a sibling directory can slip through the ordinal-ignore-case prefix test, and the exception is thrown only after the fact. Validate `relative` up front (reject `Path.IsPathRooted(relative)` and any segment equal to `..`) so the failure is deterministic and platform-independent.

`DurationSec` memoizes into two non-volatile instance fields on a shared, immutable-looking record. Concurrent readers can observe `_durationCacheChart == RuntimeChart` while `_durationCacheSec` still holds the value from a previously computed (different) chart (assignments are not atomic as a pair and can be reordered/teared across threads), returning a stale duration. Also the enumeration walks `AllNotes` (a LINQ `Concat` over three lists) twice on every cache miss. If this record is shared across threads (as the doc comment about gameplay/rendering suggests), use a `Lazy<double>`/`Interlocked` guard keyed only by the reference, or compute the duration once in the constructor/`BuildLoaded` and store it as an `init` property.

The sustain-chain validation loops are inconsistent about what counts as an invalid linkage. `ConvertLegacyNote` starts `seen` with the head id but the `allById`/`incoming` pass earlier skips nodes whose `SubNoteId == -1`, so a node that is *itself* a head (HoldHead/MixerHead) can be a valid chain link target: it passes `node.Type != expectedNodeType` only if type matches, but a HoldHead pointing at another HoldHead would be rejected as "wrong node type" — good — yet an unrelated *head* node can be silently unreachable and never reported, because the final `consumedPathNodeIds` sweep only checks path *nodes*, not heads. More concretely, `incoming` is computed for every non-`-1` `SubNoteId` including nodes whose parent is not a head (e.g. a Tap node pointing at a HoldNode), so a Tap can consume the incoming slot and cause a legitimate head to fail with a misleading `"shared by multiple sustain chains"` diagnostic instead of `"dangling/wrong parent"`. Validate that every `SubNoteId` link originates from a Hold/Mixer head (or a Hold/Mixer node) before counting `incoming`.

The 1e-9 absolute tolerance on `expected` seconds is compared against a value that can be on the order of minutes; an absolute epsilon of 1e-9 s is far below the binary64 rounding error accumulated through the recurrence (`previous.Seconds + delta*240/Bpm`) once the chart is long, so perfectly valid legacy files can be rejected with a spurious "continuity mismatch". Conversely, a genuinely bad offset in a short chart could pass. Use a relative/ULP-aware tolerance (e.g. `1e-9 * Math.Max(1.0, Math.Abs(expected))`) or compare exact rationals as `ExactBarTime` already allows.

Legacy `Note.Width`, `Note.Position` and `Center` are copied straight into the v2 semantic model without any finiteness/range check (unlike `BarTime`, which goes through `SafeBarTime`). A NaN/Infinity `Width` or a non-finite `Position` propagates into `V2Chart`, and `V2SemanticValidator.ValidateChart` may accept it if it only checks `BarTime`; the value then flows into the gameplay digest and rendering. Validate `double.IsFinite(note.Width)` (and positivity/sign if the spec requires) plus `Position`/`Center` finiteness here and throw `InvalidDataException`, since `ConvertLegacyChart` is the boundary that must guarantee canonical output.

comments.content: `SafeId` accepts any `.`/`_`/`-` after the first character, so values like `a..b`, `a.`, or window-reserved names pass through unchanged as IDs. Combined with the fact that these IDs become file-relative identifiers elsewhere this is fragile; more immediately, `ConvertLegacyPackageChart` feeds `SafeId(packId, ...)` and `SafeId(legacyChart.Name, ...)` results into `V2SemanticValidator.ValidatePack`, so the validation result depends on whether the caller passes a `chartId` argument that was already sanitized. Prefer rejecting/normalizing IDs against the same grammar the v2 decoder enforces (`[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*`, no `..`) so that `ConvertLegacy*` and `LoadStrict` accept the same ID space.

`LoadLegacyPackageChart(string legacyChartPath, string packId, string? chartId, JudgePreset preset)` silently discards the `chartId`/`packId` values' intent when it forwards `ReadOnlySpan<byte>.Empty` as the audio bytes: the resulting `GameplayDigest` is computed over no audio, so two packages with different audio but identical charts will share a digest. More importantly, the overload intentionally loads without audio, which makes the produced `V2LoadedPackageChart.GameplayDigest` not comparable with the bytes-based overload — this is a silent semantic difference that callers can easily miss. Either document the difference prominently in XML docs on this overload or make the digest computation skip audio when bytes are empty in a labelled way (e.g. parameter `includeAudio: false`).

The in-memory `LoadStrict(metaJson, chartJson, chartId, audioBytes, path)` overload does not call `V2PackageValidator.ValidatePackStructure`/`ValidateEntry`, so it skips the coverage provided by the disk path: no `V2SemanticValidator.ValidateChart` call, no `ResolveAudio`/preview resolution, no `chart.ChartId` vs entry comparison beyond the one manual string check, and no validation of the other declared charts' file ids. It also accepts `resolvedAudioBytes` of zero length with no diagnostic. This makes the two `LoadStrict` entry points validate materially different subsets of the format; either route the in-memory path through the same `ValidateEntry` with a synthetic hook set, or add explicit documentation/tests proving the gap is intentional.

comments.content: The public speed helpers are unguarded: a NaN/Infinity in any operand (e.g. a chart/second value that ends up NaN upstream, or a scroll curve sampled outside its key range) propagates silently into `DistancePixels`, which then feeds `Mathf.Max(0f, ...)` / `PositionAt` and can place the note at a garbage or NaN position for every frame. Similarly, negative `basePixelsPerSecond`/`playerSpeed` silently reverse the scroll direction with no signal. Since this is described as the shared authoritative rule used by the renderer, consider making the contract explicit — either clamp/sanitize non-finite inputs here or guard in the caller — so a bad input fails loudly instead of producing invisible/mirrored notes.

`DistancePixels` mixes two different semantics without documenting it: the result is signed by `(noteSecond - currentSecond)` (future notes positive, past notes negative), but the multiplier `scrollSpeed` can itself be negative (legacy negative `DropSpeed`, per the test `legacy negative DropSpeed preserves signed approach distance`). With a negative scroll speed a *future* note yields a negative distance, i.e. the sign no longer means "future/past", while `FallthroughSpeedPixelsPerSecond` deliberately drops that sign via `Math.Abs`. These two behaviors are easy to misuse (callers also clamp with `Mathf.Max(0f, ...)`). Please state the sign contract in the XML doc for both methods (`DistancePixels`: signed, positive = approaching; `FallthroughSpeed`: magnitude only, direction-agnostic) so the Abs is not read as masking a direction bug.

`Math.Abs` here makes a zero-speed configuration indistinguishable from a bug: the renderer (`MissFallSpeedPx`) then silently clamps to the 60px/s floor, so a chart or player setting of 0 (or a negative `playerSpeed` mistaken for a direction flag) produces an unexplained animation speed rather than an error. Also, `Math.Abs` on the aggregated product loses where the sign came from — a negative `playerSpeed` intended as a direction will be treated as a magnitude. Recommend validating the inputs (positive `basePixelsPerSecond`/`playerSpeed`, non-zero magnitude) at this single authoritative point, or at least documenting that the returned value is a magnitude and that the renderer applies its own floor.

`V2DiagnosticException` is declared here after use but it is not an auto-generated symbol — the file compiles only by declaration order within the file, not by referenced-file order. The real issue: this factory performs no null-guard on `exception`. Both call sites (`EditorValidationService` lines 22 and 38) invoke it from `catch` blocks, so this is low risk, but the record's own string fields are non-nullable reference types assigned unchecked, meaning `new V2Diagnostic(Warning, null!, "/", null!)` is representable and will silently flow into editor UI / JSON serialization. Add validation (or `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull`) to make the invariant explicit.

comments.content: The record exposes positional constructor parameters with no null/length validation, and `JsonPointer` is documented as RFC 6901-like elsewhere (`V2DiagnosticException.NormalizePointer` guarantees "/" for empty). Direct constructions in `EditorValidationService` (lines 65+) pass a `pointer` value that may be empty, bypassing the exception's normalization, so the invariant "JsonPointer is always a valid pointer" is inconsistent across producers. Consider a validating constructor or a shared normalizer so downstream editor consumers can rely on the pointer being well-formed.

Enum members have no explicit values, so numeric values are assignment-order dependent (Warning=0, Error=1). If this enum is ever serialized numerically (JSON without a string-enum converter) or persisted, inserting an `Info`/`None` level before `Warning` shifts values and breaks stored data. Downstream code only compares `== V2DiagnosticSeverity.Warning`, so nothing breaks today, but pinning explicit values is cheap insurance for a "stable" diagnostic contract.

`FromException` is the only logic in this file and has no direct test (no `FromException` reference exists under `tools/chart-editor-tests`). It is reached only indirectly through `EditorValidationService`, so a regression in field mapping (e.g. severity forced to `Error`, pointer normalization preserved) would surface as an opaque assertion failure elsewhere. Add a focused test asserting that the mapping copies `SourceName`/`JsonPointer`/`Reason` verbatim and forces `V2DiagnosticSeverity.Error`.

The decoder (`V2JsonDecoder.ReadPathNodes`) does reject empty arrays, but the model itself is public and constructible by any caller (integration/adapters, tests, future encoders); nothing on the record enforces the non-empty invariant, so the failure would surface as an unclear index error deep in evaluation rather than a clear contract violation. comments.content: `AllNotes` allocates a fresh compiler-generated iterator/enumerator state machine on every access. It is used by validation and digest computation which run over every note, and being a `get` property it looks cheap to callers but is not — repeated enumeration of `chart.AllNotes` re-creates the state machine each time. Consider materializing the flattened list once (lazily cached) or exposing it as a method/collection so call sites don't accidentally re-enumerate in hot paths.

The `_ => JudgePreset.Hard` fallback intentionally implements the spec rule "Hard and above share the Hard preset", but it also silently absorbs any future `V2Difficulty` value added to the enum and any invalid cast (`(V2Difficulty)99`) into `Hard`. That masks decoder/enum drift with no signal. Since the set of difficulties is small and frozen, enumerating them explicitly (`Hard => JudgePreset.Hard, Mega => ..., Giga => ..., Tech => ..., Custom => ...`) would make adding a new difficulty a compile-time error instead of a silent behavior change. At minimum, document on the property that all difficulties other than Casual/Normal map to Hard.

`NotesOf` falls through to `NotesRight` for any value that is not `Left`/`Center`, so an invalid cast such as `(Track)42` silently returns right-track notes instead of failing. The mapping is a pure 1:1 enum→array lookup, so use an exhaustive switch that throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` on unknown values (C# exhaustive switch expression on a non-flagged enum with `_ => throw ...`), preventing wrong data from being read/rendered silently.

Related to the empty-nodes invariant: `Left`/`Right` on `V2Note` and `EndTime` here are computed from `Center`/`Width`/`Nodes` that the model assumes are valid (finite, `Width > 0`, sorted node times). Since these records are pure DTOs with no validation, downstream consumers (evaluation/digest/runtime adapter) will produce garbage or throw on malformed data if any construction path bypasses `V2SemanticValidator`. Kindly confirm the semantic validation in `V2SemanticValidator.ValidateChart` is always run before any consumer touches these computed members (for legacy-import path in `Integration.cs` it is called, but it should be enforced for all decode/encode paths), and that tests cover empty-nodes / zero-width / NaN inputs at the model boundary.

If a duplicate-free JSON contains a non-string `type` (e.g. `"type": 5`), `ReadString` already throws, so this path is unreachable for non-strings — yet the code calls `GetString()` without null-forgiving and outside any guard. More importantly, the string was already validated but not captured; re-reading it is fragile. comments.content: Optional package paths accept an empty string (`"audio": ""`) — `ReadPackagePath` rejects empty, so an explicit empty string throws. But the schema likely intends an absent key for "no path"; if the frozen v2 contract allows `""` to mean absent (common convention), this would incorrectly reject it. Confirm the writer (`V2Writer`) never emits `""`; otherwise this is a mismatch between encode/decode. If empty-string-means-absent is permitted, normalize it here.

`ExactBarTime.FromJsonComponents` throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for negative/over-limit components and non-positive denominator. `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` derives from `ArgumentException`, so the catch here is currently fine — but note that `ReadSafeInteger` minima (bar>=0, numerator>=0, denominator>=1) already guard these. If those minima are ever relaxed, the type-based catch remains correct. No change required, but worth a comment noting this relies on both minima and the ArgumentException base type.

`hasLevel == hasUnrated` correctly rejects both-present and both-absent. Verified `checked((int)ReadSafeInteger(levelElement, ..., 1, 99))` is safe — the range 1..99 fits in int, so the unchecked cast cannot overflow. However, `checked(...)` conveys a false sense of risk; since the bound is pre-validated by `ReadSafeInteger`, the `checked` is redundant. Not a defect, but consider removing `checked` or documenting why it's there to avoid confusion.

No maximum input size is enforced: `File.ReadAllBytes` and the `ReadOnlySpan<byte>` overload's `ToArray()` fully materialize the buffer before any validation, and every `DecodePack(ReadOnlyMemory<byte>)` path allocates a `JsonDocument` over the whole payload. A maliciously large pack/chart (multi-GB) will OOM before the depth limit (128) has any effect — a resource-exhaustion risk for any loader that decodes untrusted files. Consider a size guard (e.g. reject > a few MB, or > reasonable bound for the doc types) before parsing, and note that `ReadOnlySpan<byte>.ToArray()` defeats the allocation-free intent of the span overload.

`ValidateJsonTree` recurses over the entire tree and is invoked on every decode, then `Properties`, `ReadNotes`, etc. walk the same tree again — a full extra O(n) pass over every property name and string plus per-node HashSet allocation for objects. For large charts (many notes/nodes) this doubles traversal cost. Consider merging duplicate detection into the `Properties` helper (which already enumerates each object's properties and can use `Dictionary.Add` to detect duplicates with a diagnostic) instead of a separate pre-walk; this removes the second full-tree pass AND eliminates the `Properties.Add` non-diagnostic throw risk noted below.

This `result.Add` relies entirely on `ValidateJsonTree` having already rejected duplicates. If a validation entry point ever bypasses `Parse`/`ValidateJsonTree` (or the pre-walk misses a case), `Add` throws `ArgumentException` (non-`V2DiagnosticException`), breaking the fail-closed contract with a wrong exception type. Use `TryAdd` and throw a diagnostic on duplicate to make this helper self-defensive and independent of the pre-walk.

Path-traversal hardening here rejects `..`, backslash, `:`, NUL, and empty/`.`/`..` segments, and requires NFC elsewhere only for display text — but it does NOT reject Unicode normalized `..` (fullwidth/other) or control chars. Since `Properties`/`ValidateJsonTree` reject unpaired surrogates and control chars only for display text, a path segment could contain e.g. `\u002e\u002e`-adjacent Unicode dot variants that a downstream filesystem/normalizer could fold to `..`. The current signature silently accepts impossible values; nothing crashes, but negative combo is silently clamped to the 1.0x baseline rather than being surfaced. This is acceptable as a research/optional policy as long as callers never pass negative combo. If this is meant to be defensive, add an explicit `Math.Max(0, comboBeforeHit)` before division with a comment documenting the clamp policy, and confirm the intended max combo of 300 matches the verified original data.
