comments.content: `buffScoreFactor` is only lower-bounded by `Math.Max(0.0, ...)`. A `double.NaN` passes through `Math.Max(0.0, NaN)` as NaN, `Math.Floor(NaN)` is NaN, and `(int)NaN` in C# is an unspecified value (0 on x64, int.MinValue on ARM) — undefined behavior depending on platform. `double.PositiveInfinity` or a very large factor also overflows the int cast (unspecified result/0). Since this is math kept for fidelity of an optional policy, validate with `double.IsFinite(buffScoreFactor)` and clamp the final product to `int.MinValue..int.MaxValue` before casting.

The fast path `perfectMain >= totalMainNote` returns 10000 before considering Great/Good. That is correct only when `perfectMain == totalMainNote` and the other counts are 0. With inconsistent/overlapping inputs (e.g. `ClearPercent100(100, 5, 0, 100)`), it returns 10000 while the actual weighted value would be >10000 and clamp to 10000 anyway — so the result is the same. However, with a *small* total and inflated perfect (e.g. `(50, 0, 0, 10)`), it short-circuits to 10000 masking an obviously invalid input. Negative counts are also not rejected; `weighted` can go negative and only the final `Math.Clamp` saves it to 0. For a fidelity helper this is likely acceptable, but if callers can ever pass partition counts, consider validating `perfectMain/greatMain/goodMain >= 0` and `perfectMain + greatMain + goodMain <= totalMainNote`, or at least documenting that inputs are trusted.

Two issues here:
1. Boundary inconsistency with `ClearPercent100`: for `holdingTotal == 0` this returns `Miss`, whereas `ClearPercent100` returns 0 (also effectively "empty = worst") — so they are actually consistent in spirit, but note that an empty mixer (0 ticks) yields `Miss` rather than `Perfect`/`None`; confirm against original behavior, since a mixer with zero ticks that was never played arguably should not be graded Miss.
2. `holdingHit > holdingTotal` (inconsistent input) yields `rate > 1.0` → Perfect, which silently masks bad data. Also a negative `holdingHit` with positive total falls to Miss, which is fine.

At minimum, clamp `rate` to `[0, 1]` and reject negative hit counts so the function can't return a grade from nonsensical input.

The magic literals `0.699999988` and `0.5` are duplicated with `ClearPercent100` (which uses `0.699999988` and `0.5` for weights). The float-derived constant `0.699999988` appears in two places with no named constant explaining *why* it is not `0.7`. If the original-float constant ever needs updating (or if a new threshold is added), these can drift. Extract shared `private const double GreatWeight = 0.699999988;` / `GoodWeight = 0.5` with a comment referencing the source (float `0.7f` / `0.5f`), and use them in both methods.

The loop only returns when a pair satisfies `b.Second > a.Second`; if the first pair has equal seconds (`b.Second == a.Second`) but a later pair is valid, the `if` body is skipped and the loop keeps advancing `i`, so a query inside the first segment silently falls through to the final fallback (returning a wrong bar). For `Nodes.Count == 1` the loop never runs, so the same thing happens for any query. In both cases the returned bar is not the node's actual `BarTime`, so `MixerRuntime` grace/loss deadlines are computed in the wrong bar. Also, when `@second` is before `Nodes[0].Second`, the first valid pair extrapolates backwards without clamping to `path.Head.BarTime`. The legacy `BoundsAtLegacy` explicitly handles `< 1e-9` durations and clamps outside-range times; this function should do the same.

The fallback slope uses unexplained magic constants `150 / 240`: 150 is presumably a hard-coded BPM and 240 the seconds-per-bar numerator. For a legacy chart whose actual BPM differs from 150 this yields a wrong seconds→bar mapping once the query passes the terminal node, which distorts mixer loss/grace deadlines. At minimum extract named constants; better, derive the slope from the terminal segment (or the chart's BPM data) instead of assuming 150 BPM.
comments.existing_code: return path.Head.BarTime + (second - path.StartTime) * 150 / 240;

A path that carries a `V2BpmTimeline` but no `V2Evaluator` will therefore evaluate geometry through `BoundsAtLegacy` while its bar/deadline math uses the exact v2 timeline, mixing two different time bases for the same sustain. The selection condition should mirror `SustainPath` (and be documented) so bar mapping and geometry stay consistent.

comments.content: `BoundsAt` documents a strict rule (v2 only when both `V2Evaluator` and `V2BpmTimeline` are set), but `BoundsAtRuntime` silently degrades to `BoundsAtLegacy` when either is null. This fallback input is not a v2 chart node list; its `Nodes` may be sparse endpoints only, so the silently produced bounds can be wrong and the failure is invisible. Either throw (or `Debug.Assert`) on partial setup or make the fallback explicit via a caller-side decision.

Add construction-time validation (non-empty, sorted by `Second`, non-null nodes, head matches `HeadId`).

comments.content: `BoundsAtRuntime` re-does the null checks already performed by `BoundsAt`, and it is public, so the guard is duplicated but the semantic is inconsistent (private legacy fallback). Also each call performs a BPM segment binary search plus a PCHIP interval search — for a hot per-frame/per-note path this is acceptable, but the duplicated guard should be removed so the invalid-state fallback has a single source of truth.

The lock compares `noteTime` to the armed value with exact double equality, and several contracts in this tiny class are implicit. Concrete issues:

1. Exact equality is fragile: any future caller that feeds a slightly re-derived time (e.g. a time offset/speed-scaled value, a time accumulated by summing deltas) will match nothing but itself and silently defeat the protection, or reject a legitimately simultaneous press. The "known note time" semantics are batch identity, not numeric equivalence; either compare with an explicit epsilon (e.g. `Math.Abs(noteTime - _lockedTime.Value) <= Tolerance`), or better, key the lock on a stable note identity (index/id) rather than a double.
2. NaN handling is inconsistent: when unarmed `LockedTime` is NaN, but `CanUse(double.NaN)` returns `true` while unarmed and `false` once armed with a non-NaN value (NaN != NaN). Conversely, arming with `CommitResolved(double.NaN)` permanently accepts only NaN and rejects everything else, silently freezing judging for the frame. Invalid/non-finite times should be rejected explicitly (`if (!double.IsFinite(noteTime)) throw/return`) instead of flowing into state.
3. No thread-safety: `_lockedTime` is read in `IsArmed`/`LockedTime`/`CanUse` and written in `Reset`/`CommitResolved` with no synchronization. Current usage (per-frame reset on the main gameplay thread) happens to be single-threaded, but nothing in the type documents or enforces that; if judging is ever driven from a worker/audio-callback thread, `Reset` racing with `CommitResolved` can drop a commit (lock silently cleared mid-frame) or produce a torn read of a `Nullable<double>` (struct of bool + double). Make the constraint explicit by documenting "single-threaded, reset once per frame before processing presses", or use `Interlocked.CompareExchange`/a lock to be safe.
4. Lifecycle contract is undocumented and easy to misuse: `Reset` unconditionally clears the lock and `CommitResolved` keeps only the first value (`??=`). Whether the lock is per-note or per-frame is invisible from the type, so a caller that forgets `Reset` leaks the lock across frames (judging dead until reset) and a caller that resets too eagerly makes the protection a no-op. Add a short XML-doc summary stating the intended lifecycle (e.g. "armed by the first resolved note of the frame; caller must `Reset()` at the start of every input-flush/frame") and why Mine units are excluded.

Note: the exact-equality behavior is currently pinned by `TestV2InputTimeLock` (same-time allowed, 1 ms difference rejected). If the epsilon/identity approach is adopted, those assertions must be updated to reflect the new tolerance rather than the bit-exact comparison.

Release is forwarded to `_inputs`/`HoldContacts` even when the id is not active (double release, release after `Clear()`, or a release that arrived before its press). Move already ignores unknown ids for exactly this reason. Downstream consumers (e.g. `GameplayMain.Mixer.UpdateMixerState`, which treats every Release as an input event) will then see a phantom release that can prematurely end a hold/contact. Gate the Release on `_active.Remove` succeeding.

`Press` samples are added to `_touches` and `_presses` but never to `_initialTouches`, so the documented frame-start snapshot omits contacts that began this frame. Consumers such as `UpdateMixerState` read `InitialTouches` to seed hold/mixer contacts and will miss a freshly pressed finger, and the semantics ("frame-start snapshot" vs "initial contact") are ambiguous. Either add the pressed samples to `_initialTouches` as well, or document/rename the property (e.g. `FrameStartTouches`) so callers do not rely on the wrong meaning.

The buffer is documented as owning lifetimes across input and frame sources but has no synchronization: `Queue` may be called from the input/UI thread while `CollectFrame` iterates `_pending` and mutates `_active`/`_touches` on the frame thread. Concurrent `List`/`Dictionary` mutation causes corruption or `InvalidOperationException` and can leave `_active` inconsistent with the snapshots. Either serialize access (document a single thread) or guard `_pending` and `_active` with a lock and swap pending batches inside `CollectFrame`.

Consider snapshotting `_pending` into a local list and clearing it before processing (or wrapping the loop in try/finally) so a failing callback cannot cause duplicated event application.

comments.content: `RemoveTouches` scans the whole list for every press/move and calls `RemoveAt` per match, which is O(n·k) and becomes quadratic with many simultaneous pointers/secondary samples. Run one compaction pass instead (`_touches.RemoveAll(t => t.Id == id)` or a stable in-place filter) to keep per-event cost linear.
comments.suggestion_code: private void RemoveTouches(int id) => _touches.RemoveAll(touch => touch.Id == id);

comments.content: These properties expose the internal mutable lists as `IReadOnlyList`. Callers can down-cast back to `List<T>` and mutate them, or add additional `_touches` entries via the callback while iterating from outside; the "reused and valid until next CollectFrame" contract is also unenforced. Consider returning `CollectionsMarshal`-backed spans, `ReadOnlyCollection<T>` wrappers created once, or a copy-on-demand, and explicitly documenting the aliasing contract.

A second `Press` for an already active id silently overwrites the `ActivePointer` (reset to `Began` and new position) with no release recorded for the first contact. Platforms can emit duplicate press events; this would duplicate `_presses` entries and leak an unclosed Hold contact. Either ignore a duplicate press for an active id or emit an implicit release first.

Clamping `until` up to the previous `_time` can push the frame's end past `path.EndTime` when audio regresses after the sustain already ended (e.g. `_time` was 2.0 = EndTime, then a stale frame arrives at 1.9 -> `until` stays 2.0; or a frame at 1.99 followed by a regression leaves `until` at 2.0 which is fine, but if `_time` was ever advanced beyond EndTime by an earlier caller this clamp silently reopens the interval past the path end). More importantly, the order `Min(EndTime)` then `Max(old)` means the Max can undo the EndTime cap: any pre-regression `_time` greater than `EndTime` (possible because the public API allows arbitrary `until`, and `path.EndTime > StartTime` is not validated) results in geometry being evaluated after the sustain ended. Apply the EndTime cap after the monotonic clamp.
comments.suggestion_code:
if (_time is { } old) until = Math.Max(until, old);
until = Math.Min(until, path.EndTime);

comments.content:
The `next < _time.Value` guard is effectively unreachable and its error semantics are misleading:
- `inputTime` is clamped with `Math.Max(..., _time.Value)`, so it can never be below `_time`.
- `next` is the min of `inputTime` and `tickTime`; a past *tick* (`ticks[tick] < _time`) does make `next < _time`, but the throw aborts the whole frame *after* the previous loop iterations already applied inputs, settled ticks and mutated `Placed`/`_lossBar` — leaving observable partial state, and the caller never advances its tick cursor so the next frame throws again forever.
Also, this throw is raised on the first iteration even when the past tick is *before* the clamp window only because a caller replayed a stale tick list; the message points at `ticks` but the same condition would be hit for any non-monotonic `ticks` input. Skipping already-past ticks (advance `tick` while `ticks[tick] < _time`) is safer than throwing, or at minimum validate the whole `ticks` list up front (it is documented as ascending, so a non-ascending entry is the real contract violation worth reporting) before any state mutation.

A `Began` event is allowed to resurrect known-but-dropped pointers, and any `Began` (including one at the same timestamp right after a removal) unconditionally re-adds the touch. That is intended, but note that a `Began` whose position is non-null only re-establishes contact — the *receiver* is only re-assigned when `CanCatch` passes and `(Phase == Began || Controller == Id)`. Combined with the `Controller` invalidation in `AdvanceFrame` (Controller nulled if the owner is missing from `seed`), a second finger that owns the controller and is present in `seed` but never re-reported in `inputs` keeps control, while one absent from `seed` loses it silently — a sustained stationary finger that the seed list omits for one frame will drop controller ownership even though it never left the track. Consider whether controller invalidation should be driven by an explicit release rather than by seed membership.

The early-placement gate returns *after* `_touches[input.Id] = position;` but *before* placement, so a pre-start press that is rejected still leaves a live touch entry. That touch will be used by `Observe` as soon as `time >= path.StartTime` (the pre-start early return only short-circuits `Catching`, but the touch remains in `_touches` for the subsequent cut-based `Observe` calls once the interval crosses `StartTime`), effectively letting a finger that was never granted early placement catch the sustain at start. If the intent is that unaccepted pre-start contacts must not create a receiver (as the test `unaccepted pre-start click does not create a receiver` states), the touch should not be registered either, or the rejection check must run before `_touches[input.Id] = position`.
comments.suggestion_code:
if (input.Time < path.StartTime && !input.AllowEarlyPlacement) return;
        _touches[input.Id] = position;
comments.existing_code: if (input.Time < path.StartTime && !input.AllowEarlyPlacement) return;

comments.content: `Observe` is invoked twice per cell, once exactly at `left` and once at the cell midpoint. At the cell start the bounds are evaluated exactly at a cut — which is where a boundary crossing occurs — so `CanCatch` at that instant is evaluated on the boundary value. Because `AddBoundaries` only adds roots strictly inside `(from, to)` (mixer geometry lines 20 and 38 use `>` and `<`), the crossing is excluded from the cell but `left` for the next cell is the crossing itself, so `Observe(left, ...)` sees the crossing point (inclusive on both edges) and may report the *old* membership for a cell it no longer belongs to, delaying the loss by one cell. Using `left + epsilon`-based sampling for the boundary observation, or documenting that `left` deliberately uses the tangent value, would make the transition timing deterministic instead of dependent on `CanCatch`'s 1e-10 inclusive tolerance.

In `auto` mode `Placed`/`Position` are forced each call, but `_lossBar` is only reset when `Catching` is true, and `ReceptionAt` consults `_lossBar` via `barAt(second)`. Since auto always sets `Position = bounds.Center`, `Catching` is essentially always true, so this is mostly benign — however if `path.EndTime` is reached and `auto` is toggled off mid-sustain, the stale `_lossBar` from a prior manual phase (never cleared because `Catching` was false and `Placed` false at that instant) can make `ReceptionAt` report `Grace`/`Disconnected` for an auto-held sustain. Consider clearing `_lossBar` whenever `auto` forces placement.

`ReceptionAt` uses the *current* `Catching` flag with an arbitrary `second` — a public query on an existing-but-arbitrary timestamp. Asking `ReceptionAt(t)` for a `t` far in the past (or future) returns the state of the last observed instant, not the reception at `t`, and the magic `1e-12` epsilon is unexplained. Since the method is public and consumed by other systems, this contract mismatch is easy to misuse; documenting it as "reception at the last observed time" (or removing the unused `second` argument) would prevent incorrect external reasoning about grace.

`_cuts` is sorted but not deduplicated, and `AddBoundaries` allocates a fresh `List<double>` for every touch on every `Advance` call (v2 branch) and may emit the same root twice (once for the receiver and once for a touch at the same position). For a sustained chord with many simultaneous touches and long frames this is O(touches × boundary lists) allocations per frame plus redundant cell iterations. If `_cuts` is meant to be an ordered distinct set, clearing the per-touch bar buffers and deduplicating `_cuts` after sort would reduce both allocations and duplicate `Observe` calls (each `Observe` is not free — it iterates `_touches`).

The steal path only resets the stolen value and reassigns it; the previous owner is never told its object was taken, so both callers now hold the same reference and keep mutating it (double-add to scene tree, double-release, one caller's state clobbering the other). Because the stolen entry's `InUse` stays `true`, the later `Release()` by the *original* owner will also succeed and mark the entry free while the new owner still uses it — a subsequent `Acquire()` can then hand out an object still in use. Either throw/return false when exhausted, or expose an eviction callback (`Action<T>? onEvict`) so the prior owner can detach, and track the lease owner so a stale release is rejected rather than silently freeing an actively-leased entry. At minimum this needs to be documented if callers are expected to tolerate sharing.

The pool has no synchronization: `Acquire`/`Release`/`IsInUse`/`ResetAll` mutate and enumerate the shared `_entries` list and the `_nextLeaseOrder` counter without locking. If a pool is ever shared across threads (e.g. audio/render), concurrent `Acquire` can hand the same entry to two callers, `_entries.Add` during enumeration throws, and the `LeaseOrder` counter can produce duplicate ordering. Either document/enforce single-thread affinity (e.g. `Debug.Assert` in a thread-check) or wrap the mutating methods in a `lock`.

Grouping on exact `double` equality means the start-before-end ordering only applies when start and end are bitwise identical. Times derived from different floating-point expressions (e.g. `t` vs `t + 0.36` vs an accumulated frame delta) that are mathematically equal but differ by an ulp are treated as distinct instants: the end is processed in an earlier group than the start, so the counting is order-dependent and the peak can be off by one relative to the naive/expected value. If the conservative "both coexist" semantics is intended, bucket times with a tolerance (e.g. round to a small quantum or compare with an epsilon) before grouping. If exact grouping is intentional, add a test covering near-equal but non-identical boundaries to lock the behavior.

`PeakOverWindow` silently drops non-finite hit times here, but the `ActivityInterval` path in `PeakOverIntervals` performs the same filtering internally. Consider factoring this filtering into one place so the two overloads stay consistent; currently a caller passing `NaN`/`Infinity` hits gets a quietly under-sized pool with no diagnostics, which can later manifest as visual pops at runtime rather than a clear failure.
comments.existing_code: var hits = hitTimes.Where(double.IsFinite).OrderBy(static t => t).ToArray();

comments.content: Each `SustainPath` contributes exactly one pooled object over its whole `[StartTime, EndTime]` span, regardless of length. Long sustains (which the renderer may split into multiple view/segment objects) will therefore be under-counted, and since `PeakOverIntervals` will report a low peak, `SustainCapacity` can be clamped below actual demand. Please confirm the renderer only ever uses one object per sustain path, or scale the contribution by the number of visual segments per path.

comments.content: `Get` returns the live stored instance and `TryUpdate`/`LoadJson` store the caller's/deserialized object by reference, so any caller can mutate a persisted best (e.g. `store.Get(id)!.Score = 0;` then a later `TryUpdate` with a lower score succeeds). This breaks the best-score invariant the class is supposed to enforce (even the tests exploit this at GradeTests.cs:34). Return a copy (clone) from `Get`/`GetLegacy`, and in `TryUpdate`/`TryUpdateLegacy` store a clone instead of `candidate`.
comments.existing_code:
public ScoreRecord? Get(ScoreIdentity identity) =>
        _records.TryGetValue(identity, out var record) ? record : null;

comments.content: `TryUpdate` decides acceptance using only `candidate.Score`, whereas duplicate resolution during load uses the full multi-field `PreferDuplicate` ordering. The two policies can disagree: a candidate with equal score but better Acc/MaxCombo/judgments is rejected here but would win on load; accordingly, a saved file containing such a record could be replaced (or not) in a way that is not stable across a reload. Align both paths on a single comparison helper (e.g. use `PreferDuplicate(candidate, old)` here, or document/justify score-only acceptance).
comments.suggestion_code:
if (_records.TryGetValue(identity, out var old) && !PreferDuplicate(candidate, old))
            return false;

comments.content: `LoadJson` recomputes `Grade` from `Acc` for every record, silently discarding the persisted grade. This makes load non-idempotent with respect to what was written (a stored record with grade/acc mismatch is rewritten on the next save) and can override an authoritative grade computed elsewhere (e.g. by gameplay rules that account for stage failure or different grading rules). Either recompute grade at write time only (in `PrepareAcceptedRecord`) and trust persisted grades on load, or explicitly document/quantify this migration behavior and gate it on a format version bump.

`LoadJson` mutates the shared `_records`/`_legacyRecords` dictionaries after parsing without any synchronization, and `TryUpdate`/`SaveJson`/`Clear` also touch them unsynchronized. If the store is ever loaded/saved from a background thread (the wrapper defers saves, but nothing prevents concurrent reads, e.g. UI `Get` while a load runs), enumeration in `SaveJson` can throw `InvalidOperationException` and dictionary writes can corrupt state. Make the class explicitly single-threaded (document it) or guard all public members with a lock and snapshot inside `SaveJson`.

`GradeOf` does not validate that `Acc` is finite and within [0, 100]. `NaN`/`+Infinity` fall through to `"D"` (asserted in tests), so a malformed record with a non-finite/negative `Acc` is accepted and persisted, and grade can be downgraded silently. Validate `Acc` in `TryUpdate`/`LoadJson` (e.g. `double.IsFinite(acc) && acc is >= 0 and <= 100`) and reject or clamp invalid values rather than storing them.

`LoadJson` parses the entire JSON twice (once via `JsonDocument.Parse` just to inspect `format`, then again in `DecodeVersioned`/`DecodeLegacy`). For a large score file this doubles parse cost and allocation. Reuse the already-parsed `document.RootElement` (e.g. `Deserialize<StoreData>(document.RootElement)`) instead of re-parsing the raw string.

`KeyOf` uses `:` as a delimiter without escaping. If a `packId` or `diff` contains `:`, distinct pairs can collide (e.g. `("a:b", "c")` and `("a", "b:c")`), causing one legacy record to overwrite/alias another. Validate that neither part contains the delimiter, or use an unambiguous composite key/escaped encoding.
comments.existing_code: public static string KeyOf(string packId, string diff) => $"{packId}:{diff}";

comments.content: `GradeLabel(string grade)` dereferences neither null-guards nor null returns: `grade` is non-nullable but callers pass record values which may be null after deserialization (`Grade` is settable and could be null from malformed JSON, and `PreferDuplicate` already defensively uses `Grade ?? ""`). A null `grade` here returns null into a UI text assignment. Consider `string?` with a fallback, or mark the parameter non-null and validate.
comments.existing_code: public static string GradeLabel(string grade) => grade == "Y" ? "Ψ" : grade;

comments.content:
The tolerance branch ignores `snap` entirely, so for small drags the exact `Time` is returned even when snapping is enabled. This makes snapping state-dependent: the same target second maps to `Time` when reached in one small step but to a grid-snapped bar when reached in a single large step. Example: anchor time = 1/3, tolerance = .001, grid 1/4; a click within tolerance keeps 1/3 (correct per the doc), but a drag to .3335 s (>tolerance) snaps to 1/4. Intended for click preservation, but callers that pass a large `toleranceSeconds` (e.g. 1.5 px / PixelsPerSecond while zoomed out) will prevent snapping for drags that visually move up to a pixel and a half — worth confirming/documenting that this is deliberate, and that `snap` being ignored here is acceptable.

Additionally, `toleranceSeconds` is not validated: a negative or NaN tolerance makes `Math.Abs(delta) <= toleranceSeconds` always false, silently disabling exact-time preservation. Consider `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`/normalizing to 0 for negative or non-finite values, and `ThrowIfNull(bpms)` to fail fast instead of relying on `EditorTime`'s null check.

Two issues with clamping before snapping:
1. `Math.Max(0d, ...)` silently maps any pointer position left of chart start (negative delta) to bar zero. Combined with the tolerance branch, a note at 1/3 dragged slightly left by more than tolerance snaps to 0 even though the visual displacement is tiny — a large, discontinuous jump. Callers like `CanvasGesturePreview.MoveNote` then compute `time != anchor.Time` and apply an unbounded time delta, so a negligible leftward drag can commit a full 1/3-bar jump.
2. Clamping before `SnapSeconds` passes the clamped value through `SecondsToBar`, which does its own `seconds <= 0` clamp — but if the caller is snapped and the grid is coarse, fine. More importantly, `Seconds + delta` may be NaN/Infinity if `pointerSeconds` is non-finite (`SecondsToBar` would throw `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`), so an invalid pointer value surfaces as an exception rather than being handled. Consider validating `pointerSeconds` here (`if (!double.IsFinite(pointerSeconds)) return Time;`) so a bad frame does not throw mid-gesture.

Also, clamping to 0 before snapping means the drag cannot be represented as "negative offset" — if the intent is to let callers decide the lower bound (as `CanvasGesturePreview` already does with `time < ExactBarTime.Zero`), the clamp here duplicates/conflicts with that logic.
comments.existing_code: : EditorTime.SnapSeconds(Math.Max(0d, Seconds + delta), bpms, gridDivisor, snap);

Neighbour bounds are exclusive (`time > previous`, `time < next`), so a node dragged exactly onto its previous node or its next node is rejected even though that is a legitimate (and snapping-reachable) result. Snapping makes this easy to hit: with a coarse grid the nearest grid line often equals a neighbouring node's time, and the preview then returns null, leaving the last accepted preview position while the pointer keeps moving. Consider `>=`/`<=` (or an explicit equality allowance) plus a documented minimum spacing, and add a boundary test where the snapped time equals `previous`/`next`.

The note span is derived as the *current* preview `endTime - currentTime`, so the latest bound is sticky: once a drag clamps the head to a bound, `currentTime`/`endTime` passed in are the already-clamped values. With the existing path-shift caller (`AuthoringCanvas.Gestures` passes `n.TimeExact, n.EndExact` which are overwritten every frame) the span stays constant, but the contract is fragile — any caller that recomputes the span from data that has already been clamped loses the original note length and the note can shrink. Also, when the span is negative or `durationSeconds` is below the span, `latest` is negative and the result is clamped to zero regardless of 1/3-bar exactness, silently unsnapping. Example: `Snap(FromFraction(-1, 200), 16)` (time = -0.005 bar, grid 1/16 = 0.0625) does not produce the mirrored result of `Snap(FromFraction(1, 200), 16)`. `EditorDocument.Snap` has the same pattern, but it is guarded by the non-negative document invariant; this public helper has no such guard. `BeginTail` semantics are only checked on the single transition call. Two important behaviors are untested: (1) that `UpdateWidth` truly leaves `Width`/`Center` unchanged while in tail stage (the boolean `false` return is asserted, but the frozen geometry is not), and (2) that calling `BeginTail()` a second time does not reset an already-dragged `EndTime` back to `Time`. The Tap path is verified against the draft's *initial* `Width = 1` only. `Commit` derives the committed width from the current `Width`/`Center` (and re-clamps it), so committing without a drag should still return/place that base width — but the returned value and the committed `Center`/`Width` are not asserted here, and the `BaseWidth` is never distinguished from the draft's transient `Width`. `Side = 1` is always `EditorTrack.Left`, so the track branch in `Commit` (`UnitTrack` switch: 1 => Left, 2 => Right, other => Center) is never exercised beyond the default. Since a wrong track assignment would be invisible to this suite, consider parameterizing `NewDraft` with `side`/`anchorCenter` and adding at least a Center (`Side = 0`) placement check to cover the off-track geometry clamping.

These try/catch blocks silently swallow the failure to reject. If `Execute`/`DeleteBpmCommand` does NOT throw, the assertion inside `catch` never runs; the first block just falls through, and the second only catches the case where the deletion *is* rejected (the intended path throws at the end). `TestBpmCollisionIsRejected` is inconsistent with the other rejection tests in this file (which use `ExpectException<T>`). Structurally it is correct here (the `throw` after the `catch` fails the test when no exception is raised), but it diverges from the established helper pattern in the same file. More importantly: after the collision is rejected, nothing verifies that the event at `1/1` (added on line 101) still exists or that no partial half-applied state (e.g., duplicated entries) is present. Add a check on total `Bpms.Count == 2` and that the `1/1` entry is untouched.

If a no-op `MoveNote` pushes an undoable command that leaves content equal, `IsDirty` could still be false in some implementations while the save/undo baseline has shifted. Also, the `$`-interpolated message is fine, but `snap` is a bool rendered as `True`/`False`, so a failure message reads "with snap True" — acceptable, but consider naming cases explicitly for debuggability.

Additionally, multiple successful steps are executed back-to-back before any `Undo`, so the "one step = one undo" invariant claimed in the doc comment is only verified for the TIME branch, not for CENTER/WIDTH. Consider interleaving an undo per property to actually pin that invariant.

`TryResolveFile` is not fully traversal-safe on case-insensitive or symlinked layouts, and the containment check is fragile:
1. `Path.GetRelativePath` compares the two paths string-wise; on a case-insensitive root (Windows/macOS) `GetFullPath` may return a differently-cased prefix, which is fine, but the check `relative.StartsWith(".." + separator)` does not account for a root that is the filesystem root (`rootFull == "/"` or `C:\\`) where relative could be `..`-prefixed siblings — more importantly path canonicalization here is purely lexical.
2. It does not resolve symlinks, so a symlinked directory inside `root` pointing outside will pass the check and the resolved `fullPath` escapes `root`. Callers that read/write the returned path are exposed to arbitrary file access (e.g. a package containing `link -> /etc` then `link/passwd`).
3. `IsSafePackagePath` already rejects `..` segments, so the extra `..` check here is defensive but the real gap is symlink/reparse-point resolution.

Consider resolving the final path (e.g. `FileSystemInfo.LinkTarget`/`ResolveLinkTarget`, or `Directory.GetRealPath`-style canonicalization) and re-validating containment against the real root before returning.

`IsDisplayText` only rejects runes `<= 0x1f` and `0x7f`. It still allows:
- C1 control characters (U+0080–U+009F)
- Bidi override/embedding characters (U+202A–U+202E, U+2066–U+2069) which can spoof displayed text (Trojan Source style)
- Zero-width / invisible format characters (U+200B–U+200F, U+FEFF) and other `Cf`/`Cc`/`Cs` category runes

If display text is rendered in reports/UI or logged, this permits spoofing and log injection. Reject runes with `Rune.GetUnicodeCategory(rune)` in `Control`, `Format`, `Surrogate`, `LineSeparator`, `ParagraphSeparator` (or an explicit allowlist) instead of only checking two code points.

`IsDisplayText` enumerates the string up to three times (`RuneCount`, `First`, `Last`, and the validation loop). For potentially many validation calls this is wasteful. Capture the runes once into a list/array and derive count/first/last/validation from that single pass.

`IsSafePackagePath` relies on `Uri.TryCreate(value, UriKind.Absolute, out _)` to reject URI-like inputs, but that also rejects legitimate relative paths that happen to parse as absolute URIs (e.g. `a:b` style segments are already blocked by the ':' check, so the net effect is usually fine). The more concrete gaps:
- `Path.GetFullPath`/`Path.Combine` behavior differs per platform; on Windows, segments ending with a space or dot are silently trimmed by the filesystem, which can map two distinct package paths onto the same file (collision) and bypass uniqueness checks.
- The `char.IsAsciiLetter(value[0]) && value[1] == ':'` drive-letter check doesn't catch UNC prefixes (`//server/share`) that would already be caught by `StartsWith('/')`, but does not catch `\` variants — those are caught by `Contains('\\')`, so that's covered. However, names like `CON`, `NUL`, `COM1` are not rejected, which can resolve to devices on Windows.

Consider comparing the combined path against reserved Windows device names and trailing dot/space segments.

`DiagnosticBag` exposes the internal mutable list via `Items` (`IReadOnlyList<Diagnostic>` is only a view; a caller can cast back to `List<Diagnostic>` and mutate it), and `Error`/`Warning` mutate `_items` without synchronization while `HasErrors`/`Print` enumerate it. `JsonPointer.Property`/`Index` do not validate their inputs. A null or whitespace `pointer` silently produces a malformed pointer (e.g. leading space or missing `/`), and a null `property` will throw a `NullReferenceException` inside `Escape`. Since these build RFC 6901 pointers used in diagnostics/error messages, add argument validation (`ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrEmpty` etc.) so malformed pointers fail fast near the call site instead of producing misleading diagnostic locations.

The numeric invariant is not sufficient to make the produced components canonical v2 BarTime JSON. `ExactBarTime.FromJsonComponents` (shared/Chart/V2/ExactBarTime.cs) additionally requires `numerator < denominator`, `gcd(numerator, denominator) == 1`, and `numerator == 0 => denominator == 1`. The current only post-normalization check covers `FractionNumerator == 0` (denominator is 1 in the largest-to-smallest reduce case), but the `FractionNumerator == 0 && Denominator != 1` case can only occur if numerator is 0 while denominator > 1 (impossible), so this is fine. However, the validation performed here duplicates the canonical rules partially and is not verifiable from a single location; consider reusing the shared canonical validation (e.g. `ExactBarTime.FromJsonComponents`) inside `TryFromBinary64` so that an accepted value is guaranteed to be writable, instead of relying on ad-hoc numeric bounds checks that can drift from the v2 schema.

comments.content: `LegacyPack` exposes invariants that are not enforced anywhere in this model: `Charts` can be empty and `AudioPath`/`CoverPath` may reference non-existent files. Consumers (`Program.PrintAudit`, `V2Writer.Write`, `LegacyConverter.ConvertPack`) must each re-check these, leading to duplicated validation. The overscan warning assertion does not actually prove what its message claims. The document was built with `AudioOffsetSec = 0` and a single note; only the `MoveNote` command to `Center = 5.1, Width = .6` pushes the note past the [0,5] range (other commands before it were undone). So the test name/message "overscan produces warning without changing v2 data" is misleading, and more importantly the test never asserts the *warning itself* (node type/pointer/severity) nor that `V2SemanticValidator.ValidateChart` still succeeds *because* overscan is legal. As written, the check would pass for any warning, including e.g. an unrelated warning from a different cause. Assert the warning's `Pointer`/`Source` and that no `Error` diagnostics are produced.

After the invalid `EditChartDetailsCommand` throws and the state is restored, the test asserts difficulty/level but not that the history/dirty state is untouched. `EditorDocument.Execute` rethrows before pushing the history entry, so a regression that pushed the entry before validation (or mutated `_historyPosition`) would leave a phantom undo step that this test would not catch. Also worth asserting `Charters.SequenceEqual(["Lead Charter", "Co-Lead Charter"...])` and `Unrated == false` to confirm the full `ChartDetails` snapshot was restored, not just two fields.

This `ExpectException<InvalidOperationException>` guard does not verify the key requirement of "delete last chart": that the rejection happens *before any state mutation*. Because `DeleteChartCommand.Execute` stores `_previousSelectedChartId` before `RemoveChart` throws, a regression that mutated state first (e.g. removed the chart, then threw) would leave `only` in a corrupted state yet still pass this check. Capture `only.Charts.Count`, `only.SelectedChartId` and the history position before the call and assert they are unchanged after the exception.

The resource replacement rollback test never verifies that no stale pending replacement remains after `Undo`. It only checks `PendingResourceReplacements.Count == 0` after undo (line 267) but does not re-check after `Redo` that it contains exactly one entry with the correct source, nor that the staged source path equals the external file. More importantly, there is no assertion that a *second* execute/undo cycle does not double-register the mapping (the dictionary is keyed by relative path, so a leak would silently overwrite). Add an assertion on the mapping's `ExternalSourcePath` after redo and confirm `Count == 1` after a second undo.

The "copy.Notes.Single().Id == \"normal-tap\"" assertion is weakly coupled to intent: `CopyChartCommand` clones the source chart wholesale, so the assertion would pass even if the clone accidentally shared note instances with the source (a shallow-copy bug), because the ID would still be present. The core requirement is that the copy is *independent* of the source, so the test should mutate the copy (e.g. rename the note in `mega`) and assert the source chart's note is unchanged, otherwise "separate chart" is not actually proven.

`CreateCleanDocument` passes `Path.Combine(Path.GetTempPath(), packId)` as the package directory, so the document is treated as *persisted*. These tests later call `MarkSaved(Path.Combine(root, "persisted"))` on a *draft* document, but the "opened document retains clean history semantics" branch relies on the fixture at `Fixtures/golden-pack` (line 130) without asserting `CanUndo` is false/`PackageDirectory` is set. The history-position-based dirty tracking means a document constructed "persisted" via `CreateCleanDocument` starts clean only because history position matches; this assumption should be asserted explicitly in the opened-document branch rather than implicitly relying on the golden fixture's initial state.

Length check accepts 5 arguments, but the branch that validates `--revision` only runs when `args.Length > 4`; a 5-arg invocation (`... --out dir extra`) therefore falls through with revision = 1 and silently ignores the stray extra positional argument instead of reporting a usage error. The `> 6` upper bound also never rejects a 5-arg form. Enforce an exact allowed shape (4 or 6 args) so unexpected extras are errors, not silently dropped.

`HashTree` returns a lazy `IEnumerable<string>` that reads the filesystem during enumeration, and it is enumerated twice in `SequenceEqual`. Both enumerables are lazily produced inside the same comparison, so the two directories are read interleaved — this is only deterministic because they are separate directories. More importantly, `SequenceEqual` on the two lazy sequences short-circuits on the first ordering difference, so `Check(firstHashes.SequenceEqual(secondHashes), ...)` throws on the first mismatch without a useful diff, and subsequent assertions. Materialize both hash lists before comparing (and ideally report the differing entries) so the determinism check is clear and stable.

Cleanup in `finally` can itself throw (e.g. a lingering file handle causes `IOException`/`UnauthorizedAccessException` for recursive delete). When that happens the original self-test failure is masked and the CLI reports a misleading fatal error, leaving the temp directory behind. Wrap the delete in a try/catch (best-effort cleanup) so the real result is preserved.

Using `string.Replace(source, destination, ...)` to build target paths is fragile: any occurrence of the source path substring elsewhere in a file/directory name (or a case variation on Windows) is replaced too, producing wrong destinations. Use `Path.GetRelativePath(source, path)` combined with `Path.Combine(destination, relative)` instead.

Unlike `digest`, `validate-v2` does not reject an empty/whitespace path; `V2Commands.Validate("")` will attempt to open the current directory and produce a confusing error instead of an argument error. Also note `digest` checks `string.IsNullOrEmpty(args[3])` but not `args[1]`; align both commands to validate the directory argument consistently (e.g. `Path.GetFullPath` or a non-empty check) for clearer diagnostics.

`AuditMetrics` is the type that decides whether a conversion is acceptable, but it encodes no invariant and no contract. Key problems:

1. Semantics are undocumented. `BakedSyncCount` vs `DerivableSyncCount` vs `SyncMismatchCount` (is a mismatch the set where baked==true but derivable==false, or a union?) is not stated, so consumers such as `Program.PrintAudit` can only print raw numbers and any future caller will guess.
2. There is no way to ask "is this audit clean?". All counts default to 0 via `init` and C# `default`, so an *unpopulated/default* `AuditMetrics` (e.g. a chart whose audit was never computed) is indistinguishable from a perfectly clean audit — `DerivedTotal == null` is the only hint, and only for that one field. Conversion-success logic can therefore silently accept a chart with no audit data.
3. `BakedTotal` is non-nullable `int` while `DerivedTotal` is `int?`, implying `0` baked notes is meaningful vs `null` derived, but nothing expresses that.

Recommendation: make the audit's provenance explicit (e.g. add a `bool IsComplete`/`bool HasErrors` or a factory/constructor that requires the values), document each counter, and/or expose a derived `bool IsClean => SyncMismatchCount == 0 && ContinuityErrorCount == 0` so callers cannot diverge on what "OK" means.

`Unrated`, nullable `Level` and nullable `DifficultyKey` form three partially-overlapping representations of "this difficulty has no rating":

- `Unrated = true` with `Level = 5`
- `Unrated = false` with `Level = null`
- `DifficultyKey = null` regardless of `Level`

`LegacyConverter` sets `Unrated = entry.Level == 0`, and `V2Writer.ToChartEntry` copies all three fields through verbatim into `V2ChartEntry`, so an inconsistent combination produced here propagates straight into the canonical v2 output without any check. Nothing here (or in the projection) enforces `Unrated => Level is null`.

Recommendation: encode the state as a single representation (e.g. `int? Level` where `null` means unrated) or add a validation/factory that asserts the combinations, so producers and consumers (V2 writer / validator) cannot disagree about what "unrated" means.

Structural invariants of a `ConvertedNote` are entirely unenforced at the data-contract boundary and are only partially checked much later in `V2Writer.ToNote`:

- Only "non-path notes must have zero nodes" is validated, and as a throw at write time. The converse (a Hold/Mixer with zero nodes, nodes out of chronological order, nodes whose `Center`/`Width` fall outside the note span, or a node time earlier than `source.Time`) is never checked.
- Because times are `RationalBarTime` — compared only later after conversion to `ExactBarTime` — a misordered node list will silently produce an invalid path in the emitted v2 chart rather than failing in the converter where diagnostics are still collectable.

Recommendation: validate note/node invariants where the nodes are produced (converter) or in a dedicated validation step before writing, and report them as `DiagnosticBag` entries instead of relying on a single `InvalidOperationException` at projection time.

`required` on strings only guarantees the initializer ran; it does not prevent `Title = ""`, `Id = " "` or (for non-nullable annotation checks that are not enforced at runtime) a null coming from a non-annotated path. These values go straight into `V2Pack` in `V2Writer.ToPack` and are then serialized by `V2JsonEncoder`, so an empty/whitespace `Id`, `Title` or `Audio` will produce a pack that fails v2 validation downstream or, worse, a pack with an empty id that collides with other entries rather than failing at conversion time.

Same concern applies to `ConvertedChartEntry.Id`/`File`/`Charter` and `ConvertedNote.Id`/`Type` (the latter is later matched via a `switch` that throws on unknown values). Suggest validating `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace` for identifiers at construction (factory or `IValidatableObject`-style `Validate()` method) and surfacing the failure as a diagnostic during conversion.

`Bpm`, `Value` (scroll) and note `Center`/`Width` are plain `double`s with no validation. `double.NaN`, `double.PositiveInfinity` and `Bpm <= 0` are all representable and will be written verbatim into the v2 chart by `V2Writer.ToChart`, producing a non-consumable chart (JSON encoders commonly reject NaN/Infinity) or a division-by-zero in any BPM-timeline consumer.

Also note the `Bpms`/`ScrollSpeeds` lists themselves are not guaranteed sorted or non-empty, and multiple BPM events at the same `RationalBarTime` are allowed by the type even though that is ambiguous for downstream timeline computation.

Recommendation: validate at construction (`double.IsFinite`, `Bpm > 0`), and either document or enforce ordering/uniqueness of the time lists.

`Judge`'s three-state `bool?` meaning differs by note type (required for Hold, optional/irrelevant otherwise) but the model does not say so, and the rule lives in `V2Writer.ToNote` (`node.Judge ?? throw ...` for Hold). This makes `ConvertedNode` non-self-describing: a producer cannot tell from this type whether a missing `Judge` is legal.

A chart-level conversion failure is silently dropped: `diagnostics.Error(...)` is recorded in the per-chart bag, but `ConvertPack` still returns a non-null `ConvertedPack` with the failed chart missing from `Charts`. `RunConvert` (Program.cs) only checks `converted is null`, so it happily writes a pack (and `PackageWriter` may even expect `charts.Count == pack.Charts.Count`) while the tool exits 0 / reports success for a semantically failed conversion. `entry.Diff` is used as `ChartId` (and `ConvertedChartEntry.Id`) verbatim. For a custom difficulty, the v2 `difficultyKey` is the NFC-normalized form, but `Id`/`ChartId` keep the raw (possibly non-NFC, e.g. decomposed) string. Two entries whose diffs differ only by normalization form would already be rejected as duplicates by the parser (Ordinal), yet the emitted chartId and difficultyKey can disagree in bytes; downstream `digest --chart <id>` lookups and v2 ID validation then become inconsistent. When a chain walk fails mid-way (cycle, track crossing, wrong node type, non-increasing time, or a silent `break` on a dangling SubNoteId), the partially accumulated `chain` is still fully added to `globallyConsumed` and, if it has >= 2 nodes and the last node has `SubNoteId == -1`, is also returned in `result`. Consequences:
1. The truncated chain can be emitted as a hold/mixer that ends early, even though the source linked further nodes.
2. Nodes belonging to a broken chain get marked consumed, so they no longer trigger the "standalone type 4/7 path node" error and the error/count in `globallyConsumed` masks the real structure.
3. Conversely, an error that occurs before any node beyond the head leaves the head unconsumed while its nodes get flagged as standalone, producing misleading diagnostics.
Track whether the walk completed successfully and only commit the chain to `result`/`globallyConsumed` (or mark all involved notes as errored) when the full chain from head to a node with `SubNoteId == -1` was validated.

Dangling `SubNoteId` is skipped silently here. Although the earlier pass already reported "dangling SubNoteId", this `break` leaves a partial chain that may be emitted as a shortened hold/mixer (see the global-consumed finding). Either fail the chain explicitly so it is not emitted, or document that the chain is truncated and skip it from `result`.

comments.content: Duplicate scroll events at the same BarTime are silently collapsed with "last wins" (`byTime[item.BarTime] = item`). Unlike BPM sections (which must be strictly increasing) there is no diagnostic for conflicting scroll values/events at the same time, so genuinely ambiguous legacy data (e.g. 1.0 then 2.0 at bar 3) is converted without any warning while the discarded event is lost. Emit a diagnostic (or an audit counter) when a duplicate BarTime is encountered.

Absolute 1e-9 tolerance on `Seconds` is scale-dependent: for large timestamps (minutes/hours into a chart) accumulated binary64 rounding already exceeds 1e-9, so valid legacy charts will be rejected as continuity errors, while for very early times it may accept meaningful drift. Prefer a relative/ULP-based tolerance (e.g. `max(1e-9, |expected| * 1e-12)`) or compare with `Math.BitIncrement`-based ULP distance.

Grouping by `note.BarTime` uses `RationalBarTime.Equals`/`GetHashCode`, which compare stored numerator/denominator exactly (not reduced equality), so `1/2` and `2/4` would hash differently even though `CompareTo` considers them equal, and the equality meaning depends on the object implementation rather than the rational value. If exact times are meant, group with a comparer based on `CompareTo` (e.g. build the lookup with `RationalBarTimeComparer`) and document that sync derivation requires bit-exact input times; otherwise state the intended semantics explicitly.

The bare `catch` swallows every exception, so integration regressions in `JudgePlan`/`BarSection` construction can no longer be distinguished from legitimately underivable data: `DerivedTotal` becomes null and the audit output silently says "unavailable" while the conversion still proceeds. At minimum catch only expected exception types, and report the swallowed exception as a diagnostic/audit field (with the message) so the failure is visible.

`ValidateCrossChartMetadata` only inspects `entries`, i.e. charts that were successfully converted. If two different custom diffs collide after NFC folding (e.g. via different Unicode case forms) but one of them failed conversion, no error is produced here and the pack then contains only one of them — the incoming chart silently disappears without a pack-level error. Consider validating against `pack.Charts` diffs (or ensure per-chart failures already fail the pack).

Only `Encoding.UTF8.Preamble` (the UTF-8 form, EF BB BF) is stripped. A file encoded as UTF-16/UTF-32 (with or without BOM) produces a byte stream that is not a valid JSON document, but the resulting diagnostic (`invalid UTF-8` / `invalid JSON`) does not tell the user the real cause. Worse, a UTF-16LE file starting with FF FE is treated as `invalid UTF-8` while a UTF-16 file without BOM may contain NUL bytes and be reported as JSON syntax error. Consider explicitly detecting UTF-16/UTF-32 BOMs (and rejecting them with a clear message) before the UTF-8 decode. Also note (informational) that the standalone `File.ReadAllBytes`-then-decode passes here mean the whole document is decoded up to three times (UTF-8 validation, Utf8JsonReader scan, JsonDocument.Parse) — fine for small files, but worth a comment if pack sizes are unbounded.

comments.content: Stripping the BOM before the duplicate scan/parse is correct for JSON semantics, but it shifts all `BytePositionInLine` values reported by `Describe(ex)` and by `JsonException` inside `FindDuplicateKeys` by 3 bytes for BOM files. That is minor, but if byte positions are used for editor navigation they will point into the stripped prefix. Consider noting this in `Describe` or keeping the offsets relative to the original file.

`new UTF8Encoding(false, true).GetString(bytes)` allocates the full decoded string solely to validate it, throwing away the result. On large inputs this doubles memory and is unnecessary: use `Encoding.UTF8.GetCharCount(bytes, throwOnInvalidBytes: true)` (or a stack-allocated/streamed decoder) to validate without materializing a string. Note also that `File.ReadAllBytes` has no size limit, so a huge file can cause an OOM before any diagnostic is produced.

If a file is both invalid JSON and too deep (>256 nesting), `FindDuplicateKeys` throws and the whole file is reported only once — fine. However, `JsonException` is not the only thing `Utf8JsonReader`/`GetString` can throw here: a payload whose strings are large enough triggers `InvalidOperationException`/`ArgumentException` from `GetString` when the escape buffer limit is exceeded, and `Stack<ScanFrame>` growth can throw `OutOfMemoryException`. An unhandled `InvalidOperationException` here would crash the tool instead of yielding a diagnostic. Consider widening this catch to handle `InvalidOperationException` as `invalid JSON` as well.

The duplicate scan (`FindDuplicateKeys`) and the real parse are two independent passes with duplicated options (MaxDepth 256, no comments, no trailing commas). Any future change to one option set silently desyncs the two passes (e.g. a document accepted by the scanner but rejected by the parser or vice versa). Extract a single `static JsonReaderOptions`/options factory, or better, perform duplicate detection while parsing (the parser could be driven with `Utf8JsonReader` + `JsonDocument.ParseValue`) so there is only one pass.

`FindDuplicateKeys` collects duplicates and keeps scanning after an error, but `CompleteValue`/`ValuePointer` bookkeeping relies on the token stream being well-formed. If the reader throws mid-document (e.g. depth exceeded) the partially built `duplicates` list is discarded (the catch returns null) — correct — but nothing caps the number of duplicates, so a malicious document with millions of duplicate keys accumulates a huge list plus a `HashSet<string>` per object before failing. Since a single duplicate is already fatal, stop scanning on the first duplicate (or cap the list) to bound memory.

comments.content: `diagnostics.HasErrors` is checked on the *shared* bag. If the caller had already recorded an unrelated error before calling `Load` (plausible when validating a pack: several files share one bag), this file is silently rejected even though its own content is valid, and no diagnostic is attributed to it. This makes the loader dependent on ambient state. Track whether `ValidateStrings` added errors locally (e.g. count `diagnostics.Items.Count` before/after or return a bool from the walk) instead of consulting the global flag.

`ValidateStrings` is recursive and, for an object, validates each property name twice as a string-derived value path — actually once for the name and once for the value, which is intentional, but the recursion depth is bounded only by `MaxDepth=256`, so deep nesting is safe. The real issue is that this is a full-tree second traversal creating a new `JsonPointer.Property(...)` string for every node (two per property), which is a lot of transient allocations for large chart files. Since property names were already validated by the reader through `GetString` in the duplicate scan, consider validating names there (one pass) and skipping this full second walk, or at least only allocating the pointer when an error is actually found.

Unpaired UTF-16 surrogates cannot occur in a string produced by parsing valid UTF-8 JSON (the decoder already rejected invalid sequences), so this check is effectively dead for strings; keeping it is harmless but the one place it can matter — lone `\uD800`-style JSON escapes — is actually the case `System.Text.Json` accepts and produces an unpaired `char`. Good that it is checked. However, the diagnostic only reports the first offending string and then still walks the rest of the tree; on a huge document with thousands of bad strings, the number of reported errors is unbounded. Consider stopping after N errors to keep diagnostics readable.

`TryGet` and the `Optional*` helpers throw `InvalidOperationException`/`KeyNotFoundException` when `_element` is not an object (e.g. `TryGetProperty` on a null/array/string element throws `InvalidOperationException`: "The requested operation requires an element of type 'Object'..."). All other accessors validate `ValueKind`, but `TryGet` does not, and `Required*`/`Optional*` assume the caller already invoked `EnsureObject`. If `EnsureObject()` returns false, callers in `LegacyParser` correctly bail, but any future caller (or a call like `OptionalInt32` on an array element) will crash with an exception instead of emitting a diagnostic. Add a non-object guard in `TryGet` (return `false`) and/or document that all accessors require `EnsureObject()` to have been called.

comments.content: This method walks the whole tree, but `Resolve`/`Open` only enforce it as a snapshot before use. The real security-relevant walk is unbounded on an untrusted directory (a package could contain thousands of nested dirs, or a deep tree causing very long paths / `PathTooLongException`). More importantly, the entry `EnsureNotReparse(entry, ...)` is redundant with `Resolve`'s per-segment checks and adds a full-tree scan on every `Open` call (also done twice: once here and once per path in `Resolve`). Consider limiting recursion depth (packages have a small, bounded directory shape) so a malicious package cannot make the tool hang, and mention the TOCTOU point below.

There is a TOCTOU gap: `Resolve` checks for symlinks/reparse points and existence, then callers later open the file by path (`File.ReadAllBytes`, `File.OpenRead`). Between the check and the open, an attacker who controls the package directory can replace the regular file with a symlink to an out-of-package file and cause the tool to read arbitrary local files (e.g. hashing `/etc/shadow` into the printed digest). To close this on the platforms that support it, open with `FileOptions` that follow no links (or re-validate the opened handle via `File.GetAttributes`/`GetFinalPathName` after open and compare it against the resolved path before reading).

`chunkEnd = chunkStart + size` and `chunkEnd + (size & 1)` are computed in `long` from `uint` inputs — `chunkStart` can never exceed `stream.Length` and `size <= uint.MaxValue`, so on a 64-bit process there is no overflow here (this is fine), but the seek `stream.Position = chunkEnd + (size & 1)` can move past `stream.Length` when `size` is the last odd-sized chunk at exactly EOF: `chunkEnd == stream.Length` and `chunkEnd + 1 > Length`. Setting `Position` beyond the end is legal for a FileStream, so the loop exits — OK. However `WaveDuration.Read` is only reached for `.wav` paths, yet `ProbeAudioDuration` resolves the file and probes only on `.wav`; a RIFF/WAVE file with a non-`.wav` extension is silently accepted with duration `null`. If RIFF magic is the real criterion, probe by sniffing the header rather than the extension, otherwise a validly-named `song.WAVE`, `song.wav ` (trailing space) etc. skips duration validation and produces a misleading warning.

comments.content: `_durationCache`/`_warnings` are plain mutable collections with no locking; the class is `sealed` but exposes mutable instance methods and is not documented as single-threaded. If a caller parallelizes `Validate()` (the hook `AudioDurationSeconds` may be invoked concurrently by future validators, or the context is reused across threads), e.g. `_warnings.Add` from two threads, the `HashSet` can corrupt or throw. At minimum, document that `V2PackageContext` is not thread-safe (or make it so with `ConcurrentDictionary`/lock) so future callers do not assume otherwise. Also the cache is keyed by the raw package path string; two different path spellings that resolve to the same file (e.g. differently-cased paths on Windows) will each probe separately and, more subtly, `null` results for non-WAV files are cached by raw path while the warning text uses that same raw path — make sure `Resolve` spelling differences do not produce duplicate/contradictory warnings.

The two catch blocks (and the corresponding pairs in `Digest`) are identical in shape and duplicated across both commands. Extracting a small helper (e.g. `TryRun(Func<int> body, string directory)`) that maps known diagnostic exceptions to exit codes would remove the duplication and make the missing catch-all easier to add in one place.

Collision detection groups with StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase, but the files are actually written on a case-sensitive comparison basis by the OS? On Linux, `"Audio.ogg"` and `"audio.ogg"` are two distinct files, so this rejects valid (or at least non-colliding) packages on case-sensitive filesystems. Conversely on Windows it correctly rejects. Either make the comparer match the platform (`OperatingSystem.IsWindows() ? StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase : StringComparer.Ordinal`) and phrase the error accordingly, or always use Ordinal and rely on the OS failing the copy — but the current behavior is inconsistent with the actual filesystem semantics and can produce spurious "output package path collision" errors.

comments.content: The exists-check at line ~154 and `Directory.Move(staging, output)` here are a classic TOCTOU: if `output` appears between the check and the move (another process/user creating it), `Directory.Move` throws and the partially-built package (or the pre-existing directory) state is confusing. On POSIX, `Move` onto an existing directory fails with IOException — acceptable — but there is also a partial-move hazard: if the move fails midway (e.g. cross-device rename fallback that copies then deletes), or if the move succeeds but the caller later fails, the caller cannot tell whether `output` is complete. Consider using `Directory.Move` only after verifying the target still does not exist, and on failure check `Directory.Exists(output)` to distinguish "pre-existing target" from "corrupt partial output" in the diagnostic. At minimum, the diagnostic message should say whether the target already existed.

Cleanup is not exception-safe: `Directory.Delete(staging, recursive: true)` runs inside the catch block and can itself throw (locked file, permission error, race with another process), which would propagate out of `Write` and mask the original error while also losing the `return false` contract. Additionally, a partial `Directory.Move` (cross-volume copy fallback partially completed) can leave a partial `output` directory behind that is never cleaned, so the next run's "output already exists" check permanently blocks retries. Wrap the delete in its own try/catch and also clean up a partially created `output` when the move was the failure point.

More importantly, the failure is written to `stdout` (line 48 prints to `Console.WriteLine`) while `Program.Main` reserves `stderr` (line 91, line 28) for hard errors — CI logs that only preserve `stderr` will drop individual assertion failures and only show a final aggregate count. The traversal is unbounded and relies on an `AGENTS.md` sentinel. In a shallow CI checkout or when running from a published output directory outside the repo, this loops up to the filesystem root and then throws a `DirectoryNotFoundException`; `Program.Main` catches it and returns exit code 1, which looks like a test failure rather than an infrastructure/setup error. Also, if any parent directory (e.g., `$HOME`) happens to contain an unrelated `AGENTS.md`, the method will silently return the wrong root. Consider: (a) an opt-in environment variable override (e.g., `CORE_TEST_REPO_ROOT`) or an explicit argument that `Program.ParseArguments` validates, (b) bounding the traversal depth, and (c) throwing a diagnostic that names the searched `BaseDirectory` and expected marker so CI failures are self-explanatory.

comments.content: The 49/50 magic loop counts encode the depletion boundary but do not verify the actual value before the final miss. A broken implementation that, say, drops 2.5 per Miss would still fail the 49 case only by luck of ordering, and a wrong-but-close implementation could produce e.g. 2.0 health at step 49 and still be accepted. Assert the intermediate health (`100.0 - 49 * 2.0`) so the boundary is verified numerically, not only by final depletion.

Hardcore boundary checks only the depleting step (25 misses); there is no assertion that 24 hardcore misses do NOT deplete (health should be 4.0). Without the non-depleting side the test cannot distinguish a -4 rule from a rule that depletes one miss earlier. Add the 24-miss case for symmetry with the Standard rule's 49-miss case.

This does not assert that health stays at 0 after the Perfect — the only assertion is performed after the subsequent Miss, so an implementation that heals from 0 on Perfect (e.g. 0.2) and then drops back would still pass, because -2 clamps to 0 anyway. The key data-integrity rule ("a heal cannot revive depleted health") is never checked. Assert the state immediately after the perfect heal, and add the hardcore equivalent (Perfect +0.1) to cover the second rule.

The Hardcore heal path is under-covered: Great/Good returning 0.0 is only validated by the DeltaOf table, never end-to-end on the health state, and there is no hardcore case showing that a Perfect heal cannot escape depletion. Add health-level assertions for hardcore Great/Good being no-ops and for hardcore heal-after-depletion.

The clamp boundary is only tested from above (delta = 30 �� clamped) and via invalid values (NaN, -5). Note the `Observe(10.0, true, double.NaN)` call also anchors `AudioEnded` on the first call, so subsequent observations are post-audio — fine — but three cases are left unpinned and would let regressions through:
1. `delta == 0` (paused frame) must not advance `_postAudioSeconds` nor unlatch anything.
2. `delta` exactly equal to `MaxStepSeconds` must be added once, un-clamped, and `delta` slightly above it must add exactly `MaxStepSeconds`.
3. A finite negative delta (`-5.0`) is currently mixed in with NaN, so the `delta > 0` guard is verified only for `-1e9`-style implicit cases; asserting `EffectiveSeconds` is *unchanged* (not merely that `ShouldFinish` is false) would catch a `+= delta` regression. Since this is the only test targeted at `MaxStepSeconds`, adding an `EffectiveSeconds` equality check after all three calls is cheap and much stronger.

Monotonicity is only checked *after* `ShouldFinish` becomes true, where `Observe` short-circuits at the top (`if (ShouldFinish) return;`). That early return means the test never exercises the actual latch logic on a finished condition — it would pass even if the early return were removed and `ChartEndReached`/`AudioEnded` could be reset, as long as `ShouldFinish` happens to recompute the same. To really pin the contract, assert the individual latches (`end.AudioEnded`, `end.ChartEndReached`) are still true after the regressing sample, and also cover the window *before* completion, e.g. observe a lower `songTime`/`audioEnded == false` between the two latches and assert neither latch regresses (the production code only ever `Math.Max`es `_observedSeconds` and never clears `AudioEnded`, so this is the behavior worth locking in).

Two contracts are not pinned at all:
1. The constructor throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for non-finite `chartEndTime` — no test asserts this, so a relaxed validation would go unnoticed. A small `ConstructorRejectsNonFiniteChartEnd(check)` with NaN/±Infinity is one line each.
2. The `audioEndObservable: false` path is only tested with `audioEnded == false`. The `UntrackableAudioUsesChartPath` scenario never passes `audioEnded: true`, so the guard `_audioEndObservable && audioEnded` is unverified — an implementation change that latched `AudioEnded` regardless of `_audioEndObservable` would still pass every test. Add an `end.Observe(39.9, true, Frame)` in that scenario and assert `!end.AudioEnded` to lock in that the fallback clock never fabricates an audio latch.

The `frames` bound is a bare range with no diagnostic. If the assertion fails, the failure message only says it didn't finish in 100..130 frames — it doesn't report the actual count, so triage requires re-running under a debugger. Since `check` only takes a message string, fold the value in:

```csharp
check(end.ShouldFinish && frames is >= 100 and <= 130,
    $"collapsed clock waits the remaining 2s of real time before finishing (frames={frames})");
```

The same applies to the loop-cap pattern: `while (!end.ShouldFinish && frames < 600)` means a regression that never finishes exits the loop harmlessly and reports the count above, which is acceptable — but the count is currently swallowed.

`TryUpdate`'s return value is ignored, and then `Get(identity)!` is dereferenced unconditionally. `TryUpdate` returns `false` (and stores nothing) when `identity.IsValid` is false or an equal-or-better score already exists; in that case `Get` returns `null` and the null-forgiving `!` turns the failure into a `NullReferenceException`, which aborts the entire core-test run (Program.cs catches it and returns 1 with only a generic "Core test error" message) instead of producing a readable assertion failure. Assert the update succeeded before mutating the returned record.

`GetLegacy(...)!` is dereferenced with the null-forgiving operator before any check. If the fixture key/JSON shape ever stops matching what `LoadJson`/`DecodeLegacy` expects (e.g. renamed property, empty fixture, decoding change), this throws `NullReferenceException` and aborts the whole test binary rather than reporting a failed assertion for this test case. Capture the record, assert non-null, then assert the fields.

`reloaded.Get(identity)?.Grade == "Y"` is `false` when `Get` returns `null` (null-conditional yields `null`, and `null == "Y"` is false), so a missing record silently reports as "wrong grade" instead of being distinguished from a real regrade bug — a null record would make this message misleading. Assert existence separately so failures are diagnosable.

comments.content: The stability assertion compares raw JSON strings, which couples the test to `SaveJson`'s formatting/ordering rather than the semantic invariant. It also re-saves `reloaded` a second time inside the assertion, so a nondeterministic save would be masked or, conversely, a purely cosmetic serialization change would fail the test. Compare the saved JSON of the *same* instance once and assert semantic equality (grades/fields) instead of string identity.

Error-path coverage gaps relative to the thresholds exercised: there are no assertions for negative accuracy or for `double.NegativeInfinity` (the `_ => "D"` fallback should clamp them to D), and no negative case verifying that values just below a boundary on the other side (e.g. 59.999999, 79.999999, 89.999999, 94.999999, 96.999999, 98.999998) stay in the lower grade. Without these, an accidental `>` vs `>=` or a missing clamp could slip through. Also add a case for `GradeAssetKey("Ψ")`/unknown input returning `"D"`, and the null/missing `GetLegacy` path.

`expected[note.Id]` is a bare indexer inside the loop over `chart.AllNotes`. If the fixture or loader ever yields a note id that is not in this dictionary (a new note added to the fixture, a duplicate/unexpected id, or `chart` being a different chart than the fixture), this throws `KeyNotFoundException` and the whole test method aborts with an unhandled exception. `Check` records failures instead of throwing, so one missing id destroys all remaining assertions and the report loses the real diagnostic. Guard the lookup or iterate the expected entries.

Inconsistent double comparison policy: elsewhere this file uses `Math.Abs(x - y) < 1e-12`, but BPM `Sections[i].Seconds`/`BarTime` and the `BpmAtBarTime`/`BpmAtSeconds` boundary checks are compared with exact `==`. `Seconds` is a derived value (accumulated from BPM segments), so it is not guaranteed to be an exact binary64 literal; any loader change makes these tests fail spuriously or hide tiny drift. Use the same tolerance used elsewhere and assert just-past-the-boundary lookups so an off-by-epsilon regression reads clearly.

Any single malformed chart under `--dev-testdata` aborts the whole recursive scan: `LoadFile`/`JudgePlan.Build` throw and nothing is caught, so the remaining files are never validated and the earlier `Check` failures are not visible either. Since this mode is meant to sweep a directory of real packs, collect per-file results and continue on failure so one bad pack does not mask regressions in all the others. Also note the mismatch with the dev-testdata intent: `engine.Apply(...)` is fed `unit.AffectsJudgeCounts`, and the very next assertions require every unit to be a headline unit — for stacks containing `AffectsJudgeCounts == false` units (Auto-style) the `NormalizedScore == 1_000_000` check would still pass while the first check fails, making the failure message misleading.

The switch handles `Input`, `Auto/HoldPoint/Contact/HoldEnd` and `Mine` but has no `default`. Because `UnitKind` is a plain enum and `JudgePlan` is the only producer today, a newly added kind would silently produce a unit that is never applied, and the only symptom is the later `CountPerfect == 15` / score assertion failing — with no indication which unit was skipped. Add a `default: Check(false, $"unhandled unit kind {u.Kind} for note {u.NoteId}")` so the gap is reported directly.

`Health` is full at start (`Health = MaxHealth` in the engine ctor) and each Perfect in the sweep either heals/clamps at `MaxHealth`, so this assertion can pass even if `Apply`/`HealthDelta` were completely broken (e.g. no health deltas applied at all). It adds no regression protection for the Happy path, and the suite never exercises a non-Perfect grade or a Mine hit (which is the only path here with a real negative health delta, see `HealthDelta` for `ScoreCategory.Mine`). Consider adding a negative case (e.g. one Miss or a touched Mine) to make the health/scoring paths actually meaningful.
